items.title: Phase response approach to networked neural activity models with delays
items.abstract: Networks of delay-coupled neural mass models alternate between synchrony and anti-phase locking as the delay between brain regions increases. The origin of these delay-dependent bands has remained unclear. Here, we show that a single function, the phase interaction function $H$ of an isolated node, predicts where the bands occur and explains why they repeat. For a Wilson--Cowan model with intra-nodal delay $τ$ and inter-nodal delay $ρ$, we compute the limit cycle and phase response, and hence $H$, by harmonic balance. Each band boundary is a zero of $H'$ shifted by the phase lag $Ωρ$, so the bands repeat in $ρ$ with the oscillation period. Simulations of the full delay-differential networks confirm these predictions, from two nodes, where predicted frequencies agree to second order in the coupling strength, to rings, where the theory also identifies coexisting stable twisted states that random initial conditions rarely reach. At weak coupling, the delays at which synchrony gains or loses stability are set by the node dynamics alone, whereas stable anti-phase states require a bipartite network. For a macaque connectome, metastability peaks at the edges of the synchrony bands, where the stability margin of phase-locking vanishes. The reduction is accurate for coupling strengths well below the slowest Floquet exponent of the node, beyond which a phase--amplitude description is needed. More broadly, vanishing phase-locking stability provides a simple route to metastability in delay-coupled oscillator networks and a candidate mechanism for the flexible coordination of brain dynamics.

items.title: Comparing Measurements of Pictorial Depth: Conditions for Placing Methods, Observers and Depiction Styles on One Scale
items.abstract: Two observers can agree about what lies in front in a picture yet report different amounts of apparent depth. People report pictorial depth by judging which of two points looks nearer, setting a probe to match a surface, adjusting relative sizes, or rating three-dimensionality. Two such methods can agree closely without sharing a unit. We ask when different methods, observers, depiction styles and viewing conditions can share one scale. Each set of scores, a measurement block, is a graph node. Two blocks are linked only if their shared observations pass six checks fixed in advance, among them outcome type, removal of declared offsets and position effects, proportionality and covariance. If the adjusted shared patterns are exactly proportional, a connected graph fixes every block's gain, its relative scale factor. The checks accept proportionality only within a set margin, so a link supports the gains without proving exact proportionality. One unit is still not one depth coordinate. Suppose each block scores shared stimuli with its own origin and positive unit. A matrix-rank test then decides when a common coordinate is identified: when only one overall origin and unit remain free. If each shared stimulus, an anchor, is scored by exactly two blocks, this needs two disjoint sets of anchors, each connecting every block, their compatibility assumed, not tested. They also suffice, except for anchor values satisfying exact polynomial relations (probability zero for anchor values drawn from any distribution with a density). We adapt network gain estimation from test linking, with a loop-consistency check. A reanalysis of published probe settings on 3-D renderings passes one of 171 candidate depiction-style links through all six checks, each judged by its own 95% bound, unadjusted for the 171 pairs. Links between tasks remain untested; they need shared stimuli and a joint uncertainty model.

items.title: Retrieval-Augmented Parkinson's Disease Classification from Resting-State Functional Connectivity
items.abstract: Altered resting-state functional connectivity (FC) is a candidate marker for the diagnosis of Parkinson's disease (PD). Publicly available PD datasets, however, are small and fragmented across sites, scanners and clinical criteria. Transfer learning mitigates data scarcity by reusing a model trained on larger cohorts, but represents their knowledge primarily through a single set of weights shared by all individuals. Motivated by precision neuroimaging, we propose a retrieval-augmented classification (RAC) framework that additionally places each target individual in the context of similar individuals from external cohorts. A graph convolutional autoencoder (GAE), trained on external PD and control cohorts, encodes these cohorts into a neuro-knowledge base. Each target individual is encoded using the pretrained GAE, and its nearest neighbors are retrieved from the external knowledge base. Their embeddings are combined with the target embedding using mean aggregation or attention for classification. A systematic comparison on the TaoWu cohort separated the contributions of encoder pretraining, retrieval, attention and partial fine-tuning. Pretraining improved mean classification accuracy from 60.5% to 66.0%. However, retrieval and attention did not consistently improve performance over the pretrained-only variants. Several retrieval-based configurations nevertheless showed modestly higher ROC-AUC than the randomly initialized baseline. Varying the number of retrieved neighbors and partially fine-tuning the encoder provided no consistent additional gains. Retrieval-neighborhood analysis further showed diagnostically mixed neighborhoods. These findings provide initial evidence that population-learned representations can be complemented by individual-specific retrieval in neuroimaging, although larger datasets are needed to determine when such contextual information improves classification.

items.title: Spectroscopic Survey of Small Solar System Bodies with Ariel
items.abstract: The small Solar System bodies (SSSBs) preserve records of the formation and evolution of the Solar System. In particular, the near-infrared wavelength region around 3 $μ$m provides crucial insights into the origin and transport of hydrated materials and organics, although it is difficult to observe from the ground because of strong telluric absorption. We assess the observability of SSSBs as complementary science to the ESA Ariel space mission, operating in the visible to mid-infrared wavelength range (0.5--7.8 $μ$m). Using the NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris system, we evaluate the visibility of known SSSBs from 2032 to 2035. Our analysis shows that Ariel can spectroscopically characterize up to 402 unique SSSBs under a conservative limiting visual magnitude of $V=13.6$. If observations can be extended to somewhat fainter targets ($V=16$), the number of observable SSSBs could increase to 2144. Assuming operational scenarios in which one SSSB is observed every 3, 7, or 30 days over a four-year mission, the total numbers of observable targets would be 357, 209, and 49, respectively. We further model the spectral energy distributions of candidate targets to evaluate their observational performance. We demonstrate that Ariel can resolve critical absorption features, such as those at 2.7 $μ$m and 3.4 $μ$m, with a higher spectral resolution than the previous infrared survey with AKARI. Observations of SSSBs with Ariel can provide insights into the distribution and evolution of life-forming materials in the Solar System and constitute a scientifically compelling component of Ariel's complementary science program.

items.title: Post-DART impact ejecta re-accumulation on Dimorphos and implications for Hera gravity measurements
items.abstract: Context. The DART impact might have substantially modified the surface and near-surface structure of Dimorphos, affecting the morphology and gravity field that is to be measured by ESA's Hera mission. Aims. We investigate the post-impact redistribution of ejecta and its dependence on the assumed internal structure of Dimorphos. Methods. We performed high-resolution SPH simulations of the DART impact into two low-cohesion rubble-pile models, with and without a large central boulder. We followed the processes of ejecta re-accumulation and gravity evolution for six hours. Results. The impact ejects about 13% of Dimorphos's mass, most of which is re-accreted, producing near-global resurfacing. The ejecta blanket exceeds 8 m around the impact depression but is only a few tens of centimetres thick near the antipode, with similar large-scale deposition in both interior models. Local gravity changes reach about 10% of the pre-impact value. The central boulder affects the surface gravity only within the impact depression, where the removal of overlying material enhances its gravitational contribution. Conclusions. Hera will observe a surface and gravity field substantially modified by DART, which must be considered when interpreting measurements in terms of the internal structure of Dimorphos.

items.title: Information-thermodynamic principles unveil the response of complex networks to perturbations
items.abstract: Understanding how complex networks respond to perturbations is key to uncovering their functional organization. We show that, for a maximum-entropy perturbation prior, standard diffusion cannot increase response entropy, a measure of the diversity of the system's response. To overcome this limitation, we develop a density-matrix-based information thermodynamics of perturbation responses along arbitrary dynamical trajectories. We show that this framework is grounded in an information-theoretic principle of least dissipation and introduces a generalized free energy that quantifies deviations from an instantaneous diffusive reference. We then illustrate the formalism using nonlinear complex networks, revealing regimes of enhanced response diversity that cannot be captured by standard diffusive descriptions.

items.title: Distilling neural networks into equations to predict planetary instability
items.abstract: The problem of predicting when a multi-planet system will become dynamically unstable has defied analytical progress over the past three hundred years. Recent machine learning advances achieve high predictive performance of instability dynamics, but as black-box systems cannot be interpreted to connect to existing scientific understanding. Here we show analytic equations that predict when a multi-planet system will undergo instability. We discover these equations by first training a neural network on a dataset of N-body simulations, and then distilling its latent knowledge into closed-form algebraic expressions. Our two-stage pipeline first learns an interpretable variable basis, then searches for equations using symbolic regression. The resulting equations outperform existing analytic estimates of instability and apply across wide ranges of mass ratios, spacing, and orbital eccentricities. They capture structure in the prediction landscape with a small number of variables amenable to dynamical interpretation. These results demonstrate how symbolic learning can be combined with neural networks to extract scientific insight from complex dynamical systems.

items.title: A Warped Dust Ring in the CQ Tau Disk
items.abstract: The diversity of planetary orbital architectures calls for observational constraints on radial variations in disk-plane orientation, or warps, yet such variations in dust disks remain poorly characterized. CQ Tau is a promising target because its misaligned inner disk and candidate gas warp suggest a radially extended warp. We present the ALMA 1.3 mm dust continuum image reconstructed from the real part of the visibilities, extracting the centro-symmetric disk structure. At an effective spatial resolution of $0.052'' \times 0.042''$ ($7.8 \times 6.3$ au), the image reveals a bright main ring at radii of $\sim20$--$70$ au and an unresolved compact emission component tracing the inner disk around the central star. Ellipse fits centered on the stellar position to contours tracing the inner and outer edges of the ring reveal radial variations in position angles and inclinations. At the inner edge ($\sim21$--$26$ au), the position angle and inclination span $214^\circ$--$233^\circ$ and $23^\circ$--$39^\circ$, respectively, while they span $231^\circ$--$235^\circ$ and $33^\circ$--$36^\circ$ at the outer edge ($\sim58$--$67$ au). Whereas a coplanar ring toy model fails to reproduce such variations, a warped ring model with the local tilt decreasing from $\sim4^\circ$ at $r = 20$ au to $\sim1^\circ$ at 60 au reproduces them. The high-pass-filtered real-part image reveals a pair of opposed curved negative residuals. Similar features appear only in the warped ring model, further supporting the dust warp. These results establish CQ Tau as an example of a warped dust disk and an important laboratory for investigating the connection between three-dimensional disk geometry and planet formation.

items.title: Formation of international environmental agreements and payoff allocation
items.abstract: Dealing with climate change requires that all countries engage in costly efforts to reduce their emissions. Reaching this objective has so far been elusive because it is in the best interest of each country to let the others do the effort and benefit itself from a better environment. The presence of negative externalities and strategic behavior have made game theory a natural paradigm to design an international environmental agreement (IEA) that codifies what countries should do. Considering that countries are sovereign and no supranational entity can impose an agreement, a stream of literature adopted a noncooperative mode of play to the formation of an environmental coalition. On the other hand, as joint optimization of all countries' payoff leads to the best outcome, cooperative games approach has also been proposed to share the cost of climate change. Both approaches have their pros and cons.

items.title: Mesoscale Modelling of Titan's Shangri-La region: the impact of surface properties on winds
items.abstract: The knowledge of Titan's near-surface atmosphere is sparse. The Huygens descent probe measured winds, and the multiple dune field observations and possible dust storms suggest active near-surface dynamics. The Dragonfly rotorcraft lander will fly close to the surface in the Shangri-La region, near the Huygens landing site, where complex dune orientations were observed. This study presents the first mesoscale modelling of the near-surface dynamics in this region. However, due to a lack of high-resolution topography data, synthetic maps of surface properties were built. The surface was divided into different topographical units, such as plains, mountains, etc. The slopes and height of those units were then parametrised. Maps of thermal inertia, albedo and the aerodynamic roughness height were also built. The mesoscale model is coupled to a comprehensive radiative transfer code and forced by a global climate model. No moist processes are considered in this study. Topography has a major impact on near-surface wind amplitude and direction through slope flows and valley circulations. The majority of the winds are below 0.25 m/s. These winds induce a sensible heat flux comparable to the surface solar flux. Spatially varying thermal inertia has the biggest impact on the wind and surface temperature, with high values leading to smaller diurnal amplitude. The seasonal variability is taken into account, with stronger winds in northern summer. Predicted mesoscale near-surface winds are capable of lifting dust over dune fields, with different orientations during the year, and can therefore potentially play a role in sediment transport on Titan.

items.title: Multiplex relational event models of self-reported and perceived gossip
items.abstract: Gossiping is a complex social phenomenon that unfolds through multiple types of relations. Among other things, individuals may initiate gossiping about others as a result of believing themselves to be the target of gossip. These two processes, i.e., gossiping and gossip perception, form a dynamic multiplex network, where self-reported and perceived gossip ties coexist and can influence each other over time. We develop a multiplex relational event model to study the joint evolution of these two processes. The proposed model includes endogeneous covariates that capture the influence of events occurring within one layer, as well as events occurring on the other layer, on the rate of self-reported and perceived gossiping. We analyze survey data collected annually from 44 secondary schools in Hungary. We show how a multiplex relational event model, including linear, smooth and random effects, is able to describe the social mechanisms operating within and between self-reported and perceived gossiping and to capture how these two layers influence each other over time.

items.title: UV-driven organic precursor formation and dust evolution outside the snow line
items.abstract: In the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, dust grains are often mantled with a layer of ice containing simple molecules. The irradiation of the disk by far-ultraviolet (FUV) photons breaks such molecules, producing photoproducts (radicals, ions, and intermediary molecules) in the ice layer that can act as precursors to complex organics. As grains drift towards the warmer, inner region of the disk, their consequent sublimation of ices causes organic synthesis on their surfaces, potentially enhancing grain sticking and dust growth. In addition to interstellar medium radiation, FUV emission from the central star and nearby massive stars can contribute to photoproduct formation. We perform a vertical dust size evolution simulation including grain growth and fragmentation, and calculate photoproduct formation under irradiation from these three sources, treating the central star's FUV continuum and Lyman-$α$ emission separately. We find that enhanced UV irradiation, particularly from stellar Lyman-$α$ emission, significantly increases the total abundance of photoproducts formed. This results from both the strong stellar Lyman-$α$ flux and resonant scattering by the overlying hydrogen layer, which redistributes photons and directs a fraction toward the dust layer. Turbulent mixing and fragmentation cycles further redistribute grains vertically, allowing photoproducts to form throughout the disk. We find that stellar Lyman-$α$ irradiation can produce sufficient photoproducts to produce an organic mantle with an {organic-to-rock ratio of $\approx 10\%$}, which could enhance grain sticking. Our results suggest that FUV-driven organic synthesis may facilitate dust growth and contribute to overcoming barriers to planetesimal formation.

items.title: The anomalously large transiting planet around Boyajian's star: evidence for a circumplanetary ring
items.abstract: A recent study reported a transiting giant-planet candidate with a mass of $9.4^{+4.9}_{-4.1}\,M_{\rm J}$ and a radius of $1.7\pm0.1\,R_{\rm J}$ on a wide orbit around Boyajian's star (KIC 8462852, also called Tabby's star), which is well known for its irregular, deep flux dips. The reported radius is puzzling, because cool giant planets of $\sim$10\,$M_{\rm Jup}$ are expected to have radii close to Jupiter's, so the companion appears $\sim$60--70\% larger than standard models allow. Here we explore the solution that the planet is actually ringed. We develop a fast and accurate code to compute the transit light curve due to a ringed planet, and apply it to the TESS light curve. The ring model is marginally favoured by the data by $Δχ^2>10$ and a difference in Bayesian information criterion (BIC) of $<2$. The preferred configuration is a Jupiter-sized ($1.1\,R_{\rm J}$) planet surrounded by an opaque, highly flattened ring extending to $3.1$--$4.4$ planetary radii with a nearly polar obliquity. While the ring geometry is uncertain, simple estimates suggest that a debris annulus extending out to the planet's Roche limit is needed to explain the large transit depth. The ring thus removes the radius anomaly altogether and is qualitatively consistent with the dusty, comet-shepherding environment inferred from the star's historic dimmings.

items.title: From AI-assisted to AI-native Industrial Control: Architecture, Agent Design, and Challenges
items.abstract: The integration of AI and industrial control is rapidly transforming industrial automation. However, current approaches remain predominantly AI-assisted, where AI functions are incorporated as auxiliary components without fundamentally altering the underlying architecture of industrial control systems. Consequently, the potential of AI to enable higher levels of autonomy, adaptability, and continuous evolution remains underutilized. This paper proposes an AI-native industrial control paradigm, which reconceptualizes industrial control systems by positioning AI as the intrinsic core rather than an external enhancement. The proposed paradigm is built upon an AI-native infrastructure and a collection of collaborative agentic AIs, each encapsulating a set of advanced skills. Among them, the industrial control agent plays a central role in orchestrating the system lifecycle. Through this paradigm, industrial control shifts from a closed, capability-oriented, human-driven, and passive engineering process to an open, task-oriented, intent-driven, and autonomous solution delivery mechanism. The paper further analyzes the key challenges of the AI-native paradigm from both AI and industrial control perspectives, including issues related to AI model reliability, formal verification, real-time assurance, and heterogeneous resource orchestration. Overall, this work outlines a forward-looking vision for industrial control in the AI era and identifies critical research directions toward autonomous, evolvable, and adaptive control systems in complex and dynamic industrial environments.

items.title: Competitive exploration in structured environments
items.abstract: Organisms must constantly weigh exploiting the resources they know against exploring for better ones. When foragers compete, the best behavior for each forager also depends on what its competitors do. How does competition change the strategic balance between exploration and exploitation? Here we address this question in a minimal model: two $ε$-greedy temporal-difference learners on a one-dimensional lattice, who start at a small reward at one end and are unaware of a larger reward at the other. For a lone forager, the optimal exploration rate increases monotonically with the value of the distant reward, and with its distance up to a critical distance. When two foragers share the lattice and split rewards, the choice of exploration rate becomes a game whose Nash equilibria have both foragers exploring, both staying, or one exploring while the other stays (anti-coordination). Under local best-response dynamics, pairs of foragers often converge on both exploring or both staying, even when anti-coordination would be socially optimal. This social dilemma arises for a wide range of parameters, and it persists even in a simplified model without explicit spatial structure. A minimal, naturalistic signal, in which one forager informs the other that it has found the distant reward, can remove many of the dilemmas in which both foragers explore, and can produce a Nash equilibrium whose collective payoff exceeds that of every outcome available without signaling.

items.title: Using Diffusion Similarity Networks to Identify, Track, and Predict Movement Disorders
items.abstract: Characterizing individual structural brain alterations in movement disorders like Parkinsons disease (PD) and Essential Tremor (ET) remains a significant challenge in clinical neuroscience. While brain structural connectivity (SC) derived from Diffusion Tensor Imaging (DTI) tractography maps physical white matter pathways, it fails to capture localized microstructural remodelings within gray matter structures. In this study, we use Diffusion Similarity Networks (DSNs) as a novel framework to estimate microstructural connectivity from diffusion weighted imaging (DWI). First, we evaluate the ability of DSNs to differentiate individuals with PD from healthy controls (HC). We used Similarity Network Fusion (SNF) to visualize differences between the fused networks of both groups as well as the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (BCT) to quantify changes in network topology, including transitivity, clustering coefficient, global efficiency, and betweenness centrality. Second, to evaluate the capacity of DSNs to track disease progression over time, we utilized longitudinal data extracted from the Parkinsons Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) database, mapping distinct functional subnetwork degeneration trajectories in PD patients. Finally, we developed a predictive Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework on a locally collected cohort to address the challenging task of differentiating PD from ET, utilizing DSNs as highly discriminant input features. Our results demonstrate that DSN metrics successfully capture distinct structural signatures that reliably separate clinical phenotypes, while longitudinal modeling reveals an accelerated, progressive decay in specific motor and basal ganglia subnetwork topologies over time. Furthermore, the GNN model achieved high classification performance (Balanced accuracy = 0.8684, AUC= 0.9420) in distinguishing PD from ET globally, with local explain- ability analysis successfully showing the specific brain Regions of Interest (ROIs) driving the differential diagnosis. Overall, these findings demonstrate that Diffusion Similarity Networks serve as a robust, non-invasive biomarker for movement disorders, offering deep insights into disease progression and an explainable AI tool for clinical decision support.

items.title: End-to-end automation of behavioural experiments with a collaborative robot
items.abstract: Reliable behavioural measurement is critical to neuroscience discovery, but end-to-end automation of experiments using live animals is challenging. Preparation and transfer of live animals into and out of behavioural assays require skilled, dexterous, gentle and consistent handling. This is difficult to achieve without bespoke automation systems, which resist wide adoption. We present STELA, a robotic cell featuring off-the-shelf collaborative robot (cobot) that autonomously runs the complete workflow of a Drosophila behaviour experiment, from vial to data. Designed to emulate human routine fly laboratory procedures in human workspace, it performs manipulation of fly culture vials, CO2 fly anaesthesia, vision-guided sex classification, single live fly manipulation, and loading and disassembly of a behaviour assay, all in a programmed loop. In 24-h working day, STELA completed 16 experiments (1024 individual visual learning assays in flies) compared to the human who, in an 8-hour working day, completed 6 (384 assays). Retention of flies fit for analysis was similar (93.85% versus 83.33%, respectively), but with 12-fold improvement in handling consistency by the robot. In biologically matched behaviour experiments, robotic and manual handling resulted in the same mean fly behavioural outcomes, yet the robot significantly reduced inter-individual variability in baseline and learning behaviours. STELA demonstrates that it is possible to deploy standard robotic systems to flexibly automate one of the most challenging animal experiments. It provides a low-variance, high-throughput platform for scalable experimentation, and a path to closed-loop, democratized robotic acceleration of experimental discovery.

items.title: Whole-brain normative modeling across multiple functional connectivity metrics in MEG
items.abstract: Normative modeling has recently emerged in structural and functional neuroimaging as a promising approach to characterize neuropathology at the individual level. Trained on large healthy cohorts, these models predict expected measurements from covariates such as age and sex while quantifying normal population variability. Individual measurements can then be compared against the model to identify deviations associated with pathology. While most normative models of brain function have been based on functional MRI, EEG and MEG offer more direct measurements of brain activity at higher temporal resolution. Despite the promise, how to adequately perform normative modelling at the whole-brain level on these modalities remains challenging. We here propose M/EEG-FUNCOIN to identify age- and sex-related dimensions of change in functional connectivity from a plethora of FC measures from electrophysiology: amplitude envelope correlation, phase-locking value, and time-delay embedding covariance. Using resting-state MEG data from the Cambridge Centre for Aging and Neuroscience (Cam-CAN) dataset, we show that M/EEG-FUNCOIN can: (i) characterize age- and sex-related whole-brain functional connectivity patterns in greater detail than existing methods; and (ii) effectively capture meaningful deviations in connectivity in individuals that rank high and low in cognitive ability. Altogether, these results show great potential for applications in complex, network-level brain pathology.

items.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Sleep Disorders in Psychiatry
items.abstract: Sleep disorders are prevalent among psychiatric patients and are strongly associated with neurobiological, psychological, and behavioral processes. This chapter analyzes neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE), an approach incorporating the insights gained from neuroscience with patient education to understand and manage sleep disturbances better. To establish a scientific basis for psychoeducational interventions, we discuss central mechanisms of sleep regulation such as circadian rhythms, sleep homeostasis, neurotransmitter systems, and brain networks. It illustrates how bidirectional sleep disorders and psychiatric syndromes, including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), are linked, and explains sleep disturbance as a transdiagnostic key clinical feature. In addition to cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, NIPE is used to provide a solution to insomnia by integrating mindfulness-based strategies and personalized interventions with the assistance of digital technologies. Implementation challenges and outcome assessment, as well as ethical dimensions of practice, are also considered. In fact, NIPE is a clinically relevant strategy that can both maximize patient engagement and ameliorate sleep disorder outcomes.

items.title: The transcription factor BCL11A restores differentiation potential to aged oligodendrocyte progenitor cells.
items.abstract: In young animals, oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs) in the CNS efficiently differentiate into myelinating oligodendrocytes (OLs), whereas ageing reduces this capacity, impairing remyelination following demyelinating injury and adaptive myelination involved in learning. To identify factors that restore resilience in aged OPCs, we developed gSWITCH (https://altoslabs.shinyapps.io/gSWITCH/, https://github.com/Tanay-math/gSWITCH), a computational pipeline that captures dynamic gene-expression patterns to identify 'switch' genes during lineage progression and ordered biological transitions, including time-series experiments. gSWITCH identified OPC-characteristic switch genes, which we compared between young and aged OPCs to determine whether their regulation is altered with ageing. This revealed several transcription factors with reduced expression in aged OPCs. Transcription-factor binding-site enrichment highlighted Bcl11a as a potential master-regulator of multiple switch genes. Bcl11a inhibition reduced OPC differentiation into OLs, whereas its overexpression in aged OPCs significantly enhanced OL differentiation without affecting proliferation. In aged mice subjected to demyelination injury in spinal cord white matter, Bcl11a overexpression increased OPC differentiation within lesions. We found that Bcl11a has undergone pervasive purifying selection throughout vertebrate evolution, preserving its amino acid sequence by eliminating deleterious mutations. Our study shows that reversing the age-related decline of this evolutionarily conserved factor in aged OPCs restores their impaired capacity for differentiation.

items.title: PHC2-dependent PRC1 assemblies stabilize motor neuron Hox codes.
items.abstract: Polycomb Repressive Complexes PRC1 and PRC2 establish and maintain chromatin architectures critical for cell-type specific gene expression. In the developing spinal cord, PRC1 is essential for implementing Hox-dependent transcriptional programs that diversify motor neuron identities. Although PRC1 can assemble into subnuclear condensates, whether these structures contribute to the specification and maintenance of neuronal subtype fates remains unclear. Using chick and mouse models, we show that canonical PRC1 components - BMI1, PHC2, CBX2, RING1B - coalesce into subnuclear assemblies as neural progenitors differentiate into motor neurons. Disrupting PHC2 polymerization in either neural progenitors or postmitotic neurons dismantles BMI1-containing PRC1 assemblies, triggering derepression of caudal Hox genes and a cell autonomous loss of segment-specific motor neuron fates. Mouse mutants lacking the core PRC1 subunit Ring1 fail to form BMI1-containing assemblies, despite intact PHC2 and CBX2 polymers. In contrast, motor neuron-restricted deletion of core PRC2 subunits (Ezh1/2) depletes H3K27me3 histone marks but retains PRC1 assemblies and Hox boundaries. Together, these findings indicate that PHC2-dependent PRC1 assemblies stabilize Hox transcriptional boundaries and motor neuron segmental identities.

items.title: Analysis of Perceived Student Learning Gains in a Biochemistry Lab Course-Based Undergraduate Research Experience.
items.abstract: Course-based Undergraduate Research Experiences (CUREs) provide the opportunity for students to engage in research projects and develop research skills while in a classroom or lab setting. This educational approach has been implemented and studied in many STEM disciplines but more work on assessment of student work is needed. In this study students' perceptions of their learning were compared at the beginning and again at the conclusion of a biochemistry laboratory course. Analysis of responses derived from over 300 students across five semesters was employed. Our data show improvements in skills that instructors anticipate students will develop. Over 90% of students reported increased knowledge, experience, and confidence in the Anticipated Learning Outcomes (ALOs). We also show 96% of students reported an increase in bioinformatic techniques and 85% of students report an increase for questions about wet-lab experiments presented during the course. We did not observe a statistically significant difference in Knowledge, Experience, and Confidence (KEC) between hybrid and in-person course modalities. Overall, these data provide insight into the benefits and limitations of CUREs for students. Building on studies with limited sample size 1 , this study uses quantitative analysis on perceived student learning in research-based STEM courses. We anticipate that better understanding of learning in CUREs will lead to wider adoption of this type of learning style thereby expanding research opportunities for undergraduate students, especially those traditionally underrepresented in STEM. Further studies of learning facilitated by CUREs are necessary to inspire endorsement by faculty over the commonly seen cookbook-style experiment.

items.title: Loss of PAX6 alters the excitatory/inhibitory neuronal ratio in human cerebral organoids.
items.abstract: The transcription factor PAX6 is a crucial regulator of multiple aspects of embryonic forebrain development. It has well-established roles in the regulation of excitatory and inhibitory neuron development in the embryonic cortex in mice but PAX6's roles during human forebrain development are less well understood. Using human cerebral organoids, we investigated PAX6's roles in human neurodevelopment. Homozygous PAX6 mutant (PAX6-/-) organoids were larger than controls and contained increased inhibitory cell types. Excitatory neurons were still generated in PAX6-/- organoids but they were less mature, and a subset showed dysregulated expression of inhibitory identity genes compared to PAX6+/+ controls. The inhibitory cells found in PAX6-/- organoids physically segregated from excitatory neurons and presented a distinct transcriptomic profile when compared to in vivo cortical inhibitory neurons. PAX6-/- organoids showed a dysregulated cellular response to PTN-PTPRZ1 signalling, which contributed to the observed increase in inhibitory neurons and the consequent altered excitatory to inhibitory neuronal ratio.

items.title: Assessment of Glucose Metabolism in Vivo in the Human Frontal Lobe Using Interleaved <sup>1</sup>H and <sup>13</sup>C MRS at 7T.
items.abstract: Background 13 C magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), combined with 13 C-labeled substrate infusion, offers a nonionizing, minimally invasive method for assessing fluxes through the main cerebral energy metabolism pathways. However, its human application at 7T has not been fully established, especially within the frontal lobe, where alterations are linked to various neurological and psychiatric disorders. Purpose To explore the feasibility of the interleaved 1 H/ 13 C MRS protocol for quantification of cerebral glucose uptake and downstream metabolism at 7T, and to estimate the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle flux (V TCA ) for validation. Study type Prospective. Population Three healthy volunteers (Two females and one male). Field strength/sequence 7T; single voxel spectroscopy: ACE-STEAM (indirect 1 H-[ 13 C]) and ISIS-DEPT (direct 13 C-[ 1 H]). Assessment ACE-STEAM and ISIS-DEPT were applied to acquire the time-resolved spectra in the frontal lobe. 13 C-labeled glucose, glutamate, and glutamine fractional enrichment time courses were quantified to estimate V TCA through the one-compartment model. Statistical tests The relative estimated fitting uncertainties (EFUs) were reported for the processed spectra. Nonlinear least squares minimization was used for flux fitting of 13 C traces. Uncertainty of the estimated metabolic fluxes was evaluated using Monte Carlo simulations. Results [1- 13 C]-glucose (GlcC1) was detected within 6 min on 13 C MR spectra, followed by 13 C-labeled GluH4 and GlnH4, and then GlxH3 can be quantified on 1 H MR spectra. End-of-infusion mean enrichments were 17% (GluH4), 13% (GlnH4), and 7% (GlxH3). Brain glucose concentration ranged 1.86-2.94 mM, with 61% of the mean enrichment in C1. Group-average V TCA was 0.66 ± 0.07 μmol/g/min (n = 3). Data conclusion This interleaved 1 H/ 13 C MRS protocol, combined with 13 C-labeled glucose infusion, enables minimally invasive quantification of cerebral metabolic fluxes. As a proof-of-concept feasibility study in a small healthy volunteer cohort, it may provide a useful framework for investigating neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases at 7T. Evidence level 1. Technical efficacy Stage 1.

items.title: Named neurons of the nervous system: a historical narrative review of discovery, function, and legacy.
items.abstract: Many currently applied terms in neuroanatomy are rooted in important historical breakthroughs. Some discoveries become timeless, some evolve as knowledge advances, and others disappear into history before being rediscovered by a later generation. Purkinje cells, Betz cells, Golgi cells, Renshaw cells, and Onuf's nucleus are spoken of so routinely that their eponymous significance is not always immediately apparent. Yet each one reflects a moment of curiosity, a painstaking observation under a microscope, an inspired technical breakthrough, or, at times, an intense scientific rivalry. The history of named neurons mirrors the history of neuroscience. As microscopy and histological staining techniques improved, anatomists were able to see structures that had previously been invisible, transforming the nervous system from an indistinct mass into an intricate landscape of specialized cells. Some discoveries, such as Golgi's staining method and Cajal's neuron doctrine, reshaped biology forever (Golgi, 1873; Ramón y Cajal, 1906). Others were slower to be recognized: von Economo neurons, for example, were described, forgotten for nearly seven decades, and only later recognized as a distinct neuronal population (Betz, 1881, as cited in Butti et al. 2013; von Economo, 1926; Nimchinsky et al. 1999). This review follows these remarkable journeys, exploring neurons named after their discoverers alongside those named for their appearance or function, including chandelier cells, place cells, mirror neurons, and concept cells. Together, they demonstrate the depth of many familiar names in neuroanatomy-not merely as descriptive labels, but also as windows into the history, ingenuity, and enduring curiosity that continues to shape modern neuroscience.

items.title: Polygenic prediction of cannabis-related outcomes: Evidence from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children longitudinal cohort and the European gene-environment interaction case-control study.
items.abstract: Background and aims Polygenic risk scores (PRSs) for cannabis use disorder (CUD), major depressive disorder (MDD), insomnia and chronic pain, and early age at cannabis initiation might be linked to problematic cannabis use. We tested whether: (1) higher PRS for CUD, MDD, insomnia and chronic pain are associated with earlier initiation and problematic cannabis use; (2) age at cannabis initiation explains more variance in problematic use than any single PRS; and (3) PRSs moderate the association between early initiation and problematic cannabis use. Design Observational study involving two cohorts: (1) the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) population-based birth cohort and (2) for conceptual replication, the EUropean Gene-Environment Interaction (EU-GEI) first-episode psychosis case-control study. Setting (1) United Kingdom; (2b) 16 population-based catchment areas in Europe and 1 in Brazil, with FEP cases recruited from mental health services and controls from the general population of the same catchment areas. Participants For ALSPAC, n = 8224 genotyped (51% male); subsamples with Cannabis Abuse Screening Test (CAST) at 17 years (n = 895), 20y (n = 1587), 24y (n = 836) and frequency of use at 24y (n = 2908). EU-GEI: n = 776 [controls: mean age 37.2, standard deviation (SD) = 13.5; 47% male] and 491 FEP cases (mean age 31.5, SD = 11.2; 62.5% male). Measurements Outcomes were self-reported lifetime and frequency of cannabis use and CAST score (problematic use questionnaire). Predictors were PRSs for CUD, MDD, insomnia and chronic pain. Models were adjusted for sex, age and genetic principal components (ALSPAC), and additionally for site and case-control status (EU-GEI). Results In ALSPAC, CUD PRS was associated with CAST score at 20 [beta coefficient (β) = 0.04, False Discovery Rate-corrected P-value (p FDR ) = 0.03] and CAST at 24 years (β = 0.11, p FDR = 0.005). MDD PRS was associated with CAST scores at 17y (β = 0.1, p FDR = 0.002), 20y (β = 0.06, p FDR = 0.01) and 24y (β = 0.09, p FDR = 0.01). Pain PRS was associated with the CAST scores at 17y (β = 0.09, p FDR = 0.002), 20y (β = 0.07, p FDR FDR = 0.005). In EU-GEI, CUD PRS (RRR = 1.82, p FDR = 0.001) and pain PRS (RRR = 1.27, p FDR = 0.007) were associated with weekly-to-daily use. The Relative Excess Risk due to Interaction RERI model showed evidence of additive interaction for CUD PRS, RERI = 2.4, P = 0.009, while MDD and schizophrenia PRS showed no evidence of additive interaction. Summary Genetic liability, measured by polygenic risk scores, to cannabis use disorder, major depressive disorder, and chronic pain appears to be associated with heavier and more problematic cannabis use. Age at cannabis initiation explains more variance in problematic cannabis use than polygenic liability.

items.title: Is there a natural boundary for formal thought disorder? Evidence from taxometric analysis.
items.abstract: Background Formal thought disorder (FTD) has been conceptualized as a categorical syndrome of psychosis, but this remains untested. Clarifying whether FTD is categorical or continuous and its supra-thres hold prevalence in non-clinical populations has direct implications for bears directly on mechanistic studies of FTD, psychosis prediction, and early intervention. Methods In a multi-site cross-sectional study of 520 individuals (352 clinical, 168 non-clinical), we used the Thought and Language Index to assess FTD across three subconstructs: Loosening, Peculiarities , and Impoverishment. Using complementary taxometric procedures (MAMBAC, MAXEIG, and L-Mode) with simulation of comparison data and multiple thresholding approaches (minimally important change criteria, ROC analysis, intuitive binarization), we evaluated the latent structure of FTD, optimal cutoff points to estimate FTD prevalence, and the frequency of co-occurrence of subconstructs. Results Taxometric analyses revealed a predominantly dimensional latent structure for FTD across various base rates. Among healthy individuals, Peculiarities were uncommon (1.2%), but 11.3% exhibited Loosening and 8.9% had Impoverishment even with conservative thresholds. Multi-construct co-occurrence exceeded chance across the sample but was restricted to patients at conservative clinical thresholds. Conclusions FTD exists in a continuous dimensional structure extending into healthy populations. Each dimension is measurable in healthy individuals, but multi-dimensional convergence at clinical thresholds (i.e. disorder with functional impairment) appears specific to patients. This suggests that common vulnerability factors increase the likelihood of elevations across multiple but substantially independent dimensions of FTD. As a hypothesis requiring prospective validation, clinical risk of psychosis may depend on the coalescence rather than single-dimensional severity of FTD subconstructs.

items.title: Multimodal regulation of neurite extension by extracellular matrix composition and electrical stimulation on aligned collagen fiber scaffolds.
items.abstract: Objective . Peripheral nerve regeneration is regulated by structural, biochemical, and electrical cues, yet their combined effects on neurite outgrowth remain unclear. In this study, an aligned fibrous scaffold was developed to evaluate how extracellular matrix (ECM) composition and electrical stimulation influence neurite extension and growth cone morphology. Approach . Type I collagen fibers incorporating fibronectin, collagen IV, and laminin I were fabricated by contact drawing. The contact drawn fibers were then consolidated into multifilaments, which were mounted on custom frames for cell culture. Primary dorsal root ganglia (DRG) explants were cultured on the multifilaments, and neurite outgrowth and alignment were quantified as a function of ECM composition. Functional activity was confirmed by patch clamp. High-resolution confocal imaging was performed to assess cytoskeletal organization and growth cone morphology. Electrical stimulation was applied to evaluate interactions between biochemical and bioelectrical cues. Main Results . Collagen multifilament scaffolds promoted a high degree of neurite alignment relative to DRGs cultured on isotropic surfaces. Fibronectin and collagen IV increased neurite length in a concentration-dependent manner, with maximal effects observed at intermediate ligand densities, while laminin I had no significant effect. Combinatorial ECM presentation produced non-additive responses. Electrical stimulation increased neurite length on collagen-only scaffolds but had a reduced effect or no effect with incorporation of additional ECM constituents. Growth cone morphology was altered by ECM composition, with fibronectin-, collagen IV-, and combinatorial scaffolds producing less circular growth cones, despite no significant differences in filopodia number or overall morphology-classification proportions. Significance . Neurite extension and growth cone structure are governed by non-linear interactions between multimodal cues. The scaffold system described here facilitates systematic comparison of multiple regenerative cues to inform the design of material for promoting nerve regeneration.

items.title: Sequential restriction of SNARE-mediated fusion by the COPII inner coat and SNARE chaperones.
items.abstract: SNARE-mediated fusion requires assembly of four SNARE domains (Qa, Qb, Qc, R) distributed across two membranes, with an SM (Sec1/Munc-18 family) chaperone catalyzing this assembly. We investigated topological requirements for the four SNAREs (Sed5, Bos1, Bet1, Sec22) that mediate ER-Golgi fusion using in vitro assays. In the presence of the cognate SM Sly1, we find that the R SNARE must be in trans to the Qa and Qb SNAREs. The Qc SNARE functions on either membrane but is most active in cis to Qa and Qb. These results prompted us to look upstream, at COPII-SNARE interactions. The assembled COPII coat is known to block fusion. We discovered that of five COPII core subunits, the Sar1 GTPase and Sec23/Sec24 subunits were necessary and sufficient to prevent fusion for prolonged periods, and that Sar1 was dispensable for inhibition over short periods. When Sec24 interactions with R and Qc SNAREs were disrupted, inhibition was relieved, indicating that SNARE sequestration by COPII on the nascent carrier prevents fusion. These observations help to explain how appropriate fusion events are facilitated while inappropriate events are deterred.

items.title: Systematic genome analysis enables long-overdue taxonomic reorganization of genus Orthoflavivirus; potential assignment of over 50 new species
items.abstract: Members of the Orthoflavivirus genus in the family Flaviviridae are primarily vector-transmitted RNA viruses infecting humans, other mammals and birds, including major pathogens such as tick borne encephalitis, West Nile, Zika and dengue viruses. Vector-borne flaviviruses are assigned to the Euflavivirus subgenus of orthoflaviviruses, with more divergent largely unclassified insect-specific flaviviruses, including cell fusing agent virus assigned to the second subgenus, Fusivirus. The currently classified 57 orthoflavivirus species have traditionally been assigned descriptively on the basis of their genome and antigenic relatedness, ecology and host and vector tropisms, although many more orthoflavi-like viruses remain unassigned. To investigate whether species might be demarcated using a fixed genetic divergence threshold, we examined distributions of pairwise distances in NS5 and E genes (which encode the RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and envelope protein, respectively) of classified orthoflaviviruses. Demarcation thresholds of 0.1 in the two regions would be most parsimonious with current euflavivirus classification. Exceptions include species in the tick-borne encephalitis virus complex with divergences below the threshold, and dengue virus types currently assigned to a single species that are substantially above. Application of the proposed thresholds would provide the means to establish 25 new euflavivirus and 33 new fusivirus species and reconcile several anomalies and inconsistencies in the current species taxonomy. The use of a species demarcation threshold brings consistency with the classification of viruses in other families. A robust and evolutionarily consistent framework furthermore enables taxonomic assignments of the numerous currently unassigned orthoflaviviruses that lack the phenotypic descriptions required for the current species definition.

items.title: Invisible by Design: Algorithmic Silence, Denied Citizenship, and Civic Mobilisation in the Public Sector AI Ecology
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid digitization of the state has shifted public administration from human-mediated bureaucracy to automated socio-technical systems. While critical data studies examine algorithmic bias, the communicative dimensions of automated exclusion remain under-theorized. This article introduces the concept of algorithmic silence—the systemic breakdown of bidirectional institutional dialogue when automated interfaces withhold the operational logic, weights, and rationales behind life-altering decisions. Situated within the empirical context of the Nordic digital welfare state, this study examines how marginalized populations experience, interpret, and actively resist automated exclusion. Drawing on a multi-method qualitative research design comprising digital ethnography, policy discourse analysis, and in-depth narrative field interviews with precarious public service users, we demonstrate how algorithmic silence operates as an active mechanism of administrative disenfranchisement that systematically produces denied citizenship. Crucially, rather than presenting marginalized users as passive recipients of algorithmic opacity, our findings reveal how excluded populations engineer sophisticated horizontal mutual-aid networks, collective information workarounds, and counter-public message boards to bypass top-down algorithmic gatekeepers. This study contributes to digital sociology and platform governance by shifting the analytical lens from engineering optimization to the communicative struggles defining the human cost of the automated state.

items.title: How fish exploit vortices to save energy, and under what conditions
items.abstract: Abstract How flexible swimmers exploit unsteady flows is a longstanding question in fluid–structure interaction. Kármán gait allows fish to hold station in vortex wakes at reduced energetic cost, yet how the wake organizes and stabilizes this gait remains unclear. Here, we combine comparative experiments on live and dead fish with passive bionic models, hydrodynamic reconstruction, and reduced-order modelling. Across 20 species, Kármán gait exhibited a common phase-locked organization in which wake–body interactions shaped much of the body-center and tail motion, while active regulation was concentrated in the anterior body. A forced damped-oscillator model captured the observed phase lag and near-resonant response. Bionic-model experiments identified sufficient compliance and wake–body frequency matching as mechanical constraints, whereas live-fish observations showed that stable entrainment was concentrated at an intermediate body–wake scale. These results identify Kármán gait as a physically gated, wake-forced state, with implications for fish ecology and bioinspired robotics.

items.title: High-latitude ultrasociality and the Nordic Paradox: an evolutionary-ecological framework for the psychosocial trade-offs of cooperation
items.abstract: Abstract The Nordic countries consistently rank among the world's leading societies in institutional quality, social trust, democratic performance, low perceived corruption, and subjective well-being, yet they also exhibit comparatively elevated suicide mortality. This apparent contradiction, referred to here as the Nordic Paradox , remains insufficiently explained. This article develops an evolutionary-ecological framework proposing that some of the same ecological, demographic, and institutional processes that historically contributed to the stabilization of large-scale human cooperation may also generate distinctive psychosocial trade-offs. An exploratory macro-comparative analysis of seventeen European democracies revealed that suicide mortality was positively associated with latitude, institutional integrity, and democratic performance, and negatively associated with World Happiness Report rankings, indicating higher suicide mortality in countries characterized by greater subjective well-being. Although these associations do not support causal inference, they identify a broader ecological and institutional pattern that provides the basis for an evolutionary interpretation. Integrating evidence from behavioral ecology, evolutionary anthropology, archaeogenomics, comparative institutional analysis, and the psychology of social regulation, the article proposes that high-latitude environments may have favored the long-term stabilization of cooperative systems characterized by generalized trust, strong norm internalization, and universalistic institutions, while simultaneously increasing sensitivity to reputational evaluation and psychosocial strain. Rather than offering a definitive explanation of the Nordic Paradox, the article advances a falsifiable evolutionary-ecological framework that generates specific predictions for future psychological, behavioral, comparative, and archaeogenomic research.

items.title: Road Development in the Tropical Forests of Southeast Asia and the Pacific: A Systematic Review of Forest Loss, Ecological and Health Effects, and Mitigation
items.abstract: Background: Road networks in Southeast Asian and Pacific tropical forests are expanding through highways, logging and plantation roads and unmapped access roads. This review synthesized primary evidence on road effects on forest loss, ecology and human health, and evaluated mitigation. Methods Scopus, PubMed and OpenAlex were searched on 7 October 2026 for English-language journal articles published from 2015 (PRISMA 2020). Reviewer 1 and Reviewer 2 independently screened 496 records (κ = 0.94) and assessed 80 full texts (κ = 0.80); the Adjudicator resolved disagreements. Studies were appraised with MMAT 2018, synthesized following SWiM and rated with GRADE-CERQual. Results Sixty-five studies were included, most from Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand; 19 reported forest-loss, 47 ecological and six mitigation outcomes. Forest cover loss was greater nearer roads, at higher road density or length and after construction or completion in nine studies, and no study showed less loss (moderate confidence). Loss extended to 17.7 km with secondary roads in New Guinea (moderate). Structural edge effects reached 34 m at a logging road and 350 m at a highway, whereas soil effects stayed largely on the road surface (moderate). Reptiles or amphibians led roadkill in all seven surveys recording every vertebrate class, and mortality concentrated on short sections near water (moderate). Paved roads reduced crossing by elephants and gibbons and were linked to genetic differentiation in some taxa (moderate). Crossing structures were used by mammals and a large snake (moderate); measured effects rested on single spatial comparisons (very low). No study reported a human health outcome, and fire, landslides and water quality were unmeasured. Conclusions Roads act on these forests at two scales: kilometers for access-driven clearing, and tens to hundreds of meters for edge, mortality and barrier effects. Assessment boundaries and mitigation should match each mechanism’s scale, and mitigation needs before-after evaluation.

items.title: Genetic canalization of nutrient resorption in the widespread grass Phragmites australis under salt stress.
items.abstract: Nutrient resorption is a key plant strategy for nutrient conservation, yet whether it responds plastically to non-nutrient stressors such as salinity remains unresolved. Using a common garden experiment with 110 genotypes of the cosmopolitan grass Phragmites australis , we first established that the imposed salinity treatment induced strong multilevel stress responses: above-ground biomass declined by >60%, sodium accumulated three- to fivefold across all leaf stages, and 484 metabolites showed significant differential accumulation, including canonical markers of osmotic and oxidative stress. Against this backdrop of confirmed stress, we found that nutrient resorption efficiency (NuRE) remained largely unaffected by salinity. Instead, NuRE was strongly correlated with phylogeographic lineage, ecotype, and latitude of origin, demonstrating evolutionary canalization rather than short-term acclimation. Element-specific regulatory patterns were also evident: while phosphorus resorption followed concentration-dependent control regardless of stress, nitrogen control was disrupted under salinity, and potassium resorption showed no such dependence. Our findings reveal that intraspecific variation in nutrient resorption is predominantly shaped by historical adaptation and geographic context, not by plasticity to salinity. This genetic canalization of a key functional trait implies that predictions of nutrient cycling under global change must account for the phylogeographic composition of plant populations.

items.title: Nest ecology-associated impacts of wastewater on wild bee microbiomes
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Anthropogenic pollution affects environments differently depending on proximity to the pollution source, exposure route, and species ecology. Thus, understanding an organism’s ecological role and exposure route to contaminants is central to assessing pollution impact. Treated municipal wastewater releases contaminants into waterways and alters microbial communities. Plants absorb contaminants and expose animals through foraging and nest-building activities. Nesting ecology differences of ground and wood cavity-nesting bees offer insight into niche-specific susceptibility to pollution. We compared gut microbiomes of directly exposed soil-nesting Halictus ligatus and indirectly exposed wood-nesting Ceratina spp. upstream and downstream of wastewater. We collected bees, flowers, and soil and analyzed their bacterial microbiomes using 16S rRNA sequencing. The effect from wastewater explained a much larger proportion of the variance in the ground-nesting H. ligatus microbiome than wood cavity-nesting Ceratina adults, Ceratina larvae, and pollen provisions. Conversely, soil and flower microbiomes remained stable, indicating higher stability. These findings suggest that wastewater exposure leads to strong host-associated microbiome disruption, with ground-nesting bees most affected. IMPORTANCE Because contaminants bind strongly to soil, ground-nesting bees near wastewater are likely most impacted, while wood cavity-nesting bees are likely less impacted since plant uptake of contaminants is species dependent. These results suggest that exposure routes drive contaminant susceptibility, with bee-associated microbes most vulnerable. Because bees are important pollinators and biodiversity contributors, these disruptions point to broader ecological risks in increasingly contaminated landscapes.

items.title: Genome sequence of Microbacterium sp., an endophyte isolated from Zea mays in South Africa.
items.abstract: Microbacterium species are plant-associated actinobacteria with plant growth-promoting potential. Here, the 3.42 Mb circular genome of strain ARC56GC isolated from maize leaves in South Africa is reported. Comparative genomics identified Microbacterium testaceum as its closest relative, while average nucleotide identity (ANI) analyses suggest that ARC56GC represents a genomically distinct lineage within the M. testaceum species complex.

items.title: An Sfp2-like protein underlies tube foot temporary adhesion in the sea cucumber Apostichopus japonicus.
items.abstract: Temporary adhesion by echinoderm tube feet is essential for attachment, locomotion and feeding, yet its molecular basis remains poorly understood in Holothuroidea. Here, we combined ultrastructural, proteomic, phylogenetic and expression analyses to investigate the temporary adhesive system in the sea cucumber Apostichopus japonicus. Scanning and transmission electron microscopy revealed a highly specialized tube foot disc epidermis featuring abundant secretory pores, dense microvilli, and two distinct types of adhesive secretory cells, whereas these features were absent in the non-adhesive homologous papillae. Proteomic analysis of tube foot footprints and discs, combined with bioinformatic screening, identified 20 high-confidence candidate adhesive proteins and one Astacin-domain-containing candidate de-adhesive protein. Notably, the 4,085-aa multidomain protein Aj-Sfp2-like was relatively abundant in the footprint proteome and showed extensive predicted post-translational modification. Tissue expression and in situ localization confirmed that Aj-Sfp2-like transcripts are localized to the secretory epidermis of adhesive appendages (tube feet and tentacles), whereas no such expression was detected in the non-adhesive papillae. Phylogenetic and comparative domain analyses demonstrate that Aj-Sfp2-like belongs to the broadly conserved Sfp2-like protein family, sharing a homologous modular framework with asteroid-restricted Sfp1-like proteins. These findings provide the first molecular framework for understanding tube foot adhesion and de-adhesion in holothurians and broaden our understanding of the conserved and divergent basis of temporary adhesion across echinoderms.

items.title: Beyond the reservoir: rethinking wildlife contributions to Fasciola transmission in multihost landscapes.
items.abstract: Wildlife infection with Fasciola spp. has been documented across diverse mammalian taxa and ecological settings; however, the epidemiological significance of these infections remains difficult to determine. Serological exposure, parasite DNA, adult fluke recovery, coproantigen detection, and egg shedding represent different diagnostic states and support various levels of inference. In Fasciola transmission, a patent definitive host is only one part of an indirect cycle that also requires eggs to reach wet or aquatic habitats, compatible lymnaeid snails to become infected and amplify the parasite, and susceptible hosts to ingest the viable metacercariae. From this critical perspective, we ask when wildlife infection actually contributes to persistence or transmission to a defined target population. We used the wildlife reservoir paradox to describe situations in which measured wildlife infection is poorly aligned with the realised transmission contribution, and distinguished four context-dependent functions: incidental hosts, amplifying contributors, interface connectors, and maintenance components. We then evaluated how lymnaeid identity and ecology, environmental and hydrological connectivity, and molecular evidence could strengthen or limit reservoir attribution. Finally, we refined Fasciola Interface Management (FIM) into an operational five-step workflow that asks who contaminates, where snail amplification occurs, which target populations are connected to those sites, where parasite flow can be disrupted, and whether transmission subsequently declines. The central argument is that wildlife reservoir status should be attributed to populations within defined transmission systems, not inferred from host positivity alone.

items.title: Integrating Ecology and Economics in Agent-Based Models to Support Agricultural Policy.
items.abstract: Agriculture is a complex social-ecological system with numerous interactions between policies, markets, farm management, landscapes, and ecosystems. Agent-based models are a valuable method for studying these agricultural systems, as they are able to simulate the spatiotemporal dynamics and heterogeneous actors inherent to them. This potentially also makes such models helpful tools for scientific policy advice. Here, we conduct a literature review to evaluate how agent-based models represent social-ecological systems in agriculture. We analyze 56 published models using a set of 26 criteria to determine whether socio-economic and ecological aspects of agriculture have been studied. We find that there is a particularly robust tradition of using agent-based models for economic impact analyses of policy changes, and much effort has gone into studying decision-making by land users. However, ecological models of biodiversity and ecosystem services are still often very abstract and ignore important land-use processes, impeding their usefulness for providing policy advice. Research areas that are currently underdeveloped include simulating farm management and landscape dynamics in ecological models, risk management in economic models, and bidirectional human-nature interactions in social-ecological models. Agent-based modeling of agriculture would also profit from using model coupling to represent more of the breadth of social-ecological systems.

items.title: Phylogenomics of Cypriniformes, the most diverse order of freshwater fishes: consensus, challenges and limitations.
items.abstract: Cypriniformes, the most species-rich order of freshwater fishes (∼5,000 species), represents a key lineage for understanding vertebrate diversification in freshwater ecosystems. This clade includes several highly miniaturized and understudied lineages whose phylogenetic placements have long remained contentious. Here, we present the first phylogenomic analysis of Cypriniformes with complete family-level representation and broad genus-level coverage, encompassing 316 species comprising approximately 30% of all described genera. Our dataset integrates 257 newly assembled genomes with publicly available resources and analyzes multiple sets of genome-wide markers using both concatenation-based and coalescent-aware approaches. The general concordance among analytical frameworks indicates that the backbone topology of Cypriniformes is now established, allowing clear identification of well-supported clades and regions of persistent conflict. Our results strengthen the evolutionary relationships of several miniaturized lineages, while identifying recalcitrant relationships shaped by both biological processes and model artefacts that can yield superficially similar patterns of phylogenetic conflict. Our study substantially expands genomic representation and establishes a phylogenomic foundation for future comparative, developmental, and evolutionary research in this freshwater radiation.

items.title: Severe environmental disturbances compromise ecological thresholds in aquatic environments.
items.abstract: Large-scale disturbances can profoundly alter aquatic ecosystems by modifying water chemistry, sediment dynamics, and biodiversity across connected freshwater and marine environments. The 2015 Fundão Dam collapse in Brazil provides an unprecedented context to evaluate how multiple aquatic communities respond to intense and prolonged contamination, revealing key mechanisms of community reorganization under chronic anthropogenic impacts. By a multi-taxa monitoring dataset collected from 62 freshwater and marine sites, we analyzed how different communities, comprising phytoplankton, zooplankton, macroinvertebrates, and fish, responded along a gradient of mining tailing exposure. Applying threshold indicator taxa analysis (TITAN), we identified critical environmental variables, capturing tipping points for positive and negative biotic responses to tailing-related environmental gradients. Our results showed that mining-related contaminants, combined with hydrogeochemical alterations triggered by the dam collapse, have driven long-term changes in biodiversity, reshaping ecosystem functioning. The same stressors that caused widespread negative responses in community structure also promoted localized increases in opportunistic, mainly planktonic taxa, indicating a multidirectional community reorganization. In general, small increases in metals and hydrogeochemical alterations (such as turbidity up to 17 NTU in riverine systems and 2 NTU in the marine sites), resulting from the dam collapse have driven persistent changes in biodiversity, ultimately reshaping ecosystem functioning. Integrating community-level thresholds should represent a critical approach to improve the detection of regime shifts and to support the development of habitat-specific recovery strategies for riverine and marine ecosystems affected by mining disturbances.

items.title: The Arena Model: An Account of Human Judgment
items.abstract: Psychology, economics, and behavioral science catalog human judgment through hundreds of disparate cognitive biases. The Arena Model (AM) replaces this disjointed taxonomy with a single account: judgment runs on a low-dimensional projection of a higher-dimensional world. The model derives many canonical heuristics and biases from a few fixed mechanisms. A "bias,'" per the AM account, is what happens when a mind works with fewer dimensions than its environment contains, when a researcher measures dimensions that differ from what the mind used, or when an internal signal is taken to report a property of the world. Many apparent departures from rationality resolve once unmeasured and mismatched dimensions are taken into account. Unlike descriptive frameworks that add a new mechanism for each phenomenon, the AM constrains the space of possible errors and yields clear, falsifiable predictions about the conditions under which biases will and will not appear. It also gives researchers a single, testable account in place of a growing list of unconnected exceptions. I demonstrate consistency across known biases, define the limits of the account, and propose a diagnostic test to evaluate, or invalidate, it.

items.title: Effect of breathing exercise on enema-related anxiety, fear and pain in children: a randomized controlled trial.
items.abstract: To explore the effects of breathing exercises on enema-related anxiety, fear, and pain in children. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) design was adopted. Children aged 6-12 ( n = 106) were randomly assigned to an intervention group ( n = 53) and a control group ( n = 53). The intervention group received breathing exercises. Comparisons of pain, fear, and anxiety scores both between and within the two groups were conducted using independent samples t-tests. Cohen's d formula was used to calculate the effect size of the difference between the two group averages. The intervention group received breathing exercises followed by an enema, while the control group received a standard enema procedure. Significant time, group, and time × group interactions were found for anxiety (d = 1.84), fear (d = 1,36), and pain (d = 1.23) ( p p p < 0.001), while they increased in the control group. Breathing exercises are effective in reducing children's anxiety, fear, and pain levels associated with enemas. Breathing exercises can be recommended as an effective, non-pharmacological nursing intervention for children. Clinical Trials number: NCT05508022.

items.title: Bystander Responses to Street Harassment Based on Gender, Gender Identity and Sexual Orientation: A Qualitative Vignette Study From the United Kingdom.
items.abstract: Street harassment based on gender, gender identity or sexual orientation is a common form of violence globally, experienced daily by many people. Despite the scale of the problem, there is surprisingly little research investigating street harassment from the perspectives of bystanders who observe it. In this study, 120 online participants from the United Kingdom read three vignettes depicting street harassment of a presumed cis-gender woman, a trans woman and a gay couple. After reading the vignettes, participants were asked open-ended questions regarding their potential actions and barriers and facilitators to help. We employed thematic analysis in exploring the responses and constructed five themes: (i) Perceived safety and risk; (ii) Bystander characteristics, knowledge and understanding; (iii) Perceived target need; (iv) Presence of other people and (v) Suggested bystander action. We discuss the results with a reference bystander literature, relating it to the specific context of street harassment.

items.title: The barriers and facilitators to accessing eating disorder treatment for individuals with bulimia nervosa and binge eating disorder: a systematic review and meta-synthesis.
items.abstract: This systematic review aimed to synthesise qualitative literature on the barriers and facilitators to accessing eating disorder (ED) treatment for individuals with Bulimia Nervosa (BN) and Binge Eating Disorder (BED). Searches were performed on PsychINFO, EMBASE, MEDLINE, Scopus, ASSIA and CINAHL. Included studies were appraised using the CASP qualitative checklist, and thematic synthesis was used to analyse the data. GRADE CERQual was utilised to assess confidence in the findings. Twelve studies were identified and were considered to be adequate. The synthesis produced five main themes: 'Invisibility and Illegitimacy of (Some) EDs', 'Treatment Ambivalence', 'Stigma and Shame', 'Systemic and Structural Barriers', and 'Conditions that Facilitate Access to Treatment'. Findings were rated from moderate to high confidence. Improving treatment access requires stigma-informed care, enhanced clinician training, inclusive public health messaging, and services tailored to diverse needs. A consistent barrier was low problem recognition and symptom minimisation underpinned by cultural and societal misconceptions about EDs.

items.title: Parental coping and child psychosocial adaptation in pediatric Wilson disease.
items.abstract: Objectives Pediatric data on psychosocial adaptation in Wilson disease remain limited. In particular, the relationship between parental psychosocial functioning and child quality of life and adaptation is still insufficiently understood. Methods This cross-sectional study included 50 children with Wilson disease and one parent of each child. Children completed the Revised Children's Quality of Life Questionnaire (KINDL-R) and the JSR coping questionnaire. Parents completed the General Health Questionnaire-28 (GHQ-28), Brief Coping Orientation to Problems Experienced (Brief COPE), Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS), and the Child Behavior Checklist (CBCL). Canonical correlation analysis was used to examine multivariate associations between child and parent variable sets. Results The full canonical model was statistically significant, and five canonical functions were extracted; however, only the first function reached statistical significance (Rc = 0.802, Wilks' λ = 0.202, p = 0.001). This function linked parental problem-focused, emotion-focused, and avoidance coping, together with general psychological distress, with child dispositional active, social, and emotion-focused coping, total quality of life, and, to a lesser extent, internalizing problems. Redundancy indices supported the practical interpretability of the identified parent-child psychosocial pattern. Conclusions Psychosocial adaptation in children with Wilson disease appears to be meaningfully related to parental psychosocial functioning, particularly parental coping patterns and general psychological distress. These findings support a family-oriented approach to psychosocial assessment and care in pediatric Wilson disease.
