items.title: Protein palmitoylation in disease: decoding its crosstalk with ubiquitination and phosphorylation for pathogenic mechanisms and targeted therapeutics.
items.abstract: Protein S-palmitoylation is a reversible lipid modification that governs protein stability, trafficking, and signaling. Rather than an isolated tag, it acts as a spatiotemporal routing signal within an integrated post-translational modification (PTM) network, engaging in three defined crosstalk modes with ubiquitination and phosphorylation: synergistic, antagonistic, and cascading. Although crosstalk with acetylation and myristoylation exists, this review focuses on the ubiquitination- and phosphorylation-centered networks most directly linked to palmitoylation in disease. The same palmitoylation event can stabilize or destabilize substrates, or activate or silence signaling, depending on the specific Zinc finger DHHC domain-containing protein (ZDHHC) isoform, subcellular location, local enzyme availability, and metabolic state. We further introduce the "PTM context signature", a four-variable predictive framework for disease-specific crosstalk outcomes. By dissecting palmitoylation-centered crosstalk through a disease-oriented lens, we examine how its dysregulation drives oncogenesis, inflammation, metabolic disorders, and neurodegeneration. We then translate these mechanistic principles into a network-centric therapeutic framework, evaluating ZDHHC-directed modulators, peptide-based interface disruptors, and crosstalk-informed combinations that target context-specific nodes and anticipate therapy resistance. Viewing palmitoylation as an integrated component of the cellular PTM network, rather than as an isolated lipid tag, provides a framework for understanding disease pathogenesis and for targeting PTM networks rather than single modifications.

items.title: Uncovering intergenic DNA i-motifs in the telomere-to-telomere human genome.
items.abstract: Noncanonical DNA structures such as i-motifs (iMs) are emerging as versatile functional elements within the human genome, yet their distribution and properties outside regulatory regions remain poorly characterized. Leveraging the complete telomere-to-telomere (T2T-CHM13) genome assembly, we generated an updated genome-wide catalogue of putative iM-forming sequences by implementing a bioinformatics pipeline for the systematic detection and statistical assessment of cytosine-rich motifs consistent with canonical iM-forming patterns. The analysis identified 789,952 candidates, representing a 6.39% increase over our previous hg38-based catalogue. Sequence-level comparison showed that 707,333 candidates (89.54%) had an identical sequence on the same chromosome and strand in the hg38-derived candidate set, whereas 82,619 (10.46%) were T2T-unmatched under these criteria. From this dataset, we focused on two distal-intergenic candidates selected to represent different positions within the T2T-CHM13 intergenic PSSM-score distribution and contrasting sequence architectures. The two candidates were characterized through an integrated biophysical workflow combining circular dichroism spectroscopy, UV absorption analyses (including thermal and isothermal difference spectra), nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, and size-exclusion chromatography. Both sequences adopted canonical iM folds under mildly acidic conditions (pH ≤ 6.25), displaying reversible, pH-dependent folding and distinct thermodynamic transitions. Despite similar lengths, the two iMs exhibited distinct stability and pH responsiveness, which could be rationalized by differences in cytosine density, C-tract organization, and loop architecture. Overall, this study provides a comprehensive set of iMs candidates within the T2T-CHM13 assembly, and it defines key structural and thermodynamic features of intergenic iMs.

items.title: Genetic GHSR deficiency and LEAP2 treatment enhance the glucose-lowering effects of liraglutide in male mice in a metabolic state-dependent manner.
items.abstract: Liraglutide is a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor (GLP-1R) agonist that lowers glycemia and is used to treat type 2 diabetes (T2D) and obesity. Activation of the growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHSR) increases glycemia. We aimed to determine whether GHSR inhibition enhances the glucose-lowering effects of liraglutide. We investigated the acute glucose-lowering effects of liraglutide in mice with genetic GHSR deletion or pharmacological GHSR blockade under fed, fasting, and postprandial conditions. We also examined the potential cellular basis of this interaction in murine islets using transcriptomic and immunolabeling approaches and in human pancreatic tissue using a publicly available transcriptomic dataset. Liraglutide similarly reduced glycemia in ad libitum-fed GHSR-null and control mice. Following food deprivation, liraglutide more effectively attenuated postprandial increases in glycemia in male, but not female, GHSR-null mice than in control mice. Liraglutide reduced glycemia in fasted GHSR-null male mice but not in WT males. In male mice, pretreatment with a LEAP2 (liver-expressed antimicrobial peptide 2) analog, an endogenous GHSR antagonist and inverse agonist, enhanced the glucose-lowering effects of liraglutide under postprandial and fasting conditions. GHSR and GLP-1R showed limited co-expression in murine islets. In human islets, their co-expression was also limited and enriched in δ-cells, but was also detected in β-cells, where the proportion of GHSR+/GLP-1R+ cells was higher in donors with T2D. GHSR inhibition enhances liraglutide's glucose-lowering effects in a sex-dependent manner, highlighting GHSR as a potential target to improve GLP-1R agonist efficacy.

items.title: I See What You Taste: The Influence of Social Learning on Food Acceptance in Children.
items.abstract: Picky eating is common in childhood and characterized by limited diet quality. Because children acquire food preferences partly through social learning, such as observing others' expressive responses to food, this study examined whether children's ability to interpret taste cues, food-related social cues, and general facial emotions are associated with picky eating and a proxy of fruit and vegetable (FV) consumption. A total of 273 child-parent pairs were recruited at the NEMO Science Museum in Amsterdam. Parents reported on their own picky eating and their child's picky eating. Skin carotenoid measurements were used as a proxy of FV intake in both children and parents. Children completed one general task assessing facial emotion recognition and three eating-related tasks assessing basic taste strip identification, recognition of tastes from others' facial expressions, and social modeling. Parental picky eating and the proxy of FV intake were positively related to the corresponding child measures. Poorer identification of basic tastes was associated with higher levels of child picky eating, even after controlling for parental picky eating and parental FV intake proxy. Facial emotion recognition and recognition of tastes via others' facial expressions were not associated with child picky eating or child FV intake proxy. In the social modeling task, most children selected food paired with a positive facial expression; however, this choice was unrelated to facial emotion recognition, child picky eating, or child FV intake proxy. Together, these findings suggest that picky eating in children is related to poorer taste identification rather than to difficulties in recognizing facial expressions. Longitudinal studies are needed to determine whether these findings are consistent over time, after which interventions targeting taste-related processing or taste-related uncertainty could be considered.

items.title: Remak bundle size, structure, and function are regulated by the Schwann cell basal lamina.
items.abstract: Remak bundles are groups of small-diameter unmyelinated nociceptive axons ensheathed by Schwann cells (SCs). Whereas the development and maturation of myelinating SCs have been extensively studied, the formation of Remak bundles remains poorly understood. By preventing the secretion of type IV collagen from SCs, we observe normal myelin but abnormal Remak bundles. There is a decrease in Remak bundle density, an increase in bundle size, improperly ensheathed axons, and a decrease in mechanosensitivity. While Remak bundle formation appears to be independent of integrin signaling, the loss of type IV collagen leads to a decrease in postnatal SC proliferation. Inducing the emergence of supernumerary SCs rescues Remak bundle architecture and mechanosensitivity. Taken together, our results demonstrate that SC-secreted basal lamina critically regulates Remak SC number, bundle size, and structure. Our findings provide insight into the functional role of Remak bundles and highlight their potential involvement in peripheral neuropathies and neuropathic pain.

items.title: Modeling somatic mutations associated with neurodevelopmental disorders using mosaic human brain organoids and assembloids.
items.abstract: Somatic mosaicism, the presence of genetically distinct cell populations within a single individual, has emerged as a key driver of human brain diversity and pathology. Originally associated with focal epilepsies and malformations of cortical development, recent evidence shows that somatic mutations can also contribute to neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative diseases. High-throughput sequencing and single-cell multi-omics have revealed that the brain is a landscape of clonal expansions and somatic variants. To model the functional consequences of these mutations, new approaches are needed. This review focuses on emerging approaches that use human brain organoids and assembloids to model mosaic brain tissue and investigate cell-autonomous and non-cell-autonomous effects of genetic variants.

items.title: Evaluating the impact of intraoperative neuromonitoring on neurological outcomes and extent of resection in pediatric supratentorial brain tumor surgery: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: Surgical resection of pediatric supratentorial brain tumors requires balancing maximal tumor removal with preservation of neurological function. Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) methodologies and indications are well-established in adults but remain understudied in children, whose developing brains pose unique challenges. This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluates the impact IONM on extent of tumor resection and postoperative neurological deficits in pediatric supratentorial brain tumor surgery. A systematic review of studies was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO ID: CRD420251101609). Studies published between January 1990, and June 2025 were included. Data were pooled using a random-effects model, and heterogeneity was assessed with I2 statistics. A total of 41 studies comprising 1,908 pediatric patients were included. The pooled gross total resection (GTR) rate was 76.9% (95% CI: 69.1-82.6) in the monitored group, compared with 52.8% (95% CI: 45.2-60.4) in the unmonitored group. The pooled incidence of postoperative neurological deficits was 15.1% (95% CI: 8.7-22.8) in the monitored group and 23.1% (95% CI: 12.4-38.8) in the unmonitored group. Stratified analyses showed that eloquent cortex involvement was associated with lower GTR rates and higher neurological deficits; however, these associations appeared less pronounced in monitored cohorts. These descriptive pooled estimates suggest that IONM may be associated with higher GTR rates and lower postoperative neurological deficit rates in pediatric supratentorial brain tumor surgery, particularly in eloquent brain regions. However, because the included studies did not directly compare monitored and unmonitored patients within the same cohorts, these findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a causal benefit of IONM. Rather, they provide a foundation for future prospective comparative studies to evaluate the potential impact of IONM and to develop pediatric-specific protocols aimed at preserving long-term neurological function.

items.title: From one risky choice to the next: Trait dominance, feedback, and response-locked EEG in corporate leaders.
items.abstract: Repeated risky choice can reflect both the direction of choice and whether a previous choice is repeated, but these patterns are not always distinguished in research on trait dominance. In this secondary analysis, 28 male corporate leaders completed a repeated monetary gambling task with complete feedback while EEG was recorded. Mixed-effects models examined associations of trait dominance, choice history, and feedback with subsequent High-risk choice, Stay/Switch behavior, response time, and response-locked FCz activity. Higher dominance was associated with greater odds of choosing High after both previous High- and Low-risk choices, with no reliable difference between the two history-specific associations. In the direct transition model, a 1-SD increase in continuous dominance corresponded to 47% higher odds of Current High choice (OR = 1.47, 95% CI [1.25, 1.73]). On the Stay/Switch scale, higher dominance predicted staying after High but switching after Low, indicating a High-directed pattern rather than uniformly greater repetition of the preceding risk level. Recent outcomes also remained consequential: absolute valence and comparative favorability were associated with subsequent choice, and responses were 12.7% slower after Gains than Losses, whereas dominance was not reliably related to response time. EEG findings were more qualified: mean FCz voltage was more positive in the predefined High-dominance group, whereas peak latency showed a feedback-dependent dominance contrast between Gain-Correct and Gain-Error trials; no individual condition-specific dominance slope survived Holm correction. Trait dominance was therefore associated most clearly with the direction of repeated risky choice, while recent experience continued to shape the next decision.

items.title: FlyBase: Development and metamorphosis into the Alliance.
items.abstract: FlyBase (flybase.org) is an openly accessible, centralized resource for genetic, genomic and functional data about Drosophila melanogaster. Finally, we give an update on the status of transitioning FlyBase into the Alliance of Genome Resources.

items.title: Generative Large Language Models for Psychiatric Concept Detection in Spanish-Language Electronic Health Records: Development and Evaluation Study.
items.abstract: The accurate detection of clinical symptoms in electronic health records (EHRs) is pivotal for advancing large-scale genetic and longitudinal studies in psychiatry. Free-text clinical notes are an essential source of symptom-level information, particularly in psychiatry; however, the automated extraction of symptoms from clinical text remains challenging. We aimed to evaluate the ability of open-source generative large language models (LLMs) to detect psychiatric symptom-level concepts from clinical text in Spanish and to develop a new fine-tuned, open-source LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information. We tested 11 open-source generative LLMs for their ability to detect 109 psychiatric concepts from clinical text, using annotated EHR notes from a psychiatric hospital in Colombia. The LLMs were evaluated both "out-of-the-box" and after fine-tuning and compared against a traditional natural language processing (tNLP) method developed from the same data. To develop a fine-tuned LLM that can be shared without risk of exposing patient information, we created a novel synthetic dataset, leveraging real concept annotations while generating fully synthetic clinical text, and fine-tuned a top-performing LLM on these data. Fine-tuned model generalizability was assessed through cross-site evaluation using data from a second independent hospital in Colombia. We show that while base LLM performance was poor to moderate (zero-shot: 0.2-0.6 macro-F1; few-shot: 0.2-0.74 macro-F1), it improved significantly after fine-tuning (0.75-0.86 macro-F1), with several fine-tuned LLMs outperforming the tNLP method. In total, 100 psychiatric concepts could be reliably detected (F1>0.8) using either a fine-tuned LLM or tNLP. Using the synthetic dataset, we developed Mistral-small-psych, a new LLM capable of detecting psychiatric concepts from Spanish clinical text with performance comparable to models trained on real EHR data (macro-F1=0.79) while remaining fully distributable. In cross-site evaluations, most LLMs generalized well, with small out-of-domain performance losses (macro-F1 decrease of 0.02-0.16). This work provides the first large-scale, cross-institutional evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs for psychiatric concept detection in Spanish EHRs, introduces a privacy-preserving pathway for building shareable clinical natural language processing models, and presents a new open model for extracting symptom-level psychiatric information from Spanish clinical text.

items.title: Stronger mnemonic prediction errors can disproportionately impair memory updating in older adults.
items.abstract: Mnemonic prediction errors are discrepancies between memory-based expectations and actual events that can trigger memory updating. However, the conditions under which these prediction errors result in successful memory updating, and whether these effects vary between younger and older adults, remain less understood. In two experiments, the present study investigated how prediction strength affects memory for events that violated memory-based expectations in younger and older adults. Prediction strength was manipulated by first presenting three-word sequences (i.e., trains), each with exemplars from the same category (Bluejay-Hawk-Eagle), either once or four times. Predictions based on memory for trains were then confirmed by repeating sequences entirely (Bluejay-Hawk-Eagle) or violated by repeating the first two words and changing the ending word (Bluejay-Hawk-Robin). Differences in prediction strength, created by varying repetitions, were validated using retrospective judgments (Experiment 1) and prospective predictions of original train endings along with confidence ratings (Experiment 2). Prediction error effects on memory updating were assessed by presenting the first two words of trains as cues for recalling changed ending words. Stronger predictions impaired memory for changed endings disproportionately for older adults, and older adults were less able to recollect that endings had changed when asked directly. Regardless of prediction strength and age, change recollection was consistently associated with better memory for changed ending words. Collectively, these findings suggest that stronger mnemonic predictions exacerbate the negative impact of prediction errors on the resolution of proactive interference, an ability that is often impaired in healthy aging. items.title: Listeners expect grammatical variation across dialects.
items.abstract: Dialect variation is universally attested among languages, yet the cognitive processes underlying listeners' adaptations to different dialects, particularly in morphosyntactic variation, remain underexplored. This article investigates how listeners represent and adapt to their interlocutor's dialect based on their linguistic experience, examining monodialectal speakers of Dominant American English and bidialectal speakers of Dominant American English and African American Language. In Experiment 1, participants rated written sentences to indicate the likelihood that a speaker of a given dialect would say them. All participants demonstrated knowledge of African American Language's regularized subject-verb agreement rules, rating sentences like "They was happy" as more likely than "He were happy." However, bidialectal participants showed greater differentiation between the sentences than monodialectal participants. This finding suggests that listeners do not simply relax grammatical expectations when exposed to linguistic diversity; rather, they form specific expectations of a dialect's grammatical rules. In Experiment 2, we tested whether these expectations influence perception. Participants transcribed sentences where agreement was acoustically ambiguous ("She sit[s] still"). Participants were more likely to transcribe regularized subject-verb agreement ("She sit still") when listening to an African American Language speaker compared to a Dominant American English speaker, regardless of their linguistic experience. Bidialectal participants were more likely to transcribe regularized subject-verb agreement overall. In Experiment 3, we found that such effect patterns were likely driven by morphosyntactic cues, rather than social cues to the race of the speaker. These results suggest that listeners form mental models of others' grammars to guide comprehension, with the precision of these models depending on their linguistic experience. items.title: FMRI-guided focal transcranial magnetic stimulation of anterior cingulate cortex reduces opioid seeking and restores connectivity.
items.abstract: Relapse remains a major challenge in opioid addiction treatment. Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has emerged as a potential therapeutic strategy for addiction, yet results had been mixed due to empirically selected stimulation targets and limited knowledge of neural circuit engagement. Here, we used a focal rat TMS platform to test whether high-density theta-burst stimulation (hdTBS) of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), a corticostriatal node implicated in opioid relapse by prior causal and longitudinal functional MRI studies, decreases relapse-like oxycodone seeking and associated circuit dysfunction. Male rats self-administered oxycodone intravenously for 14 d and then underwent 13 d of electric barrier-induced abstinence, a procedure that suppresses drug taking while preserving drug availability and drug-associated context. During abstinence, the rats received seven daily sessions of sham stimulation or ACC-targeted hdTBS, with relapse tests and longitudinal functional MRI acquired during early and late abstinence to assess the behavioral and circuit-level effects of stimulation. Sham-treated rats showed a time-dependent increase (incubation) in oxycodone seeking and reduced ACC connectivity with dorsal and ventral striatum. In contrast, ACC-targeted hdTBS prevented incubation of oxycodone seeking and reversed abstinence-associated ACC-striatal connectivity reductions. Stimulation-sensitive functional circuits showed spatial correspondence with tracer-defined ACC projection patterns, suggesting that anatomical connectivity is critical to the circuit-level effects of focal stimulation. These findings support ACC-centered corticostriatal circuits as mechanistically informed targets for neuromodulation in opioid addiction and introduce a preclinical framework for linking stimulation, behavior, and longitudinal circuit remodeling.

items.title: Open source laser-scanning photostimulation for neuroscience with Zapit.
items.abstract: Optogenetic tools are indispensable for understanding the causal neural mechanisms underlying animal behavior, providing millisecond-precision control over genetically defined neural populations. Random-access laser-scanning optogenetics is a powerful and underutilized method for transiently manipulating cortical activity in mice. Despite the utility of this technique, no general-purpose open-source implementation currently exists, and potential users need expertise across optics, real-time hardware control, and programming. This represents a major barrier to adoption, particularly for newly established research groups. Here we present 'Zapit', the first open-source general-purpose platform for random-access laser-scanning optogenetic experiments in head-fixed mice. Zapit is fully documented, has a user-friendly GUI, works in stereotaxic coordinates, and comes with easy-to-build hardware options that extend functionality beyond any published system. We validate Zapit's performance through electrophysiological recordings and cortical photoinhibition in behaving mice. Zapit is a novel and innovative tool with the potential to democratize laser-scanning optogenetics and significantly increase uptake throughout the scientific community.

items.title: An integrative computational approach for obstacle avoidance during action selection.
items.abstract: Action selection in cluttered environments, where individuals must simultaneously pursue goals and avoid obstacles, presents a significant challenge for the brain. To understand the underlying mechanisms of action selection in such contexts, we propose a computational model that extends stochastic optimal control theory through a novel framework for obstacle avoidance. The model decomposes action selection into a weighted combination of individual control policies, each generated for either target approach or obstacle avoidance. By integrating value information from goals, obstacles, and actions into a unified measure of "relative desirability", the model dynamically determines the contribution of each policy to the overall action selection process. We evaluated the framework using simulated target-reaching tasks in cluttered environments based on previous human studies. The results showed that the model qualitatively captures key features of human motor behavior, including the influence of obstacle properties on movement trajectories and the transient tendency to initiate movements toward obstacles before avoidance.This work offers new insights into the dynamic interaction between approach and avoidance behaviors, providing a basis for future studies of action selection in more complex and naturalistic settings.

items.title: Temporal resolution shapes inferred higher-order interactions and information representation in neural population activity: A data-driven approach using minimally complex models.
items.abstract: Studying limited datasets derived from complex interacting systems, such as neural population activity, represents an important and challenging task. The level of detail in recorded activities is highly influenced by the temporal resolution at which the activities are studied. However, does more detail always lead to a correct assessment of the system? This study examines how temporal resolution influences the inference of higher-order statistical dependencies and information representation in population-level neuronal activity. Using a minimally biased data-driven statistical inference framework, minimally complex models, we studied grid cell populations in the medial entorhinal cortex across a broad range of temporal resolutions. Results based on 23 grid cell recordings including different animals and behavioral states show that at an intermediate temporal resolution (𝒪(102) ms), the inferred model captures significant higher order dependencies alongside efficient information representations, whereas the finest and the coarsest temporal resolutions lead to poor information representation. The informative temporal resolution can be identified by two criteria: the bin size at which the inferred interaction structure is most consistent across population sizes, and the peak of the model's information representations, which agree closely across recordings. These findings indicate that temporal resolution is a critical factor in the inference of higher order neural structure and highlight that resolution-aware modeling is crucial for accurate analysis and characterization of collective dynamics in complex neuronal systems.

items.title: From raw to scaled human spinal cord morphometry: An original system for identifying complex anatomical patterns.
items.abstract: Understanding the segmental anatomy of the human spinal cord remains challenging due to its interindividual variability and the lack of standardized definition of a spinal cord segment. In this human cadaveric study, we dissected 40 spinal cords, identified and measured the length, thickness and width of each segment comprised between C2 to S5. This extensive dataset enabled us to characterize the distribution and variability of the measurements, as well as to conduct ratio and correlation analyses. By converting segment length measurements into an original coordinate system, and thickness and width values into scaled data relative to easily identified anatomical features, we showed that L4 and C6 can be considered relevant landmarks of the cadaveric SC. We also divided the sample into three subgroups according to the total SC length: a short group (n = 9), an intermediate group (n = 15), and a long group (n = 16). This distinction revealed unexpected morphological features regarding the transverse dimensions, showing that variations in total SC length did not result in proportional changes in average segment thickness or width. Overall, these new morphometric findings highlight the gross morphological complexity of a generally oversimplified structure and provide additional anatomical landmarks, improving our understanding of SC cadaveric anatomy.

items.title: A well-resolved phylogeny of Cuscuta subgenus Monogynella based on data drawn from all three plant genomes.
items.abstract: Cuscuta (dodders) consists of ~200 species circumscribed into four subgenera (Monogynella, Cuscuta, Pachystigma, and Grammica) and is the only parasitic genus in Convolvulaceae (the morning-glory family). This group shows a significant diversity in plastid functionality and represents a rare mixotrophic system among parasitic plants. Apart from a few placeholders in broadscale phylogenies, subg. Monogynella had not been extensively examined until a recent molecular systematics study. Despite this effort, a few lineages still remained poorly resolved and some backbone relationships lacked support. To obtain greater resolution and support for the phylogeny alongside studying the effect of hemiparasitism on different organellar genomes, we selected 31 samples, chosen to represent the phylogenetic diversity of each clade, and sequenced them using high-throughput sequencing. We assembled plastid genomes and retrieved mitochondrial genes and nuclear ribosomal arrays (NRAs) for phylogenomic analyses. Plastomes in this subgenus show similar lengths and gene composition and retain the bulk of photosynthesis genes. About 33 mitochondrial genes were recovered from assemblies and are more conserved in comparison to plastid genes. In addition, complete NRAs were also found to be well maintained. The members of subg. Monogynella show no evidence of hybridization. Trees obtained from all three matrices corroborate previously published molecular phylogenies with increased resolution and backbone support across the board. These results characterize the state of the organellar genomes and particularly plastomes in subg. Monogynella, bridging the gap in this field of study of Cuscuta and allowing us to compare these patterns across other heterotrophic lineages.

items.title: Following the rules? Different thermal and temporal life-stage responses of biometrics across four decades in a songbird population.
items.abstract: Global warming is widely associated with changes in body size and shape, with these variations typically framed within the context of Bergmann, Allen and the Temperature-Size rules. However, evaluating phenotypic change only against these rules can limit our understanding of how immediate plastic reactions to temperature interact with long-term trends. Also, phenotypic responses may differ among life stages, due to their different thermal sensitivity and life-history role. We examined body size and shape variations across life stages in a Mediterranean great tit (Parus major) population monitored over four decades, during which mean annual temperatures increased by approximately 1.7°C. Adults were the life stage most responsive to temperature and their mass declined by 0.84% for every 1°C of warming, while wing length shortened. Instead, tarsus length, a measure of structural size, increased with temperature in both nestlings and adults at a comparable magnitude, consistent with Allen's rule. Nestling mass near fledging showed no thermal response. Among reproductive traits, clutch size tended to decrease with temperature without reaching statistical significance and egg mass showed no thermal response, yet total clutch mass, an integrated measure of reproductive output, declined significantly with warmer laying temperatures. Long-term temporal trends did not consistently mirror these thermal effects. Adult mass declined across the study period, matching the direction of its thermal response, whereas adult tarsus length shortened over time despite lengthening with temperature. Wing length and nestling mass both remained stable. Egg mass declined and clutch size increased across the study period, despite their lack of thermal response. These results demonstrate that while warming can proximately affect body size, long-term temporal trends can be decoupled from immediate thermal effects, and that mass and structural size do not necessarily vary together. This creates an underappreciated mosaic of phenotypic responses across life stages and generations, with potential consequences for fecundity, morphology and fitness. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating ontogenetic perspectives into evolutionary ecogeographic theory and raise questions about which 'rules' will govern the trajectories of avian populations under climate change.

items.title: Other effective area-based conservation measures may enhance global conservation networks.
items.abstract: Other effective area-based conservation measures (OECMs) are expected to have a crucial role in achieving the global ambition to protect 30% of the planet by 2030. While the number of OECMs is growing rapidly, their contribution to systems of conservation areas remains unclear. Here, to fill this gap, we developed a typology of the structural roles OECMs can play in conservation networks-enlarging, connecting, buffering and aggregating protected areas (PAs), and quantified their contributions using spatial data for 6,234 OECMs reported across 14 countries. We found nearly one-third of OECMs directly adjoin and enlarge PAs, while a smaller subset (~3%) connect or buffer isolated PAs or aggregate fragmented PAs. Although OECMs currently make limited contributions to increasing connectivity, two-thirds of OECMs lie less than 10 km from a PA, providing opportunities to consolidate conservation networks in the future. Our analysis provides a global assessment of how OECMs strengthen conservation networks and offers simple, policy-relevant insights into how to maximize the benefits of area-based conservation as countries pursue the 30 × 30 target.

items.title: A fully marine stem amphibian from the Late Triassic of China.
items.abstract: Land vertebrates colonized the sea repeatedly through geologic time with various levels of marine adaptation, from partial use of marine resources to fully marine lifestyles. Mammals, reptiles and birds all have species that survive without food or fresh water from land; however, amphibians, including both crown and stem species, lack such a member partly because of their salt-intolerant skins. Here we report the first fully marine species of a stem amphibian, Gerrothorax maritimus n. sp., based on two nearly complete skeletons from the Late Triassic (about 237 million years ago). Its articulated occurrence far from land, together with associated strontium isotope record, suggests life in fully marine regimes. It descended from a lineage with complete body armour, which would limit skin-based water, gas or salt exchanges typical of amphibians and instead enforced the use of the gill and gut that can become more tolerant of salt-this probably prepared them for marine adaptation.

items.title: Quantitative imaging supports that endoskeletal mineralization in sharks is an adaptive trait.
items.abstract: Modern sharks (Selachimorpha) exhibit a broad suite of adaptations that enable them to inhabit diverse marine environments. Notably, their cartilaginous endoskeleton displays varying degrees of mineralization, potentially reflecting adaptations for buoyancy, locomotion, and feeding. Here, quantitative computed tomography was applied to assess endoskeletal mineralization in representatives from all nine orders of sharks spanning 26 out of 35 families. Our findings reveal that skeletal mineralization is highly variable between species and is more closely associated with ecological factors such as depth distribution, than with phylogenetic relationship. We find that deeper-dwelling species generally exhibit lower degrees of mineralization, suggesting adaptations for buoyancy regulation and energy conservation. Our study provides insight into the variation of skeletal mineralization in the ecology and evolution of sharks.

items.title: Reconstructing Cenozoic grasslands in North America and western Eurasia: evidence for cold-season grasses from 3D phytolith morphology.
items.abstract: Pooideae, the largest grass subfamily, radiated in the Northern Hemisphere from the Paleocene onward and today dominates cold-season and high-altitude grasslands. Fossil phytolith assemblages suggest pooid-rich ecosystems during the Oligocene-Miocene, but the lack of quantitative phytolith identification has limited reconstruction of early grassland composition and ecology. We combined 3D geometric morphometrics of grass silica short-cell phytoliths (GSSCPs) with machine-learning classification and phylogenetically informed climate modelling. A dataset of modern GSSCPs was used to classify Eocene-Miocene phytoliths from Türkiye and the US Great Plains and reconstruct paleoclimate. 3D GSSCP morphology distinguished modern grass subfamilies and tribes. Fossil assemblages contained mainly phytoliths assigned to Bambusoideae and Pooideae (including Poeae I and II). In modern grasses, Crenate and Polylobate phytolith dimensions correlated with temperature and precipitation. Fossil Crenates and Polylobates yielded climate estimates warmer and wetter than today. Ancestral state reconstructions indicated milder winter conditions at early Pooideae nodes, with cold tolerance arising early. Major temperate grass lineages (Poeae I and II) were established earlier than previously recognized, and Pooideae-rich grasslands were present by the Oligo-Miocene under warmer, wetter climates than today. These findings demonstrate the value of 3D phytolith morphometrics for interpreting early grassland evolution.

items.title: Entamoeba invadens infection contributes to juvenile mortality in captive sea turtles.
items.abstract: Sea turtles are globally threatened marine reptiles, and infectious diseases are increasingly recognized as important causes of juvenile mortality. However, the etiology and pathogenesis of many diseases, including amoebiasis, remain poorly understood. Systemic amoebic lesions have been reported in sea turtles, yet the causative Entamoeba species has never been identified at the species level using molecular methods. We therefore investigated the etiology and pathogenesis of fatal amoebiasis using carcasses of 15 captive juvenile sea turtles (three loggerhead, Caretta caretta, and 12 green turtles, Chelonia mydas), integrating histopathological and molecular approaches. Histopathology revealed severe necrotizing enteritis, hepatitis, and pneumonia with abundant amoebic trophozoites and cysts. Polymerase chain reaction, Sanger sequencing, and in situ hybridization identified Entamoeba invadens in the intestine, liver, and lungs; 18S rRNA amplicon sequencing also detected E. invadens in fecal and intestinal samples. Phylogenetic analysis showed that the sea turtle-derived sequence clustered with E. invadens sequences from other reptile hosts. Bacterial and fungal aggregates were also observed within necrotic lesions, and 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing detected diverse bacterial communities without a consistently dominant taxon, consistent with secondary microbial translocation following intestinal barrier disruption rather than primary bacterial infection. These findings provide the first evidence that E. invadens causes fatal systemic amoebiasis in juvenile sea turtles and are consistent with polymicrobial invasion following parasite-induced intestinal damage. This study establishes a pathological and molecular basis for diagnosing systemic amoebiasis in sea turtles and has important implications for wildlife disease ecology and sea turtle conservation.

items.title: Long-term effect of low ciprofloxacin concentration on nitrogen removal performance, enzymatic activity, microbial community and antibiotic resistance gene of sequencing batch reactor.
items.abstract: Ciprofloxacin usually exists at low concentration in surface water and wastewater. In this research, the nitrogen removal, enzymatic activity, antioxidant response, microbial succession, functional gene and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) of sequencing batch reactor were investigated under long-term exposure of 100 μg/L ciprofloxacin. The NH4+-N removal efficiency almost unchanged during 188-day operation. However, the ammonia-oxidizing rate, nitrite-oxidizing rate, nitrate-reducing rate and nitrite-reducing rate decreased by 17.34 %, 18.38 %, 24.98 % and 38.81 % on day 188 by comparison with 0 µg/L ciprofloxacin, respectively. Similarly, the activities of ammonia monooxygenase, nitrite oxidoreductase, nitrate reductase and nitrite reductase decreased by 25.76 %, 27.79 %, 30.65 % and 39.81 %, respectively. The increase of antioxidant enzymatic activity under long-term ciprofloxacin stress eliminated excess reactive oxygen species to alleviate oxidative damage. The relative abundances of Nitrosomonas, Nitrosospira, Nitrobacter and Nitrospina decreased with the increase of operation time. The relative abundances of nitrogen-removal key genes (e.g., amoA, nxrA, narG and nosZ) decreased with the increase of operation time, as well as the key enzymes in TCA cycle with their encoding genes. The total abundance of the top 30 ARGs increased by 7.57-fold by comparison with 0 µg/L ciprofloxacin, especially for efflux pump genes. The enrichment of ARG-encoded efflux pumps and antioxidant defense competed for the limited electrons and ATP, which led to an energy/electron trade-off with nitrogen metabolism. The present results are helpful to deeply understand the linkage among the nitrogen removal, microbial community and resistance genes under long-term exposure of low antibiotic concentration.

items.title: UV-aged tire wear particles and their leachates jointly enhance antibiotic resistance gene dissemination.
items.abstract: Tire wear particles (TWPs) represent a major source of environmental microplastics, yet how ultraviolet (UV) aging influences their effects on the transfer of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) remains unclear. Here, the promoting effects and underlying mechanisms of UV-aged TWPs and their leachate on bacterial conjugative transfer were investigated. Aging significantly increased the specific surface area and oxygen-containing functional groups of TWPs, and promoted the release of heavy metal ions and organic additives into leachate. In conjugation assays, 60-day-aged TWPs enhanced the transfer frequency of plasmid RP4 by 15.3-fold; whereas the corresponding leachate alone caused a 62.0-fold increase. Mechanistically, aged TWPs acted primarily as a physical oxidative stressor, promoting conjugative transfer through reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation and disruption of cell membrane integrity. Aged leachate acted mainly as a chemical signaling stressor, inducing biofilm formation and collective behavioral responses that created a protective microenvironment conducive to plasmid exchange, although they also contributed to oxidative stress. Combined exposure further produced a response greater than that of either pathway alone, establishing a physicochemical dual-stress framework that drives ARGs transfer. Collectively, these findings suggest that environmental aging critically shapes the ecological risks of microplastics, positioning aged TWPs as potential vectors for ARGs dissemination and underscoring the need to consider both particle-associated and leachate-mediated pathways in future risk assessments.

items.title: Glycosylation and Glucuronidation Metabolisms of Tetrabromobisphenol A Show the Opposite Effects on Transintestinal Barrier Transport in Human.
items.abstract: Tetrabromobisphenol A (TBBPA), a widely used brominated flame retardant, poses potential environmental and health risks. Glycosylation and glucuronidation are ubiquitous metabolic modifications in organisms. Through these processes, TBBPA could produce derivatives sharing the same skeleton but with various substitutions. The structure-activity relationship underlying their differential intestinal transport and absorption is an interesting issue. This study investigated the intestinal absorption, metabolism, and transport of TBBPA, and two derivatives with different degrees of glycosylation, TBBPA di-β-d-glucoside (TBBPA DG) and TBBPA mono-β-d-glucoside (TBBPA MG), using in vitro Caco-2 cell model. The intestinal absorption and metabolism degree followed the order of TBBPA>>TBBPA DG≈TBBPA MG. The occurrence of glucose moieties significantly (p<0.001) reduced intestinal uptake and metabolism. The distributions of metabolites of corresponding parent compounds also varied: TBBPA DG' metabolites mostly remained in the apical chamber (84.6%), representing the lumen, TBBPA's predominantly entered the basolateral chamber (76.0%), representing the bloodstream, and TBBPA MG's showed an intermediate pattern (42.6% apical chamber vs. 48.3% basolateral chamber). Importantly, glucuronidated metabolites were preferentially transported to basolateral chamber, likely due to strong binding to the membrane transporter, as suggested by molecular docking. These findings elucidate the structure-dependent intestinal fate of TBBPA and its derivatives and provide direct evidence that glucuronidation metabolism enhances the transintestinal barrier transport of TBBPA and its derivatives in humans. This highlights that intestinal metabolism, rather than absorption alone, dictates the form and quantity of compounds entering systemic circulation.

items.title: Potential influence of landscape structure on water quality and phytoplankton community in highly degraded urban lakes: Implications for restoration.
items.abstract: Urban lakes are of particular concern in urban landscapes, as they provide ecological, social and economic benefits, but are under strong human pressure. The current study examined eleven urban lakes that differ in their morphometric and hydrological characteristics and were located across various macroregions of Poland. The aim was to examine potential relationships among landscape structure, water quality, and phytoplankton communities across three buffer zones (10 m, 100 m, and 1000 m), selected to reflect different spatial scales of land use/land cover (LU/LC). The urban lakes were characterised by different phytoplankton biomass, with a maximum of 181.3 mg/l. Most of them were dominated by toxic or potentially toxic cyanobacteria. Land use/cover explained the greatest percentage of variability (24.3%) in phytoplankton composition in the 100 m buffer zone. However, this relationship was only suggestive and did not reach the conventional level of statistical significance. In contrast, LU/LC explained little of the variation in physicochemical parameters across three spatial scales, accounting for up to 0.6% in the 10 m buffer zone, but with no statistically significant relationships. Phytoplankton play a more important role than other water quality parameters and can serve as a more sensitive indicator, providing complementary information for assessing the impact of landscape structure. Despite the large proportion of forest and seminatural areas, the urban lakes were classified as highly degraded, exhibiting poor or bad water quality, which can be more related to historical pollution than to current landscape structure. Our results indicate that a 100 m wide buffer zone may be a useful study-specific spatial scale for considering shoreline and surrounding LU/LC management. They can be prioritised for protection and restoration activities, as well as for planning future spatial development. Restoring natural vegetation within this zone may reduce the nutrient inflows and slow the process of cultural eutrophication. However, further studies with a larger number of lakes are needed to confirm these relationships.

items.title: Zn-modified biochar coupled with biological nitrification inhibitors mitigates nitrous oxide emissions from alkaline soil through modulation of ammonia-oxidizing microorganisms.
items.abstract: Biochar (BC) has generally been employed to mitigate the nitrous oxide (N2O) emissions from agricultural soils, but its response is soil-dependent. Thereby, in soil with proficient nitrification tendency, Zn-modified BC coupled with biological nitrification inhibitors (BNIs) could be more effective in mitigating N2O emissions. The effects of coupled application of Zn-modified biochar and BNIs on N2O emission and its underlying microbial mechanism remain largely unknown. In our study, a 24-day incubation experiment was established representing nine treatments; with three biochars amendments using three settings of BNIs, referred to as: 1) control (without amendment/inhibitor, 2) control with methyl 3-(4-hydroxyphenyl) acrylate -MHPA, 3) control with methyl 3-(4-hydroxyphenyl) Propionate-MHPP, 4) pristine BC without inhibitor, 5) pristine BC with MHPA, 6) pristine BC with MHPP, 7) Zn-modified BC without inhibitor, 8) Zn-modified BC with MHPA, 9) Zn-modified BC with MHPP, all at agronomically recommended dosage. N dynamics were evaluated following the addition of urea. The inclusion of Zn-modified BC in combination with MHPA and MHPP substantially reduced N2O emissions by 94.52% and 96.85% relative to control. Quantification of N-cycling genes indicated that the treatment without BC amendment stimulated the growth of ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) and ammonia-oxidizing bacteria (AOB) across the entire incubation period. The input of Zn-BC with MHPA and MHPP substantially inhibited the population of AOA and AOB. LEfSe cladogram elucidated the distinct shift in bacterial assemblage across the treatments. Overall, our results demonstrated that Zn-modified BC + MHPP played a key role in the dynamics of ammonia-oxidizing functional microbiome and N turnover, potentially considerably mitigating N2O emissions.

items.title: Construction of ecological corridors for the Amur tiger (Panthera tigris altaica) and red deer (Cervus elaphus) in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park and conservation recommendations.
items.abstract: This study selected an apex predator-Amur tiger (Panthera tigris altaica), and a typical herbivore-red deer (Cervus elaphus) as the focal species to construct ecological corridors in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park (TLNP). The aim was to build ecological corridors based on the predator-prey relationship, enhance habitat connectivity, promote species dispersal and gene exchange, and mitigate the threat of habitat fragmentation to biodiversity. The resistance surface was constructed based on the habitat preferences of the focal species. Ecological sources were identified by combining Morphological Spatial Pattern Analysis (MSPA) with the dispersal abilities of the species. Finally, ecological corridors and key nodes were identified based on Circuit Theory. The results revealed that (1) There were 9 ecological sources for both the Amur tiger and red deer respectively, which were mostly located near the border in the southeastern and northwestern areas of the TLNP. The Amur tiger and the red deer each had a total of 15 corridors, more than half of which required crossing roads. (2) For the Amur tiger and the red deer, 4 and 32 pinch points were identified, along with 6 and 7 barrier points, respectively. The barrier points of the red deer were primarily found where roads and ecological corridors met; (3) Wildlife passages should be constructed in sections of S502, S318, and G331 with high ecological corridors density. This study can provide a scientific basis for the construction of ecological corridors in the TLNP and hold significant practical value for guiding wildlife passage site selection, mitigating human-wildlife conflict, and promoting transboundary population exchange.

items.title: Contrasting water use stability among dominant woody species across hillslope habitats in an alpine catchment of the upper Heihe River Basin.
items.abstract: Topographic position modulates soil moisture distribution and seasonal dynamics in alpine ecosystems, thereby shaping vegetation water-use patterns. However, whether dominant woody species occupying different hillslope habitats differ in the stability of their water-use strategies remains poorly understood at the hillslope scale. We investigated two dominant conifers, Picea crassifolia and Juniperus przewalskii, and a widespread alpine shrub, Dasiphora fruticosa across upslope, midslope, and footslope positions during the pre-rainy, rainy, and late-rainy seasons in an alpine catchment of the upper Heihe River Basin. By integrating δ2H and δ18O of soil and xylem water with a MixSIAR Bayesian mixing model, together with leaf δ13C, we quantified water sources for each species and evaluated water-use stability across hillslope positions and seasonal stages. Despite differences in dominant uptake depth, both conifers maintained relatively stable water-use strategies across slope positions and seasons. J. przewalskii persistently relied on deep soil water, which contributed 47% to 53% of total uptake, whereas P. crassifolia predominantly used shallow soil water, accounting for 44% to 65%. In contrast, D. fruticosa showed strong plasticity, with deep water uptake increasing from 16.2% to 41.0%, although this flexibility was constrained at upslope positions where available water was largely confined to shallow soil layers. Variability in leaf δ13C further indicated stronger physiological stability in the two conifer species within their respective hillslope habitats than in the shrub species, particularly at upper slope positions under greater evaporative demand. These findings suggest that water-use stability was associated with the sustained dominance of reliable soil water sources.

items.title: Seasonally shifting methane-control regimes across urban rivers and urban wetland rivers in the GBA, China, revealed by environmental, isotopic, and microbial evidence.
items.abstract: Urban rivers (UR) and urban wetland rivers (WR) are increasingly recognized as CH4 sources, yet the processes underlying differences between these aquatic habitats remain poorly resolved. We investigated excess CH4 concentration (ΔCH4), estimated diffusive flux, environmental conditions, stable carbon isotopes, and sediment microbial functional potential in the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA), China. CH4 dynamics exhibited a clear seasonal shift between contrasting spatial patterns. UR showed an amplified CH4 state during the first two seasons, the wetland outlet (WO) in wet season 1 and than both WR and WO in dry season 1. In UR, ΔCH4 decreased with dissolved oxygen (β = -0.194, p = 0.020) and increased with total nitrogen (β = 0.272, p = 0.003), indicating strong nutrient-redox control on CH4 accumulation. Stable-isotope signatures overlapped broadly among potential production and oxidation processes, while WR displayed more 13C-depleted CH4 than UR during wet season 1 despite lower ΔCH4, indicating that source signatures did not translate directly into net CH4 accumulation. Consistently, mcr and CO2-reducing methanogenesis genes and methanogenic taxa were relatively enriched in early UR seasons, whereas pmo-family genes and methane-oxidizing taxa were distributed more broadly across WR and WO. Together, these complementary lines of evidence reveal a seasonally reversible transition from nutrient-redox-driven CH4 amplification in urban rivers to more complex wetland-associated regulation involving carbon supply, redox heterogeneity, and methane-oxidation potential.

items.title: Environmental numerical models for predicting chemical transport and fate: From multimedia mass balance to machine learning.
items.abstract: The increasing release of persistent and emerging chemicals into the environment has intensified the need for robust frameworks capable of predicting their transport, fate, and environmental behavior across multiple spatial and temporal scales. Over the past decades, environmental multimedia mass-balance models have played a key role in mechanistic simulations of chemical fate. Rapid advances in machine learning (ML) have introduced data-driven alternatives with enhanced capacity for handling high-dimensional, nonlinear datasets. The relative strengths, limitations, and appropriate application domains of these two paradigms remain insufficiently discussed. We examine classical and emerging numerical environmental models for chemical transport and fate, with a focus on multimedia mass-balance models and machine learning. We review the theoretical foundations, structures, and applications of widely used mass-balance models at local, regional, and global scales. We evaluate recent ML applications in parameter estimation, concentration prediction, source identification, and degradation modeling. We synthesize these models according to their thermodynamic basis, spatial segmentation, temporal treatment, and chemical applicability. We highlight the differences in model interpretability, data dependence, uncertainty propagation, and policy relevance. We identify key limitations that affect model reliability, including limited availability and uncertainty of parameters, incomplete characterization and propagation of uncertainty, and restricted generalization beyond the model assumptions or training data. We further discuss emerging hybrid strategies that integrate machine learning with mechanistic mass-balance models. When appropriately designed, independently validated, and accompanied by uncertainty analysis, these approaches can potentially improve parameterization, reduce systematic bias, and support scenario-based projections; however, they may also introduce additional uncertainty associated with ML predictions and model coupling. This review provides a methodological reference for future environmental fate modeling, supporting the development of more reliable tools for predicting the environmental fate of chemicals and for decision-making.

items.title: Progestin-only contraceptive use is associated with reduced sociosexual behavior of female zoo-housed bonobos (Pan paniscus).
items.abstract: In female primates, sexual activity is modulated by the balance between progestins and estrogens and typically peaks around ovulation, when estrogens peak and the female is fertile. Yet, in many species, sexual activity also occurs outside the fertile phase and during pregnancy, raising questions about the hormonal mechanisms underlying non-reproductive sexual behavior. Bonobos (Pan paniscus) provide a valuable model for addressing this question, as females frequently engage in sexual interactions for social bonding, rather than reproduction. In zoo-housed populations, females often receive contraceptives with various hormonal compositions, including combined estrogen-progestin contraceptive and progestin-only formulations. This variation offers an interesting framework to investigate how ovarian hormones influence sociosexual behavior. We analyzed behavioral observations from 40 adult females across seven zoos and found that individuals receiving a progestin-only contraceptive exhibited significantly lower frequencies of sociosexual behavior compared to females receiving combined contraceptives or no contraception. Longitudinal data from 5 females further supported this pattern: sociosexual behavior substantially increased in females switching from progestin-only to combined contraception, nearly tripling their rates. Together, these findings show that the balance between estrogens and progestins modulates non-reproductive sexual activity in female primates, with important implications for understanding the impact of contraceptive use on social dynamics in managed populations.

items.title: Resource-driven release from lag phase triggers the world's fastest and largest coastal plant invasion.
items.abstract: What determines the duration of invasion lag phases remains one of the major unresolved questions in invasion ecology. Lag phases are often attributed to genetic adaptation, propagule limitation, or demographic stochasticity, yet the mechanisms by which environmental conditions regulate establishment success remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the explosive expansion of Spartina alterniflora along the coast of mainland China, the most rapid plant invasion recorded globally. Combining field experiments, demographic theory, and historical invasion records, we identify resource-regulated Allee effects as a mechanism governing the invasion lag phase. Experimentally, sediment accretion substantially increases clonal propagation and sexual reproduction, weakening demographic constraints associated with establishment and accelerating the transition from sparse founder patches to highly reproductive meadows. A theoretical model reveals that sediment-driven positive feedbacks weaken demographic constraints during establishment and shorten the duration of Allee effects. Historical invasion records spanning both sides of the Pacific Ocean support the predicted negative relationship between sedimentation rate and lag-phase duration. Invasion lag phases can arise solely from interactions between species traits and environmental resource availability. Contrary to the prevailing view that Allee effects are fixed properties of species, our results show that their duration is regulated by environmental resource availability. More broadly, environmental resources can govern ecological transitions by controlling transient dynamics during establishment, providing an explanation for why some introduced populations remain dormant for decades, whereas others rapidly become dominant ecosystem engineers.

items.title: Sources and sinks: Geoclimatic dynamics shaped the assembly of endemic fauna in the world's Third Pole.
items.abstract: The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP), a biodiversity hotspot shaped by tectonic and climatic forces, has seen significant progress in understanding its floristic origins. However, a comprehensive, multitaxon perspective on how its terrestrial fauna assembled remains lacking. Here we integrate time-calibrated phylogenies of over 20,000 species from five major groups (invertebrates, amphibians, reptiles, birds, and mammals), to reconstruct the evolutionary history of 527 terrestrial animal species endemic to the QTP. Our finding reveals that the QTP has functioned both as a center of in situ diversification and as a "biogeographic sink" that receives species from surrounding regions, however, with pronounced subregional differentiation: the Hengduan Mountains acted primarily as a diversification source, while the Himalaya and the Plateau Platform acted as sinks, accumulating lineages from adjacent regions. The Eocene-Oligocene climatic transition, rather than late Neogene uplift, initiated sustained faunal diversification and biotic exchange. Across subregions, distinct uplift histories and monsoon regimes drove asynchronous evolutionary trajectories, showing that even geographically adjacent regions can exhibit distinct accumulation patterns of lineages. Notably, integrating our faunal evidence with recent floristic assembly data reveals a consistent "plants first, animals later" pattern across the QTP and its subregions, suggesting that early-arriving plant lineages created ecological niches that facilitated subsequent faunal colonization and diversification. This framework advances our understanding of how mountain biotas assemble over time, with implications extending far beyond the QTP.

items.title: Behavioral evidence for two-stage sleep in spiders.
items.abstract: Sleep is a fundamental behavioral state found across the animal kingdom, yet most of what we know about sleep is heavily vertebrate-biased. Studies are scarce or nonexistent in all but a few invertebrate lineages. A recent study of an REM sleep-like behavior in a jumping spider has reported unexpected parallels to sleep expression in vertebrates. So far, experimental evidence that these behavioral indicators truly represent sleep was lacking in spiders. Here, we present a comprehensive investigation into sleep behavior in the spider Portia fimbriata (Salticidae). We demonstrate diurnal activity, a free-running circadian rhythm, robust sleep architecture, regularly occurring REM-like behaviors, elevated arousal thresholds during those REM-like states, as well as rebound effects following sleep disruption. We conclude that the behavior we observe in spiders is behavioral sleep, providing evidence for an REM-like sleep substate in a terrestrial invertebrate. These results contribute to fundamental questions about the evolution and function of sleep across animals.

items.title: New molecular and historical evidence on ancient Egyptian embalming.
items.abstract: Mumia vera aegyptiaca was a mummy-derived medicinal substance widely used in medieval and early modern medicine, yet its material composition and biological activity remain poorly understood. Here, we integrate Egyptological and pharmaceutical-historical analysis of 41 textual sources with LC-MS/MS-based metabolomics, molecular networking, machine-learning-assisted annotation, and bioactivity testing to investigate ancient Egyptian embalming materials and historical Mumia vera samples. We analyzed 24 objects from university and pharmacy museum collections, including historical Mumia vera products, mummified body parts, embalming residues, bandages, and two mummified skulls. Comparative metabolomics revealed substantial heterogeneity among materials labeled as Mumia vera, but also recurrent molecular signatures consistent with aged conifer resins, including oxidized abietane-type diterpenoids. Several samples contained Aloe-associated metabolites, including aloeresin A/D- and aloin-related compounds. These data reveal Aloe-associated metabolites in ancient Egyptian embalming-related materials and support the presence of Aloe spp.-derived exudates in selected samples. The convergence of molecular and textual evidence further raises the possibility that a previously unresolved Egyptian term from the 2nd millennium BC may refer to Aloe sp. or an Aloe-derived product. Comparative metabolomics also linked an inconspicuous powder sample to a specific mummified head, although their curatorial association had not been securely documented. Finally, a historical Mumia vera aegyptiaca extract modestly protected MDCK cells from influenza virus-induced cytopathic effects, whereas the isolated major compound 7-oxodehydroabietic acid was inactive on its own. Together, these findings show how integrating textual scholarship, pharmaceutical history, and molecular analysis can refine the interpretation of ancient Egyptian embalming practices, museum objects, and historical medicines.

items.title: Tolerance measured at one developmental stage mispredicts climate resilience in an animal with a complex life cycle.
items.abstract: Forecasts of whether marine species can evolve fast enough to survive climate change rely largely on single-stage tolerance assays, tacitly assuming that tolerance measured at one developmental stage reflects adaptive capacity across the organism's life cycle. We test this assumption in a common marine bivalve (Mercenaria mercenaria) and find that it fails in sign, not degree: larval and post-metamorphic tolerance to end-century ocean acidification are strongly negatively correlated (r = -0.53, 95% CI [-0.69, -0.33]) across family-level, pedigree-conditioned and animal model estimates, with pervasive rank reversals among the top performers of each stage. A multivariate analysis of the among-family covariance matrix G shows why: under acidification, 57% of the among-family variance collapses onto a single dominant axis that loads positively on every larval trait and negatively on every post-metamorphic trait, whereas under ambient conditions the same families show no cross-stage covariance at all. Acidification therefore does not merely depress performance-it reorganizes the genetic architecture into a cross-stage conflict. Under ramping RCP 8.5 forcing this conflict geometry dictates the direction-not merely the magnitude-of adaptation: only balanced multi-stage selection preserves family diversity, whereas single-stage selection systematically erodes the opposite axis. In complex life cycles, resilience is a geometric property of ontogeny that forecasts cannot compress into a single-stage without inverting the sign of the answer.

items.title: Baseline microbial ecology encodes probiotic responsiveness through distinct metabolic and network configurations.
items.abstract: Probiotic efficacy in inflammatory bowel disease varies widely between individuals, and the sources of that variability remain poorly understood. D-lactate is a microbiota-derived metabolite that accumulates during intestinal inflammation and is associated with epithelial barrier dysfunction, which motivated our use of a consortium selected to contribute none of it. Here we show that its benefit is not an intrinsic property of the administered strains but is determined by the pre-existing ecological state of the recipient microbiome. Across three independent mouse resources, preventive administration reduced disease severity and histopathological damage only where baseline communities carried higher diversity and more complex co-occurrence architecture; in those animals the consortium preserved community structure and metabolic output, restoring disease-disrupted metabolites, and selectively raising butyrate and propionate. Sustained exogenous D-lactate did not abolish protection, placing D-lactate as a tractable readout of ecological restoration rather than its effector. Responsiveness is encoded in the baseline microbiota and predictable before intervention, establishing probiotic efficacy as a stratifiable property of the host microbiome.

items.title: Rational design in single-atom nanoalloys for electrochemical carbon dioxide and nitrate conversion: a minireview.
items.abstract: Single-atom nanoalloys (SAAs), consisting of atomically dispersed guest metals embedded within conductive metallic host lattices, have emerged as a promising class of electrocatalysts for the sustainable conversion of carbon and nitrogen. Compared with conventional alloy nanoparticles and single-atom catalysts, SAAs provide local atomic coordination and intermetallic charge transfer, enabling efficient regulation of intermediate adsorption, proton-coupled electron-transfer kinetics, and catalytic selectivity. However, few reviews have systematically elucidated the rational design of atomically engineered metal sites for carbon and nitrogen conversion. To bridge this gap, this minireview focuses on rationally designed SAAs for electrocatalytic carbon dioxide reduction, nitrate reduction, and C-N coupling, emphasizing the relationships among electronic structure modulation, intermetallic charge transfer, coordination environments, and intermediate adsorption. Moreover, the fundamental reaction mechanisms of carbon dioxide reduction, nitrate reduction, and C-N coupling are discussed to emphasize the pathways among reaction intermediates. Finally, current challenges and future opportunities are discussed, including scalable synthesis, durability enhancement, structural uniformity, electrochemical technologies Integration, and fundamental understanding. By integrating these perspectives, this minireview aims to provide a comprehensive framework for the rational design of next-generation atomically mixed nanoalloys for sustainable electrocatalytic carbon and nitrogen.

items.title: Rhizospheric fungus Aspergillus terreus mitigates lead (Pb) toxicity in red bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) by modulating growth, photosynthetic pigments, and biochemical stress markers.
items.abstract: The lead (Pb) contamination is a serious risk to the agricultural productiveness and food security by affecting the metabolism of plants, halting photosynthesis, and causing oxidative stress. This research examined how the rhizospheric fungus Aspergillus terreus (isolate F2) could minimize the adverse effects of Pb phytotoxicity on the growth and physiology of red bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) under greenhouse conditions. The plants were cultivated in soil with 25 and 75 ppm of lead acetate and inoculated with a suspension of A. terreus spores in a completely randomized block trial (three replicas). Lead stress caused significant retardation of plant growth, with reductions of up to 43% in shoot length and up to 37% in dry weight at the higher Pb concentration (75 ppm), while root length and fresh weight declined by up to 24% and 34%, respectively. The photosynthetic pigments-chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b, carotenoids, and xanthophylls-declined by approximately 24-58% under Pb stress, with the greatest reductions observed for chlorophyll b and carotenoids at 75 ppm Pb. Increase in secondary metabolites (flavonoids and phenolics) was a form of stress response, and soluble sugars became considerably reduced. Lipid and proline levels were high in the Pb stress, proving oxidative damage and osmoregulatory processes. Inoculation of A. terreus considerably reverted these effects, and growth parameters, pigment levels, and metabolic balance were returned. Lactophenol cotton blue staining and light microscopy were used to confirm that the root sections were colonized by fungi. The isolate was molecularly determined through ITS rDNA sequencing and phylogenetic analysis using MEGA-11. Multivariate techniques [principal component analysis (PCA), hierarchical clustering, Pearson correlation, and treatment profile radar charting] verified the total treatment group separation of all 15 measured variables with PC1 and PC2 explaining 73.3% of total variance; chlorophyll a, fresh weight, and soluble sugars were the best distinguishing variables. These results reveal that A. terreus is an ideal bioinoculant in the reduction of Pb phytotoxicity and a viable and environmentally friendly approach to bioremediation of heavy metal-contaminated farm soils. These results indicate that A. terreus is an effective bioinoculant for alleviating Pb-induced physiological and biochemical stress in Phaseolus vulgaris L.; however, as Pb concentrations in plant tissue and soil were not measured, direct evidence of Pb immobilization or removal remains to be established in future studies.

items.title: Olfactory Responses of Araecerus fasciculatus (Coleoptera: Anthribidae) to Cocoa Beans Volatiles.
items.abstract: Araecerus fasciculatus (Coleoptera: Anthribidae) is a cosmopolitan insect that infests various stored grains, including cocoa beans, producing significant economic losses. Cocoa beans are marketed under two processing methods: washed or fermented. However, during storage they may become infested by insects. In this study, the olfactory response of A. fasciculatus to volatile compounds emitted by unfermented washed, fermented, and infested cocoa beans was evaluated. Volatile compounds from cocoa beans were collected using dynamic aeration and analyzed by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). Behavioral responses to beans, extracts, synthetic blends, 3-methylbutanoic acid, heptanal, and a binary blend (3-methylbutanoic acid plus heptanal) were evaluated in a Y-tube olfactometer. Antennal activity was determined by electroantennography (EAG). Chemical analysis revealed the presence of ketones, alcohols, esters, terpenes, acids, hydrocarbons, aldehydes, and pyrazines, with volatile profiles varying according to postharvest handling. In behavioral bioassays, unfermented washed beans did not attract either sex, fermented beans attracted both males and females, and infested beans attracted only males. The EAG analysis demonstrated that the volatile extract from fermented cocoa beans, as well as 3-methylbutanoic acid and heptanal, elicited the antennal responses. The binary blend did not elicit a significant attraction compared with the control, whereas each compound tested individually produced stronger responses. Males and females were attracted to 3-methylbutanoic acid at 0.001 µg, while heptanal attracted females at 0.1 and 0.01 µg and males at 1 and 10 µg. These findings identify key compounds in relation to the doses tested, providing insights for future management of A. fasciculatus in grain storage facilities.

items.title: Pathogenicity of Aspergillus nidulans isolated from the liver of diseased goat (Capra hircus).
items.abstract: Aspergillus nidulans, an environmentally ubiquitous opportunistic pathogen, can induce invasive aspergillosis in humans and animals, with numerous human infection cases documented. Here, we isolated A. nidulans strain XM06 from the liver of a diseased goat with suspected fungal infection. XM06 formed dark‑green colonies with white fluffy margins and a powdery center on PDA, and PCR amplification yielded products corresponding to putative homologous virulence genes, including Cat1, Alp2, and Aspf1. Using a mouse infection model, we characterized its pathogenic potential. The infected mice exhibited reduced body weight and average daily feed intake (P 0.05). Fungal burdens were highest in the spleen and liver (P < 0.05). Histopathological lesions including congestion, necrosis and inflammatory infiltration were observed in multiple organs. Antifungal assays revealed small inhibition‑zone diameters for amphotericin B and comparatively larger inhibition zones for itraconazole, caspofungin and voriconazole against strain XM06. This work provides preliminary pathological and in vitro drug-response data for goat-derived A. nidulans, offering baseline information for studying animal invasive aspergillosis. Notably, our mouse infection assay only demonstrates the pathogenic potential of XM06 and cannot confirm that this isolate caused the original disease outbreak in goats.
