items.title: Auditable large language model scoring of annual-report evidence packs: human calibration, baselines, and reproducibility checks
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can convert long documents into structured research variables. Auditability becomes difficult when evidence selection and model scoring are not stored. We study an inspectable scoring workflow that converts archived annual-report Evidence Packs into a five-dimension digital-transformation disclosure score. The design combines report selection, PDF-to-text normalization, bounded paragraph retrieval, and DeepSeek rubric scoring through a strict JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) interface; the original canonical prompt/run binding is not available. We evaluate three measurement questions and one secondary utility check: reproducible Evidence Pack construction, LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs, ordinal error/confusion diagnostics, and non-causal panel-use stress tests. The evaluation panel contains 476 firm-year observations from 64 firms for 2013–2024. The post-validation score shows high internal coherence for the additive rubric (Cronbach’s α = 0.893; first principal component explains 0.704 of standardized dimensional variance), substantial within-firm variation (mean within-firm standard deviation (SD) 2.901; 92.19% non-zero), and strong LLM–human agreement on shared Evidence Packs (total-score Spearman 0.910, Pearson 0.921, mean absolute error (MAE) 1.273; dimension-level weighted kappa 0.665–0.823). Human–Human total-score reliability, measured by the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC), is ICC(2,1) = 0.811. Baseline comparisons show lower error than frozen lexicon-count and firm-grouped term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) Ridge alternatives (MAE = 1.273 vs . 6.387 and 2.737). A 96-record rule-based retrieval audit shows high mean dimension coverage (0.936) but incomplete heuristic paragraph recall@30 (micro recall = 0.419); four audited zero-hit packs are false empty (4.17%). The main reliability claim is therefore bounded to shared archived evidence. Calibration, error-distribution, and confusion-grid analyses indicate that disagreement is concentrated near adjacent rubric levels, with extreme mismatches rare, supporting score ordering conditional on shared archived Evidence Packs. Secondary fixed-effects and event-time checks show only that the score can enter panel workflows; pre-entry differences and year-effect sensitivity require non-causal interpretation. The main contribution is an evidence-bounded audit template rather than an exact endpoint-rerun claim.

items.title: Dietary L-Tryptophan Improves Growth, Antioxidant Status, Intestinal Barrier, and Resistance to Aeromonas hydrophila Infection in Largemouth Bass.
items.abstract: Tryptophan (Trp) has been well documented to positively regulate nutrient metabolism, immune responses, and intestinal microecological homeostasis in mammals. However, relevant studies regarding its functions in largemouth bass remain limited. Herein, we assessed the impacts of dietary Trp on growth, antioxidant status, intestinal barrier, and disease resistance in largemouth bass. Fish were fed a basal control diet (C) or basal diets supplemented with 0.1%, 0.2%, 0.4%, and 0.8% L‑Trp for 60 days. Dietary L-Trp supplementation significantly improved FBW, WGR, and SGR of largemouth bass, with the maximum values found in the 0.4%Trp group. Based on the WGR and SGR data, quadratic regression analysis further identified 0.49% as the optimal dietary L-Trp inclusion level. In terms of antioxidant capacity, the 0.4%Trp group exhibited markedly higher serum and intestinal activities of CAT, GSH-PX, and SOD, as well as a higher content of T-AOC, compared to the C group. Moreover, the 0.4%Trp group significantly upregulated intestinal Nrf2 expression and downregulated Keap1 expression. Relative to the C group, dietary Trp supplementation significantly elevated intestinal villus height and muscular layer thickness in the 0.1%, 0.2%, and 0.4% Trp groups. Consistently, the mRNA levels of intestinal tight junction genes ( ZO-1 , Claudin-1 , and Claudin-4 ) were upregulated in the 0.4%Trp group. Supplementation with 0.4%Trp significantly downregulated the expression of proinflammatory cytokines ( TNF-α , IL-1β , and IL-8 ) and upregulated the expression of antiinflammatory cytokines ( TGF-β1 , IL-10 , IL-22 , and AHR ). Intestinal microbial analysis further revealed that dietary L-Trp supplementation enriched the abundance of beneficial bacteria, reduced pathogenic microbial populations, and improved intestinal microbial diversity and richness. Finally, dietary L-Trp supplementation effectively improved the survival rate of largemouth bass following an Aeromonas hydrophila challenge. This was associated with enhanced serum activities of LZM, AKP, and ACP, as well as increased intestinal T-SOD activity. Additionally, L-Trp supplementation upregulated the expression of Nrf2 , TGF-β1 , IL-10 , and IL-22 . In contrast, the 0.4%Trp group reduced the MDA content and downregulated expression of Keap1 , HSP70 , TNF-α , IL-1β , and IL-8 . Collectively, 0.4% dietary Trp strengthens antioxidant defense, remodels intestinal microbiota, improves intestinal physical and immune barriers, and enhances resistance against A. hydrophila infection in largemouth bass.

items.title: Mild Cognitive Impairment Identification in Geriatric and Primary Care Clinics and Driving Assessment Outcomes.
items.abstract: Mild cognitive impairment (MCI) can affect complex daily activities, including driving. This quality-improvement project compared documented MCI case counts in an outpatient geriatric clinic and a traditional primary care clinic and described Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) referral documentation and driving assessment outcomes. A retrospective Epic electronic health record (EHR) review (Epic Systems Corporation, Verona, WI, USA) covered 2021-2023 and adults aged 65 years and older. Electronic G31.84 queries identified candidates; preserved basic and instrumental daily function and verified Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores of 19-25 were required for inclusion. Scanned MoCA tests and both DMV forms were located by manual chart review. Completed written and behind-the-wheel testing and overall pass/fail outcomes were distinguished. Counts and proportions were summarized descriptively, with exact binomial 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for assessment outcomes. Clinic totals were 3,233 geriatric and 3,943 primary care visits. The geriatric query identified 60 candidates. Scanned MoCA tests were located in 36; 24 without located tests were excluded. Two scores were 11, leaving 34 eligible patients. The primary care code query returned zero patients. All 34 were offered DMV assessment through shared decision making; 17 (50.0%) had documented referrals with DMV notification and initial reporting forms in their charts. The later provider form was documented for 10 of the 17. Eight completed testing (47.1% of referred patients; 80.0% of those with the later form documented). Two passed (25.0%; 95% CI, 3.2%-65.1%) and six failed (75.0%; 95% CI, 34.9%-96.8%). Eight patients continued driving without a documented referral; the reasons were undocumented. Documented MCI case capture differed between clinics. Findings among assessment completers support routine clinical review of driving safety, individualized referral for formal evaluation, and coordinated follow-up. The failure proportion from this small, selected subgroup cannot be generalized to the wider MCI population. Prospective evaluation should examine patient safety, experience, and continued mobility.

items.title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices Regarding Marburg Virus Disease Among Healthcare Workers in Dilla University Teaching Hospital, Ethiopia: A Cross-Sectional Study.
items.abstract: Healthcare workers are a first contact for patients with infectious diseases and may be at occupational risk during hemorrhagic fever outbreaks. The Marburg virus disease (MVD) outbreak in southern Ethiopia, ongoing during data collection in December 2025, highlighted the need to assess healthcare workers' knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding MVD. Therefore, this study assessed knowledge, attitudes, and practices and examined factors associated with practice among healthcare work. A cross-sectional study of 238 healthcare workers at Dilla University Teaching Hospital was conducted from December 1 to December 22, 2025. Descriptive statistics, frequencies, and percentages summarized participant characteristics and KAP responses. Binary logistic regression examined factors associated with good practice. Variables with p value ≤ 0.25 in bivariable analysis were included in the multivariable model. Adjusted odds ratios (AORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, and significance was set at p < 0.05. About 51.7%, 57.1%, and 55.0% of participants had good knowledge, positive attitudes, and good practice toward MVD, respectively, based on study-specific cutoffs. Most identified direct contact with blood and body fluids as an MVD transmission route (92.0%). However, gaps were observed regarding environmental risk factors and MVD distribution and origin. Most recognized reporting suspected cases (91.2%), avoiding contact with infected individuals or their possessions (91.2%), and using personal protective equipment (87.8%). In multivariable analysis, modification of working habits from concern about acquiring MVD (AOR = 2.19, 95% CI: 1.21-3.99) and good MVD knowledge (AOR = 1.96, 95% CI: 1.13-3.39) were positively associated with good practice. Findings indicate gaps in MVD-related knowledge and infection prevention among healthcare workers at Dilla University Teaching Hospital. Targeted competency-based training, simulation, IPC resources, and facility-level preparedness systems are warranted to strengthen readiness for MVD and other viral hemorrhagic fever events.

items.title: A Highly Sensitive and Specific Rapid Lateral Flow Assay for the HIV Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors Bictegravir, Cabotegravir, and Dolutegravir.
items.abstract: Second-generation HIV-1 integrase strand transfer inhibitors (INSTIs)-bictegravir (BIC), cabotegravir (CAB), and dolutegravir (DTG)-are leading components of highly potent antiretroviral therapy, and CAB is also used for long-acting chemoprevention. Rapid detection of clinically relevant INSTI concentrations could support point-of-care assessment and real-time clinical decision-making. We developed a lateral flow assay (LFA) that detects BIC, CAB, and DTG in whole blood and plasma and evaluated its performance against predefined concentration thresholds and high-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS). A single LFA cassette design was developed using a monoclonal antibody to distinguish BIC, CAB, and DTG concentrations below trough, at minimal-to-moderate trough, and at ideal concentrations. LFA results were read visually at 20 min and were compared with LC-MS/MS-quantified INSTI concentrations for 124 clinical plasma specimens. For 24 plasma samples from US participants receiving treatment involving one of the three INSTIs, the LFA interpretations matched all LC-MS/MS results except for one DTG specimen, which was interpreted by LFA as 1.0-1.6 μg/mL but measured 2.1 μg/mL by LC-MS/MS. Among 100 plasma remnants from routine national surveillance in Eswatini, the LFA correctly interpreted DTG concentrations in 95 specimens. Four specimens had DTG LC-MS/MS concentrations slightly above the LFA-determined range, differing by ≤ 0.1 μg/mL, and one specimen measured at 1.20 μg/mL by LC-MS/MS was interpreted as ≥ 1.6 μg/mL by LFA. In total, 6 of 124 specimens (4.8%) had LFA-interpreted INSTI concentrations that varied slightly from the LC-MS/MS results, with no statistically significant difference in overall performance by Wilcoxon signed-rank test (W = 8.00, p = 0.94, one-tailed). The LFA design successfully provided clinically useful interpretations of BIC, CAB, and DTG concentrations with minor discrepancies in < 5% of samples. Importantly, all low-concentration samples of < 1 μg/mL were correctly interpreted by LFA. The assay shows promise as a point-of-care tool for assessing clinically relevant INSTI concentrations.

items.title: Participatory Epidemiology of Major Camel Diseases and Their Management in Somalia: The Case of Banadir and Lower Shabelle Regions.
items.abstract: This study investigates major camel diseases, their community-perceived epidemiological characteristics, and management practices in the Banadir and Lower Shabelle regions of Somalia. Data were collected from 17 key informants through semistructured interviews and from 18 participants across three focus group discussions (FGDs). Semistructured interviews captured key camel diseases, their local names, disease impacts, coping mechanisms, and locally used disease management approaches, while FGDs were used to conduct participatory exercises to rank and characterize diseases based on severity and clinical signs. Kendall's W was used to assess consensus among participants, revealing the strength of the agreement across groups. Ten diseases were most frequently reported, including trypanosomosis, mastitis, pneumonia, ringworm, camelpox, mange, tetanus, wry neck, parasite infection, and anthrax. For disease management practices, about 15 out of 17 respondents reported using both modern medicines and traditional practices such as burning, administering Dobera glabra seeds, and applying camel hump ghee. In addition, 13 out of 17 informants indicated that farmers do not conduct regular animal health checkups. Preventive measures included isolation, relocation, and recitation of the Holy Quran. Regarding veterinary consultation, 10 out of 17 respondents reported poor veterinary consultation, citing limited awareness and poor accessibility as potential causes. Of the eight diseases assessed by pairwise ranking, farmers rated anthrax (Kud) as the most severe (mean 6.67 ± 0.58 out of 7), followed by tetanus (Taagow, 6.00 ± 1.00), with strong, statistically significant agreement across the focus groups (Kendall's W = 0.849; p = 0.013). Wry neck and trypanosomosis were rated moderately severe, while pneumonia, mange, mastitis, and camelpox scored lowest. Matrix scoring showed strong, statistically significant agreement among the three informant groups across all disease signs (Kendall's W = 0.74-1.00; p < 0.05). The strongest associations were dyspnea and nasal discharge with pneumonia (mean scores 15.00 ± 1.00/20 and 16.67 ± 2.08/20), odor change with trypanosomosis (15.00 ± 3.00/20), and fever with camelpox and trypanosomosis. The findings also revealed clear seasonal variation in camel diseases, with most conditions peaking during the rainy seasons of spring (Gu) and autumn (Dayr). In contrast, trypanosomosis, tetanus, and mange occurred throughout the year, while anthrax was predominantly associated with the dry Jiilaal season. Major challenges reported include limited veterinary services, high treatment costs, and inadequate feed and drug supplies. These findings reflect substantial indigenous knowledge and point to the need for integrated interventions including improved veterinary services, affordable drugs and vaccines, and farmer capacity building to strengthen camel health in the region.

items.title: Rhizospheric Bacteria From Artocarpus heterophyllus Exhibit Antimicrobial Traits and Antagonistic Activity Against Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii , Causal Agent of Jackfruit Bronzing Disease.
items.abstract: The Jackfruit bronzing disease represents a significant phytosanitary constraint affecting Artocarpus heterophyllus production. In this context, the exploration of plant-associated microorganisms as a source of potential biological control agents aligns with sustainable agricultural strategies. This study is aimed at isolating, characterizing, and evaluating the in vitro antagonistic interactions, and antimicrobial potential of indigenous rhizospheric and endophytic bacteria with the potential to be developed as biocontrol agents for the control jackfruit bronzing causal agent Pantoea stewartii subsp. stewartii. A total of 138 bacterial isolates were obtained from rhizospheric soils and internal plant tissues, with a predominance of rhizospheric bacteria (78.3%). In vitro antagonism assays revealed that only rhizospheric isolates exhibited inhibitory activity against the phytopathogen, identifying 12 strains with consistent antagonistic capacity. These isolates were further characterized to elucidate the potential mechanisms involved in microbial antagonism. Functional analyses demonstrated that the antagonistic isolates possessed multiple extracellular enzymatic activities, predominantly lipase, followed by amylase and cellulase activities, whereas protease activity was absent. Additionally, selected isolates exhibited biosurfactant production, suggesting their role in pathogen inhibition. Antibiosis was confirmed through the production of diffusible antimicrobial compounds. Furthermore, molecular screening revealed the presence of nonribosomal peptide synthetase (NRPS) gene fragments in several strains, supporting their genetic potential to synthesize bioactive secondary metabolites. Phylogenetic identification based on 16S rDNA gene sequencing assigned the isolates to bacterial taxa known for their ecological versatility and functional attributes. Overall, this study provides evidence that rhizospheric bacteria associated with jackfruit harbor significant antagonistic and antimicrobial capabilities against jackfruit bronzing causal agent. These findings contribute to the understanding of microbial interactions and functional traits associated with plant microbiota. This study provides the first assessment of microorganisms associated with jackfruit.

items.title: Zoonotic Potential of Non- Helicobacter pylori Helicobacter Species Associated With Dogs and Cats in Human Infections: A Systematic Review.
items.abstract: Non-Helicobacter pylori Helicobacter (NHPH) spp. are clinically relevant organisms found in humans and several animal hosts. Dogs and cats are natural hosts of multiple gastric and enterohepatic NHPH spp. and may represent potential sources of human exposure. This systematic review aimed to synthesize the clinical, epidemiological, and molecular evidence concerning human infections involving dog- and cat-associated NHPH spp. and to evaluate the evidence for a possible epidemiological association with companion animals. PubMed and Scopus databases were searched for studies published from 2000 through the final search on April 15, 2026. Eligible studies reported human infection with NHPH spp. involving H. heilmannii sensu stricto (s.s), H. felis, H. bizzozeronii, H. salomonis, or H. canis. The following information was extracted: study and patient characteristics, NHPH species, human samples, diagnostic techniques, molecular confirmation, immunological state, clinical results, and exposure to dogs and/or cats. The risk of bias was evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal checklist appropriate for each study design. Of 350 records identified, 51 studies met the inclusion criteria. The evidence consisted predominantly of case reports. H. heilmannii-related organisms were the most frequently reported, followed by H. canis, H. felis, H. bizzozeronii, and H. salomonis. Gastric NHPH infections were predominantly associated with gastric disease, while H. canis was mainly associated with systemic and extragastric infections, especially in immunocompromised or clinically vulnerable patients. Molecular confirmation was reported in 66.7% of studies (34/51), with one additional study providing molecular confirmation for only 2 of 22 cases. Dog and/or cat exposure was documented in 41.2% of studies (21/51). Although several studies identified the same NHPH spp. in humans and companion animals, paired strain-level molecular evidence remained limited and was insufficient to establish the direction of transmission. Numerous gastrointestinal and systemic infections in humans have been linked to NHPH spp. found in dogs and cats. According to available data, dogs and cats may act as reservoirs or sources of human NHPH infection, given the recognized zoonotic potential of these pathogens. However, direct animal-to-human transmission and its direction have not been conclusively established. This is largely due to the limited availability of strain-level molecular comparisons and paired human-animal sampling. To clarify transmission routes and improve integrated One Health surveillance, consistent molecular identification and comparative genomic studies are therefore required.

items.title: Intrinsic Goals for Autonomous Agents: Hierarchical Exploration Captures Future Volitional Action in Drosophila
items.abstract: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.

items.title: Analysis of Biomarkers from Visual Explorations in Individuals Suspected to Be in the Prodromal Phase of Parkinson's Disease
items.abstract: Identifying prodromal Parkinson's Disease is a precondition for any future treatment that modifies the course of the disease, since such therapies would ideally act on the initial pathogenic events, early enough to delay the clinical onset of the disease rather than only slow its progression. In this work, a visual exploration model is retrained on an expanded corpus. Without any further training or threshold recalibration, it is then tested on an enriched cohort of patients with high risk of being in the prodromal phase of Parkinson's Disease, testing whether the learned signal follows a continuum of disease rather than only separating patients from controls. The resulting score distribution is analysed as an external evaluation of the hypothesis that the oculomotor signature targeted by the model is already partly present before clinical diagnosis. With every subject scored on data not used to train the model, the scores are ordered as controls < high-risk patients < Parkinson's Disease, with 42% of the high-risk patients exceeding the decision threshold. A SHAP decomposition of the scores into classifiers and gaze features shows that high scores in this cohort are driven mainly by reduced saccadic excursion, fewer fixations and longer fixations, the hypokinetic oculomotor profile that characterises Parkinson's Disease. The model score is also compared against the prodromal markers used for recruitment. The score is not correlated with hyposmia, constipation, depression or REM sleep behaviour disorder; these results, interpreted in the context of the selection induced by the recruitment criteria, are discussed as evidence that within the high-risk cohort the score is largely not explained by the available ancillary clinical variables. The results suggest that the visual biomarkers analysed are a complementary indicator to identify patients at risk of being in the prodromal stage.

items.title: The dominance of feedback mechanisms for perception in the central visual field: the flip tilt illusion by backward masking and the Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight algorithm
items.abstract: The flip tilt illusion is the misperception of the orientation of the alignment between a pair of dots by 90 degrees. It occurs when the dot-pair contains one black dot and one white dot, is typically visible only in the peripheral visual field. It is predicted by the central-peripheral dichotomy (CPD) theory. Along the visual pathway from retina to downstream stages, our brain admits only a tiny fraction of visual input information for recognition due to a processing bottleneck that starts from the output of the primary visual cortex (V1) along the visual pathway. Accordingly, perception downstream from V1 relies on impoverished information, selected largely by gaze shifts to center the selected content at fovea and additionally by the capacity of the bottleneck even in the central visual field, likely making perceptual hypotheses about the visual scene ambiguous or illusory. To overcome, downstream areas send feedback to upstream areas such as V1 to query for additional information, thereby re-assessing the weights of the initial hypotheses. This perceptual algorithm is termed Feedforward-Feedback-Verify-reWeight (FFVW). To save resources, the feedback query is limited largely to the central visual field. The peripheral visual field is thus vulnerable to perceptual ambiguities and illusions. The CPD theory further predicts that impairing the feedback renders the flip tilt illusion visible in the central visual field. This paper reports a confirmation of the prediction. The feedback is disrupted by masking the visual inputs after a short viewing duration t. Furthermore, the FFVW algorithm is studied by a computational model of the perceptual data as a function of t. It reveals that the initial feedforward sweep of visual information explains the flip tilt illusion for t shorter than 20 ms, whereas the feedback mechanism dominates perception for longer t.

items.title: New developments in the geometry and topology of 3D head-direction coding
items.abstract: The head-direction (HD) system is a neuronal compass that represents head orientation in 3D. Its encoding of 3D head orientation can be decomposed into a multiplexed representation of 2D head tilt relative to gravity and 1D head orientation in the horizontal plane (azimuth). Defining azimuth during 3D motion is not trivial, and recent studies have indicated that the HD system implements a so-called dual-axis/tilted-azimuth (DA/TA) rule, a representation that is well supported experimentally but remains mathematically and mechanistically difficult to interpret. Here, I introduce a new formulation of DA/TA based directly on the elements of a rotation matrix describing 3D head orientation. In this formulation, TA is represented by a 2D vector, whose direction encode TA and whose norm depends on tilt, consistent with a tilt-dependent gain of HD tuning reported by experimental studies. I provide a geometrical interpretation of this formulation and use it to characterize the topology of the resulting representation. More generally, I introduce a framework in which head orientation is represented by a rotation matrix and neuronal responses arise from linear combinations of its elements followed by nonlinear transformations. Within this framework, the linear stage specifies which aspects of 3D orientation are encoded, and therefore allow relating neuronal representation to linear algebra concepts. Classical HD tuning, gravity tuning, and DA/TA can all be described within this common framework. Together, these results provide a new mathematical, geometrical, and topological perspective on 3D HD coding.

items.title: Partial Fragmentation of Comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS)
items.abstract: We present time-series observations of the long period comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS) obtained in 2025-2026, bracketing the comet's fragmentation in early November 2025. We show that a simple radiation pressure model can explain many of the comet's properties: the rapid fading after fragmentation, the increasing mean particle size in the projected photometry aperture, and the time dependence of the surface brightness profile. Small dust particles ($\lesssim 100 μ$m) dominate the coma, with average dust velocity $\sim$ a few $\times$ 1 meter s$^{-1}$. The nucleus radius is estimated at $\sim$0.5 km and the dust properties are consistent with, but do not prove, an origin in nucleus rotational breakup, followed by being swept down the tail by radiation pressure.

items.title: LunarRF: A Terrain-Aware Propagation Engine and Pole-Wide 3GPP Surface Coverage Atlas of the Lunar South Pole
items.abstract: Artemis surface operations will depend on 3GPP cellular links, yet no public product shows where such links are physically possible across the lunar south pole. We present LunarRF, a GPU system for terrain-aware surface coverage, and the pole-wide atlas produced with it. A footprint engine casts 8192 radial profiles from one of 11,827 candidate masts enumerated by stated rules on the orbit-adjusted LOLA elevation model, takes the viewshed, and evaluates ITU-R P.1812 Delta-Bullington propagation on every profile, continuous through the radio horizon. An order-independent resolver merges the footprints per 20 m cell, making the run shardable and resumable. The atlas covers the disc south of 80°S at 20 m for four SFCG-recommended surface bands and the IM-2 demonstration band, 1.8 to 25.375 GHz, under a stated link budget, storing per cell the best-server power and identity, redundancy count, line of sight and coverability. The engine is validated against a parabolic-equation solver, ray tracing and analytic solutions. Swapping Deygout for Delta-Bullington, or adding terrain noise at the level of the published height-error map of the DEM, moves the coverable class on under 1% of a mast's disc in the mean. With every candidate active, 90.5% of the disc is coverable at 1.8 GHz, 59% at 5.855 GHz and 10% at 25.375 GHz, or 84, 43 and 5% after the measured 3-4 dB engine optimism. A mast covers about 90% of its visible area within its budget-set range, and no band is terrain-limited. The nine current Artemis regions are 85-99% coverable at 1.8 GHz and 22-85% at 5.855 GHz. The atlas and candidate table are released with a DOI.

items.title: Is the arXiv Apocalypse upon us? A break in preprint growth coincident with agentic AI
items.abstract: As an experiment in agentic assisted analysis, we used an agentic AI model to analyse the effect of agentic AI on arXiv submissions; data acquisition, analysis and the first draft were carried out by the model under the author's direction. Monthly arXiv submissions have grown exponentially for three decades, at about $9\%$ per year. Fitting a piecewise log-linear trend with seasonal modulation to the full record, we find two post-pandemic breaks in growth rate. The first, in mid-2022, precedes ChatGPT and is carried by the expansion of AI research within computer science (CS); outside CS, growth from 2022 to 2025 remained at $8\%$ per year. The second, between December 2025 and February 2026, follows the release of models capable of extended autonomous work and is absent from the AI categories themselves. Since December 2025 submissions without a CS listing have run $17\%$ above trend, and in September 2026 total submissions reached a record $40\,363$. The excess is largest in mathematics, where submissions doubled within a year, and follows a gradient from formal and theoretical fields to experimental ones that is not ordered by surveyed rates of AI-tool adoption. In mathematics the increase is distributed across subfields and authors, two-thirds of it arising from a larger number of distinct authors rather than from a few prolific submitters. Across fields the clearest signature is a shift to single authorship: solo-authored papers rose by $70\%$ within a year in mathematics and condensed matter, and by $44\%$ in quantitative biology even as its total output fell, but not in experimental particle physics. The analysis is deliberately agnostic of LLM-detection methods: it uses only submission counts and metadata, with treatment timing fixed by calendar dates, and is therefore free of the outcome-triggered timing bias of author-level studies.

items.title: Temporal rhythms of uncertainty: Evaluating Mars claims in the Australian colonial press
items.abstract: Favourable oppositions of Mars gave nineteenth-century astronomers recurring opportunities to test claims about the planet, while telegraphic news and newspaper reprinting carried those claims well beyond the professional observatories. Historians have established the importance of these events to the development of mass-media astronomy. Here, I examine a related question in the Australian colonial press: how did the standing of particular claims change as brief reports, local responses and fuller accounts appeared at different times? Drawing on colonial newspaper coverage from 1875 to 1899, I follow episodes surrounding the major Mars oppositions of 1892 and 1894. Reports of observations attributed to "Professor Pickering" in 1892 prompted both rapid circulation and immediate scrutiny. In 1894, a cable about William W. Campbell's spectroscopic work provoked local disagreement before more detailed accounts became available. These sequences show that a Mars opposition concentrated attention without imposing a uniform progression from anticipation to discovery and subsequent caution. Newspapers carried assessments and renewed speculation at the same time. The Australian case extends work on event astronomy by showing how the timing and form of information arriving in a colonial press network affected the public evaluation of astronomical claims.

items.title: Modelling Emotional Dynamics in the Life of Amrita Pritam: A Nonlinear Perspective on Longing and Companionship
items.abstract: Amrita Pritam (1919-2005) was a prominent writer of modern Indian literature, particularly in Punjabi and Hindi. Her literary-biographical context provides a setting for exploring memory, longing, companionship, and emotional regulation through simple dynamical models. This study develops three single-state ordinary differential equation models centred on two important relational references in her life: Sahir Ludhianvi, associated with memory, absence, recollection, and longing, and Imroz, associated with companionship, care, continuity, and support. The first model describes Sahir-related longing through memory-driven excitation and natural emotional decay (fading); the second models Imroz-related companionship through nonlinear stabilisation around a preferred emotional state; and the third unifies both influences within a single-state framework. Analytical solutions, equilibrium conditions, local stability analysis, and numerical simulations are used to examine emotional-state decay and persistence, convergence to stable equilibria, and threshold effects on system behaviour. The results indicate that memory-related reinforcement may sustain the modelled emotional state under suitable stimulus conditions, whereas Imroz-related companionship may drive the system towards a stable upper equilibrium when initial conditions lie within the admissible range. The unified model illustrates how memory-driven longing and companionship-driven stabilisation associated with Sahir and Imroz can jointly shape a modelled emotional trajectory. This study is conceptual and mathematical, not empirical or psychological. It neither measures private emotions of Amrita Pritam nor estimates parameters from biographical data. Instead, it introduces a simple nonlinear framework for exploring memory, fading, companionship, equilibrium, and threshold effects in a literary-biographical context.

items.title: Post-fragmentation Morphological and Broadband Color Evolution of C/2025 K1 (ATLAS)
items.abstract: Comet C/2025 K1 (ATLAS) underwent major fragmentation after its 2025 October 8 perihelion passage at q ~ 0.33 au. We present four epochs of Johnson-Cousins BVR imaging obtained with the Mount Laguna Observatory 40-inch reflector on 2025 November 26, November 29, December 5, and December 8, sampling the subsequent evolution of the integrated fragment-coma complex. The images were homogenized to common circular two-dimensional effective point-spread functions before morphology was measured along the projected fragment axis. We evaluated 324 profile-extraction configurations and removed solutions whose localized peak landed on the search-window boundary. The fragment-axis surface-brightness enhancement relocates inward between November 26 and 29 and outward between December 5 and 8; the sign of both changes is recovered in every valid configuration and at all tested common target PSFs from 5.3 to 6.0 arcsec. Calibrated BVR photometry using Gaia DR3 synthetic Johnson-Kron-Cousins standards independently shows a repeatable November 26-29 change in broadband spectral shape: B-V decreases while V-R increases. The curvature index S'_(V-R) - S'_(B-V) changes by +3.47 (+1.50/-1.65) percent per 1000 Angstrom, with 99.1 percent of Monte Carlo realizations positive, while the full B-R reflectivity gradient remains approximately constant. Repeating the color comparison at a fixed projected radius of 2205 km produces nearly identical changes. The combined results are consistent with continued restructuring of the unresolved post-fragmentation inner coma, while broadband imaging alone cannot uniquely separate dust-color evolution, molecular emission, and changing contributions from unresolved fragments.

items.title: Planetesimal Delivery to Giant Planet Circumplanetary Disks: Bulk Ice Enrichment and an Ice-rich Iapetus
items.abstract: The regular satellites of Jupiter and Saturn are substantially enriched in ice relative to the rock-rich solids of the outer Solar System. In addition, the satellites interior to Titan and distant Iapetus are icier than Titan itself. Collisional processes and subsequent migration can readily alter compositions deep in the planetary potential well, but producing a distant, ice-rich satellite with Iapetus's radius of about 700 km is a challenge \citep{mosqueira2026a}. We show that differential ablation and capture of icy and rocky fragments from differentiated outer Solar System bodies can explain the bulk Jovian and Kronian satellite ice enrichment and supply the substantial ice-rich inventory needed for Iapetus. For 1\,m--1\,km fragments with the canonical size-distribution index \(p=3.5\) and a source containing 30\% ice by mass, the fixed radial distance Saturn calculation deposits material with ice fractions of 0.66 (delivery of vapor-only rock) or 0.50 (with retained rock melt) at 20 Saturn radii and nearly pure ice at 60 Saturn radii. Following three-dimensional trajectories over repeated passages through the pressure-supported gas gives ice fractions of about 0.4 near 20 Saturn radii and 0.9 near 60 Saturn radii. The matching Jupiter calculation yields a similar bulk ice enrichment, with a corresponding compositional gradient across the Galilean satellite region. These delivery profiles supply ice-enriched material for satellite formation. Yet satellitesimal inward migration subsequently modifies the material incorporated into satellites and thus alters their bulk compositions. We briefly discuss the implications for the PDS~70 planetary system.

items.title: Designing sustainability under Earth-system rate constraints
items.abstract: Sustainability debates are monopolized by quantities: total energy use, material stocks, or recycling volumes. These metrics are informative, but they obscure a more fundamental constraint. On a materially closed but energetically open Earth, long-term viability is governed by rates: power density, areal power density, and the rate at which dispersed materials can be repurified under dif- fuse solar fluxes. We develop a physical framework that links technological metabolism, material dilution, and recycling limits through these rate con- straints. This perspective clarifies why many contemporary technologies remain viable only through stock drawdown and high-power buffering, and why green growth strategies often shift rather than resolve the underlying mismatch between industrial activity and Earth-system dynamics. We argue that long-term sustain- ability requires both quantitative reduction in aggregate industrial throughput toward rate-bounded regimes and the development of technologies qualitatively compatible with biospheric operating conditions.

items.title: Erasmus Reinhold on Copernicus and the “saving of appearances”: A preliminary reassessment
items.abstract: This study offers a preliminary reassessment of Erasmus Reinhold’s role in disseminating Copernican astronomy and his epistemological conception of astronomy’s purpose. While confirming Reinhold as a highly technical astronomer deeply engaged with De revolutionibus , it challenges the view that he was indifferent to cosmological questions. Reinhold praised Copernicus not for heliocentrism itself, but for laying new foundations to revive astronomy, particularly geocentric astronomy. Inspired by Copernicus, he may have envisioned a proto-Tychonic system that rejected celestial spheres without compromising planetary harmony. Unlike Andreas Osiander’s instrumentalist interpretation, Reinhold understood “saving the appearances” as the pursuit of uncovering the true law and harmony underlying planetary motions—a search for the real geometry of the cosmos. Though influenced by an epistemology that privileged mathematics, his concept of harmony was not purely mathematical, as it remained rooted in a geocentric worldview. This reassessment highlights the complexity of Reinhold’s thought and stresses the importance of considering contemporary receptions of his work to better understand his legacy during a pivotal moment in early modern astronomy.

items.title: A Low‐Sidelobe W‐Band Gaussian Corrugated Horn With Stable Phase Center for Terahertz Quasi‐Optical Systems
items.abstract: ABSTRACT High‐quality Gaussian beams with low sidelobes and stable phase centers are essential for efficient beam focusing and low‐loss energy coupling in terahertz quasi‐optical systems. However, conventional corrugated horns usually require costly electroforming processes. The complex corrugated structures impose stringent fabrication requirements and increase manufacturing costs. In addition, phase‐center drift over frequency degrades the focusing efficiency and beam‐coupling performance of broadband quasi‐optical systems. In this study, a fabrication‐oriented W‐band Gaussian corrugated horn antenna is proposed. The horn antenna employs a multistep rectangular‐to‐circular waveguide converter, which achieves broadband TE 10 ‐to‐TE 11 mode conversion while reducing fabrication difficulty and tolerance requirements through a machining‐friendly stepped geometry. By optimizing the corrugated tapered and parallel sections of the horn, stable HE 11 ‐mode radiation, low‐sidelobe Gaussian beam generation, and a stable phase center are achieved over the 75–110 GHz frequency band. A prototype antenna was fabricated using mechanical machining and laminated assembly techniques. The measured results show that the proposed antenna achieves a reflection coefficient below −20 dB, a gain of 24–26 dBi, a normalized sidelobe level below −31 dB, and a cross‐polarization level better than 35 dB across the operating band, while the phase‐center variation remains within ±20 mm. The proposed design significantly reduces the fabrication complexity and manufacturing cost of terahertz corrugated horns while maintaining excellent radiation performance.

items.title: Hardware architectures for posit arithmetic: evolution, trade-offs, and artificial intelligence
items.abstract: The IEEE 754 floating-point standard has been the backbone of scientific computing for decades. However, the rapid growth of deep learning (DL) and edge computing has highlighted its drawbacks, mainly in high memory bandwidth and energy usage. To solve this, the posit number system was introduced in 2017. It uses "tapered precision" to dynamically allocate more bits to the "Golden Zone," where artificial intelligence (AI) weights usually fall. Although theoretically better, early posit hardware faced a major "hardware tax" because decoding variable-length regime bits was too slow. This paper presents a detailed survey of posit hardware architectures from 2017 to 2025. We trace its evolution from basic scalar generators to advanced vectorized accelerators and compute-in-memory (CIM) designs. We highlight major improvements, such as leading difference detectors (LDD) and Radix-4 dividers, which have successfully reduced decoding delay by over 40% and energy consumption by 80%. Our comparative study shows that 16-bit posits can effectively replace 32-bit IEEE floats for memory-bound tasks. It saves 50% memory bandwidth without losing accuracy in applications like ResNet inference and climate modeling. Finally, we conclude that with recent RISC-V posit vector units (PVUs), posits demonstrate competitive potential relative to BFLOAT16 and FP8 formats, particularly in memory-bound edge applications.

items.title: Particle Acceleration in Tycho's SNR
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Supernova remnants (SNRs) have long been considered prime candidates for cosmic‐ray sources in our Galaxy. Observations of SNRs in TeV gamma‐rays can help in solving the problem of the origin of cosmic rays and are key to understanding the mechanism of particle acceleration at a propagating shock wave. Tycho's SNR belongs to a rare subclass of Galactic SNRs' known as historical supernovae; the supernova was observed by Tycho Brahe in 1572. Tycho's SNR has been widely studied across the electromagnetic spectrum. Non‐thermal emission from Tycho's SNR has been detected in radio and X‐rays. These studies show a shell‐like morphology of Tycho's SNR, whose configuration results in the efficient cosmic ray acceleration at the supernova shock. Thus, Tycho's SNR has become a candidate for the investigation of particle acceleration in SNR shocks at high and very high‐energies. At TeV energies, the SHALON telescopes discovered emission with a hard spectrum, extending from 800 GeV up to 80 TeV, correlated with the supernova shells contributing to the very‐high‐energy gamma‐ray flux. A nonlinear kinetic model of cosmic‐ray acceleration in SNRs was applied to Tycho's SNR to compare the observed TeV gamma‐ray emission spectra with the model predictions. The collected experimental data support the theoretical prediction of a hadronic mechanism of generation of very‐high‐energy (800 GeV–100 TeV) gamma‐rays from Tycho's SNR.

items.title: The Gradual Refinement of Kepler’s Triangulation Method: Early Developments in His First Encounter with Tycho
items.abstract: Johannes Kepler’s early work with Tycho Brahe’s Mars observations in Benátky in 1600 marked a pivotal moment in his methodological development. This paper traces Kepler’s evolving approach to triangulation, emphasizing how he progressively refined the method to determine planetary distances with greater accuracy. Through a systematic analysis of Kepler’s calculations, this study reconstructs the steps by which Kepler transitioned from simple triangulation methods to a more sophisticated approach involving multiple observations with one celestial body at a fixed position. By following Kepler’s early reasoning, errors, and refinements, this paper sheds light on the intellectual processes that ultimately led to the breakthroughs presented in Astronomia Nova .

items.title: Neuromorphic Computing Architectures for Low-Power Edge Inference in IoT Applications
items.abstract: The blistering advancements witnessed in the Internet of Things (IoT) ecosystem have led to the urgency of search outcomes that provide energy efficient, low latency, and smart processing support that manifests itself right at the edge. The traditional edge computing devices built on von Neumann architecture are inherently limited by being optimized to be adjacent in memory and processing components, which results in the high power required and latency, which are highly undesirable in devices with limited power resources; wearables, smart sensors, and remote-monitoring systems. A Neuromorphic computing approach based on the human brain blueprint presents a better alternative due to its implementation of spiking neural networks (SNNs) that allow asynchronous and event-driven computation, thus dramatically lowering power demand and yet being able to run real-time inference. This paper includes a holistic comparison of the most recent examples of the neuromorphic hardware platforms, such as Intel Loihi, IBM TrueNorth, and BrainScaleS system, with regard to their learning architectures, energy consumption, throughput, and suitability to the edge-based IoT applications. An empirical case study is carried out, which is a keyword spotting case study and event-based gesture recognition case study using Google Speech Commands and the DVS Gesture dataset sets, respectively. The neuromorphic systems presented a significant energy per inference improvement up to 15x and reduced latency at about 30 on traditional ARM Cortex-M7-based ANN implementations at very slight sacrifices in terms of classification accuracy. In addition, the Loihi platform showed on-chip learning utilizing spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which made the platform capable of dynamic and adaptive inference in fluctuating IoT applications. This paper also examines the integration issues of neuromorphic systems which include the compatibility with sensor modalities, immature software toolchains, and complexities to convert ANN to SNN. The results indicate that neuromorphic systems are highly suitable in ultra-low-power edge intelligence and provide a paradigm of scalable and biologically inspired, next-generation IoT systems. The lines of future research are described in such aspects as hybrid neuromorphic edge-cloud learning, unification of benchmark requirements, and designing secure, programmable, and reconfigurable neuromorphic co-processors to support adaptive edge AI.

items.title: THE AUTOMATED ADMINISTRATION MAGAZINE
items.abstract: This magazine disseminates project results from a four-year research project on governance of AI and automated decision-making in the public sector. The Automated Administration (ADM-GOV) is a project with researchers from Swedish and Finnish universities, led by Lund University and funded by the Future Challenges in the Nordics Programme.For the past four years, we have been studying how AI and automated decision-making (ADM) can be implemented in the public sector without undermining fundamental rights, good governance, and trust in public institutions. You find results from studies on various related aspects reported on in this magazine – in articles, commentaries and interviews. In addition, given the impact AI tools have on the very means for production of texts, images and graphic design, in what we think of as a formative period, a secondary purpose with this magazine has been to conduct a meta exploration of normative boundaries of how AI impacts human creative output. By pointing to normative boundaries, we argue that some of the changes in norms – legal but importantly also informally social – are somewhat blurry at the moment, and in need of clarifying explorations. items.title: Glutamatergic Neurons in caudal Pontine Reticular Nucleus (PRNc) Mediate Backward Locomotion in mice
items.abstract: Locomotion is essential for animals to adaptively navigate their environment. However, despite extensive investigation into neural mechanisms underlying forward movement, the brain circuits controlling backward locomotion, a critical motor behavior for navigating confined spaces and avoiding threats, remain poorly understood. Here, using a specially designed behavioral paradigm for backward locomotion in mice, we find that glutamatergic neurons in the caudal pontine reticular nucleus (PRNc) are selectively activated during backward, but not forward, locomotion. Activity increase of these neurons is temporally aligned with backward movement, with its amplitude correlated with speed. Optogenetic manipulations further demonstrate that these neurons are both sufficient and necessary for initiating and sustaining backward walking. Moreover, anatomical tracing reveals that the PRNc broadly integrates bilateral cortical and subcortical inputs and projects extensively to brain-wide and spinal cord networks. These findings suggest PRNc as a previously unrecognized brainstem center in direction-specific locomotor control circuits. Key findings of this work and our initial identification of this brainstem locomotor node were presented at the Society for Neuroscience Annual Meeting in November, 15th, 2025 (SfN Neuroscience 2025, San Diego, CA; Program No. PSTR027.02).

items.title: JOINT ACTION AWARENESS IN MACAQUES DURING A MULTIPLAYER VIDEO-GAME CONTEXT
items.abstract: In behavioral neuroscience, research in nonhuman primates often relies on video game like paradigms, including studies of social interaction and joint action. In social studies, establishing whether animals monitor their partner and are aware of their reciprocal interactions in these abstract laboratory settings is essential for interpreting the processes underlying cooperative performance. Here, we examined spontaneous head orienting behavior in two macaques performing a cooperative visuomotor task under highly controlled conditions. The animals sat side by side with their heads unrestrained and used isometric joysticks to control their respective cursors displayed on a shared screen. Depending on trial instructions, they performed either individual actions (SOLO action, SA) or joint actions (JA) to obtain a reward. We quantified spontaneous head rotations toward the partner as an ethologically relevant behavioral indicator of social monitoring. Partner directed head turns occurred more frequently during JA than during SA trials. Crucially, their rate increased with the number of errors made by the partner during JA trials. Together, these findings indicate that macaques monitor their partner during abstract, computer-mediated cooperative interactions and that this monitoring is driven by the performance of the partner. Such spontaneous, context specific orienting toward the partner supports the interpretation that macaques are aware of their dyadic engagement, even in video game like settings. Our results therefore highlight the suitability of controlled visuomotor paradigms for investigating the cognitive-motor processes underlying joint action in nonhuman primates.

items.title: The social ecology of development: The changing structure of preschoolers’ everyday experiences at home
items.abstract: Everyday social interactions shape human psychological development. Research, however, has primarily relied on controlled settings or brief observations; consequently, the nature of naturalistic everyday experiences remains largely unstudied. To address this gap, we developed an automated multimodal processing pipeline to analyze a large egocentric corpus of naturalistic everyday experiences from 107 children aged three to five years in Germany (267.52 hours). The pipeline detects faces, persons, proximity, and speech types to classify time into interacting, available, or alone states. Results indicate a significant ecological reorganization: social interaction dominates at age three and declines towards a more even distribution between states at age six. Conversational agency remains stable throughout preschool, with children sharing it nearly equally with conversational partners. Crucially, social interactions change in their structure in that isolated social cues become significantly less predictive of interactions with age. Thus, preschool social interactions become less frequent but more diverse with development.

items.title: Examining Linking Language and Causal Implications in Observational Psychological Capital Research
items.abstract: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by Haber et al. (2022) in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology. Haber et al. found that causal relationships were implied through the language used to link exposures and outcomes and through recommendations for action. This small-scale conceptual replication applies Haber et al.’s approach to psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the domain of IO psychology. Specifically, we evaluate the causal strength of the language used to describe the nature of the connection between given variables when reporting findings and when making recommendations for action in 50 PsyCap articles. The majority of action recommendations were found to have strong causal implications (85% in abstracts, 84% in discussion sections), and most linking sentences implied some level of causality (64% in abstracts, 58% in discussion sections). This was despite very few articles explicitly stating an intention to estimate causal effects (10%) and many explicitly warning against drawing causal inferences (42%). No significant relationship was found between the causality implied in the linking sentences and the strength of causal implication of the action recommendations. These findings have important implications for how research is implemented, and very real consequences for those who are the focus of such implementations. Increased transparency about causal interests and reasoning is needed to uphold the credibility of findings and the integrity of applications of observational PsyCap research.

items.title: Factors Associated with Stunting, Underweight, and Wasting Among Children Under Five in Bangladesh: Evidence from the MICS 2025 Survey
items.abstract: Background: Childhood malnutrition remains a major public health concern in Bangladesh despite two decades of progress. Using the latest nationally representative data from Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) 2025, this study assesses the prevalence of stunting, underweight, and wasting among children under five and examines their association with child, maternal, household, and regional characteristics.. Methods: We analyzed data on 21,736 children under five years of age from MICS 2025. Rao-Scott chi-squared tests and survey-weighted multivariable logistic regression were used to examine associations between socio-demographic factors and each malnutrition outcome. Results: Weighted prevalence was 24% for stunting, 23% for underweight, and 13% for wasting. Stunting peaked at 12-35 months (AOR = 2.13, 95% CI: 1.82-2.50 for 12-23 months), whereas underweight was highest at 48-59 months (AOR = 1.88, 95% CI: 1.60-2.22). Girls had lower odds than boys of stunting (AOR = 0.92, 95% CI: 0.85-0.99), underweight (AOR = 0.93, 95% CI: 0.86-1.00), and wasting (AOR = 0.84, 95% CI: 0.76-0.92). Children from the richest households had substantially lower odds of stunting (AOR = 0.48, 95% CI: 0.41-0.56), underweight (AOR = 0.50, 95% CI: 0.42-0.58), and wasting (AOR = 0.71, 95% CI: 0.59-0.86). Maternal higher secondary education or above was protective against stunting (AOR = 0.57, 95% CI: 0.47-0.69) and underweight (AOR = 0.63, 95% CI: 0.51-0.76). Children in Sylhet had higher odds of stunting (AOR = 1.37, 95% CI: 1.15-1.64) and underweight (AOR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.18-1.67) than those in Barishal. Conclusions: Household wealth, children sex and birth order, maternal education, and geographic division are the main correlates of child malnutrition in Bangladesh. Equity-focused, region-specific interventions and continued national surveillance are needed to accelerate progress toward SDG 2.2.

items.title: Acceptability, Safety and Feasibility of a Sedentary Behaviour Intervention (REACH-SCI) in Individuals with Spinal Cord Injury: A Mixed-Methods Study
items.abstract: Purpose: Individuals with paraplegia often have high levels of sedentary behaviour, which increases cardiovascular disease risk. This study assessed the acceptability, safety and feasibility of a sedentary behaviour intervention (REACH-SCI) in individuals with paraplegia. Materials and methods: A pre-post feasibility study was conducted in wheelchair-users with paraplegia (n=18) to evaluate an 8-week intervention comprised of a wearable activity tracker, educational booklet, goal setting, motivational support sessions, peer support and activity tools (Trial registration: NCT06957483 ). Acceptability was assessed via semi-structured interviews and questionnaires, safety via adverse events, pain and fatigue, and intervention feasibility via components being delivered as intended. Intervention engagement and preliminary efficacy were also assessed. Results: The intervention and study procedures were acceptable and safe, intervention components were delivered as planned, and the study was feasible in terms of participant recruitment, retention and data completion rates. Engagement with intervention components was generally high, except for peer support. The intervention demonstrated preliminary efficacy for improving sedentary behaviour, physical activity, cardiovascular disease biomarkers and psychosocial outcomes. Conclusions: An intervention to reduce sedentary behaviour in individuals with paraplegia was acceptable, safe and feasible. The effectiveness of REACH-SCI should be evaluated in a definitive trial to inform clinical care and public health guidelines.

items.title: Health workers' and administrators' experiences of duty handover on maternity wards in public health facilities in Hoima District, Uganda: a qualitative phenomenological study
items.abstract: Background: Duty handover is a high-risk point in the continuity of maternity care, and breakdowns in handover communication have been linked to delayed care and avoidable harm. Qualitative evidence from maternity wards in low-resource Sub-Saharan African settings is limited, and to our knowledge no study has examined handover experiences on maternity wards in Hoima District, Uganda. This study explored the experiences and challenges of health workers and administrators regarding duty handover on maternity wards in public health facilities in Hoima District, Uganda. Methods: We conducted a qualitative phenomenological study. Fifteen in-depth interviews with maternity ward health workers and five key informant interviews with administrators were carried out across six public health facilities. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim and analysed using a modified Colaizzi seven-step method. Reflexivity and bracketing were addressed through a pre-fieldwork assumptions statement and bracketing interview, a reflexive journal kept throughout data collection, and independent double-coding of a subset of transcripts. Results: Two themes were identified: duty handover practices on maternity wards, and challenges experienced by health workers during handover. Handover was inconsistent in structure, duration and adherence to protocol, and relied heavily on informal telephone communication rather than structured face-to-face reporting. Standardised tools were used in some facilities only. Participants identified time constraints and workload, inadequate training, limited resources and supervision, negative staff attitudes, and difficulty accessing patient information as key challenges, and linked communication breakdowns to delays and errors in care. Patients and families were largely not involved in handover. Conclusions: Duty handover on the maternity wards studied was inconsistent and constrained by capability-, opportunity- and motivation-related barriers operating together. Standardised and locally adapted handover tools, targeted training, stronger supervision and facility- and national-level guidance appear necessary to protect continuity of care in comparable low-resource maternity settings. Keywords: duty handover; maternity care; patient safety; qualitative research; phenomenology; Sub-Saharan Africa; Uganda

items.title: Improving Antenatal Syphilis Screening and Treatment Coverage in Public Health Facilities in Kampala, Uganda: A Pre-Implementation and Implementation-Phase Study
items.abstract: Introduction: Congenital syphilis (CS) remains a major cause of preventable adverse pregnancy outcomes globally, driven by poor antenatal care (ANC) quality, health-system barriers, and untreated maternal infection. In Uganda, syphilis screening and treatment coverage remains below national targets. We evaluated service-delivery impact of a multi-component syphilis testing and treatment intervention implemented across four public health facilities in Kampala, Uganda. Methods: Guided by the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR), the intervention introduced same-day dual HIV/syphilis antibody testing, on-site treatment, and partner notification at three ANC facilities with women with serological evidence of syphilis or unknown syphilis status and infant follow-up at a tertiary referral hospital. Facility register data were compared between a pre-implementation period (January-December 2020) and the implementation period (June 2021-July 2022) using a modified Poisson regression model adjusting for site. Results: Syphilis screening among women attending their first ANC visit increased from 55.2% to 88.3% (+33.6%; 95% CI 21.0-46.3; p Conclusions: A same-day rapid test-and-treat intervention substantially improved maternal syphilis screening and treatment coverage, even during the COVID-19 pandemic, but partner and infant treatment completion remained major gaps in the care cascade. Structural interventions, including integrated maternal-infant care pathways and targeting of high-risk mothers along with their male partners, are needed to close these gaps and advance progress toward the elimination of mother-to-child transmission of syphilis.

items.title: Anopheles Mosquito Distribution and Malaria Outbreak Risk Assessment in Georgia, USA (2001 2025): Implications for Surveillance and Preparedness.
items.abstract: Competent malaria vector species in Georgia represents an emerging public health threat. Despite the successful elimination of endemic malaria transmission from the United States, the entomological conditions necessary for reestablishment of local transmission still persists across ecologically permissive regions of the south-eastern United States. However, no comprehensive, county level assessment of Anopheles mosquito distribution and associated malaria outbreak risk has been conducted across the state. This study analyzed 2,716 Anopheles collection records, representing 11,265 individual specimens, from 24 years of surveillance data (2001 to 2025). Results classified Fulton County as a high risk hot spot and critical convergence zone for malaria outbreak with the most significantly highest risk score (25), Anopheles population density (2,561) and elevated MIR activity (> 4.1%). Glynn and Lowndes counties were designated as moderate risk (15 and 12, respectively), driven primarily by substantial Anopheles populations. Conversely, DeKalb County, despite exhibiting the highest individual infection rate (MIR: 6.67%), was classified low risk (Score: 10) due to lower Anopheles abundance. Our results underscore the need for improved mosquito surveillance in high-risk counties, to address the dual health threat of arboviral and potential human malaria outbreaks under current climate change scenarios in Georgia.

items.title: Estimating healthcare cost savings from greenspace in Washington
items.abstract: Greenspace is increasingly recognized as public-health infrastructure, yet its potential contribution to healthcare cost savings remains poorly quantified beyond a relatively small number of studies. To contribute to these investigations, we estimated potential avoided healthcare expenditures associated with residential greenness in Washington using a benefit-transfer framework. We applied decile-specific relative healthcare-cost ratios from a Northern California cohort of approximately five million Kaiser Permanente members to population-weighted distributions of satellite-derived normalized difference vegetation index across Washington census block groups. Ratios were calibrated to Washington’s 2020 statewide per-capita healthcare expenditure, allowing estimates to reflect the state’s own cost baseline. Estimated annual per-capita costs declined from $6,472.75 in the least-green decile to $5,939.39 in the greenest, a difference of $533.35. Simulated interventions yielded estimated annual statewide savings of $45.6 million from raising the lowest decile to the next decile, $157.7 million from lifting the four lowest deciles to Decile five, and $56.9 million from urban-core greening in Washington’s five largest cities. These estimates are modeled associations, not causal forecasts, and depend on transferability between regional populations and on normalized difference vegetation index as an incomplete proxy for meaningful nature access. Nonetheless, the findings highlight increased and equitable greening efforts as a potentially consequential component of preventive health and infrastructure policy.

items.title: Estimating the burden of non-susceptible pneumococcal community-acquired pneumonia using probabilistic modelling and routinely collected hospitalization data
items.abstract: Abstract Background Global estimates have established antimicrobial resistance (AMR) as a major public health threat, but translating this burden into locally actionable estimates remains challenging where integrated epidemiological and microbiological data are scarce. We developed a bottom-up probabilistic framework combining routinely collected hospitalisation data with pathogen attribution and antimicrobial non-susceptibility estimates to quantify AMR burden at the pathogen, syndrome, and resistance level. Methods We integrated statewide bacterial community-acquired pneumonia (bCAP) hospitalisations in São Paulo, Brazil, during 2022–25 with pneumococcal attribution estimates from a structured evidence review and age-specific penicillin and ceftriaxone non-susceptibility from statewide surveillance. Monte Carlo simulations propagated parameter uncertainty, and global sensitivity analysis identified its main drivers. Findings Among 444,198 bCAP hospitalisations, 192,026 were estimated as pneumococcal CAP (pCAP). Of these, 74,985 were attributable to penicillin-non-susceptible and 45,224 to ceftriaxone-non-susceptible pneumococci. Estimated pCAP burden was 49,789 (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 11,103–87,186) among children younger than 5 years and 142,237 (39,147–262,706) among individuals aged 5 years or older. Across all scenarios, pneumococcal attribution was the dominant driver of uncertainty. Interpretation This bottom-up framework converts routinely available but fragmented data into locally relevant AMR burden estimates while quantifying and attributing uncertainty. It revealed a substantial burden of non-susceptible pneumococcal pneumonia and identified pathogen attribution as the principal evidence gap limiting precision. The approach could complement global AMR estimates by providing actionable subnational estimates and is potentially scalable to other pathogen, syndrome, and resistance combinations.

items.title: Encountering a newcomer attenuates shared evaluative standards: experimental evidence of rapid emergence and partial persistence
items.abstract: Abstract Collective activity requires individuals to converge on common yardsticks for judging the world; however, it remains unclear how these evaluative standards (ES) respond when a group encounters unfamiliar members. Using a newly developed dot-estimation task informed by Sherif’s classic norm-formation studies, this study experimentally tracked (a) how shared ES emerge through dyadic interactions and (b) how they respond to a newcomer whose judgements systematically diverge. Participants first completed rounds with a partner whose estimates gradually aligned with their own, with perceptual bias shifting reliably toward that partner’s standard within a single block of thirty trials. However, when a newcomer with divergent estimates entered, participants partially shifted toward the newcomer’s standard, while their responses suggested carryover from the prior interaction. Impressions of the divergent newcomer did not depend on whether participants had previously established a shared standard with another partner, indicating that brief behavioural alignment does not by itself generate derogation of a divergent other. Taken together, these findings show that shared ES form quickly through dyadic interaction and, although attenuated by exposure to a newcomer, persist in part within individuals. Understanding the micro-dynamics of their formation and partial persistence helps explain how groups negotiate common standards and how those standards may attenuate—without fully unravelling—when group composition changes.

items.title: ‘I'm Not Smoking; I'm Just Vaping’: Deciphering the Reasons for and Against Vaping and Intention to Quit Among Young Consumers
items.abstract: Abstract Vaping has become a defining feature of youth culture and a fast‐expanding consumer practice, yet little is known about how young people rationalize their continued use despite awareness of health risks and social controversy. Drawing on behavioral reasoning theory (BRT) and insights from social identity theory (SIT), this study examines how young consumers construct, compare and prioritize reasons for and against vaping under conditions of uncertainty, thereby deciphering their intention to quit. Using a mixed‐methods design, it combines 21 in‐depth interviews with a survey of 804 young adult vapers in the UK. The findings indicate that conspiracy beliefs, scepticism and perceived uncountability are positively associated with relative disadvantage, which in turn predicts ambivalence and subsequently intention to quit. Ambivalence, in turn, is linked with stronger intention to quit, particularly among individuals with a strong future time perspective, whereas fear of social exclusion appears to weaken the effect of relative disadvantage on ambivalence. The study advances BRT by using evaluability as a conceptual lens to explain why certain reasons become more salient. By integrating cognitive reasoning with social identity, it offers theoretical and policy insights for enhancing health communication and fostering more informed behavioural engagement among young consumers.

items.title: Changes in Observed Social Behaviours Following an Eight-Week Music-Based Programme for Autistic Children in Vietnam: An Exploratory Single-Group Study
items.abstract: Children with autism and their peers find shared musical activities an accessible way to have shared experiences, to engage in reciprocal activities, and to participate in a nonverbal way. However, scores achieved within a music education program do not automatically translate into scores that can be used to measure long-term gains in children’s social communication in everyday situations. The purpose of this study was to investigate changes in scores for a social-behavior observation index, which was specifically developed for the music program, as well as the scores for individual items, for a group of autistic children from Vietnam after an 8-week music-based education program. The program consisted of 16 sessions of singing, of learning and doing Vietnamese traditional rhymes and folk songs, of playing with musical instruments, of moving, and of cooperation in musical games. The ratings for eight different behaviors of 10 children with autism (T01–T10) were summed up on a three-point researcher-made observation index, resulting in total scores ranging from 8 to 24. The paired data of total scores for each of the children were analyzed using an exploratory paired analysis. Descriptive statistics were calculated for the total and for the paired data. In addition, the paired data were analyzed using an exact two-sided test, namely the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Finally, the mean ratings for the individual items at the endpoint were reported. The mean composite score of the 10 children with autism increased from 12.5 (SD 1.08) at pretest to 20.8 (SD 2.39) at posttest. The mean difference of paired scores was 8.30 (SD 1.49). All paired difference scores of the 10 children had a positive sign, hence higher scores at posttest than at pretest. The exploratory p-value was .002. The highest mean rating for the individual items at the posttest was for participation in activities at 2.90. The lowest mean rating was for emotional expression and for emotional and behavioral regulation, both at 2.20. However, without a comparison group of children with autism, without sufficient evidence supporting the use of the observation index and without documentation for several of the sources used in this study, the findings of this study are best considered as a preliminary account that needs to be further developed in a more rigorous and context-sensitive manner.
