items.title: Circuit architecture and regulation of the Drosophila brain neuroendocrine system.
items.abstract: Insect neurosecretory cells (NSCs), located in distinct regions of the brain and the ventral nerve cord (VNC), are a major source of neuropeptides and peptide hormones (NPHs) that facilitate communication between the nervous system and peripheral tissues. NPHs, in turn, regulate growth and development, and modulate diverse behaviors and physiological processes including feeding, locomotion, social behaviors, metabolism, and reproduction. Given their central role in regulating systemic homeostasis, NSCs are tightly regulated. Recent advances in connectomics and single-cell transcriptomics have enabled comprehensive identification of NSCs in the Drosophila melanogaster brain and identified factors that modulate their activity. Here, we review the current state-of-the-art on insect NSCs and the inputs regulating them, predominantly focusing on adult Drosophila. We highlight: 1) major synaptic inputs, 2) neuromodulatory inputs, 3) gut-derived NPHs, and 4) cell-autonomous internal sensors that influence NSC activity. Finally, we discuss open questions in the field and how advances in omics approaches can bridge the gap in our understanding of NSC regulation between Drosophila and other insects.

items.title: Mechanisms of Seizure Generation and SUDEP in Cortical Dysplasia: A Role for Cortical Up and Down States.
items.abstract: Sudden unexpected death in epilepsy (SUDEP) remains the primary cause of epilepsy-related mortality, yet the preictal brain dynamics that distinguish fatal from nonfatal seizures are not well understood. Identifying the network mechanisms determining these outcomes is critical for developing SUDEP risk biomarkers. Using a neuron-specific PTEN knockout mouse model of cortical dysplasia-which exhibits spontaneous seizures and SUDEP-like events-we employed long-term video-EEG monitoring to analyze cortical state transitions and network signatures. We found that nonfatal seizures are preceded by a progressive "ramp-up" of cortical up and down states, characterized by alternating neuronal depolarization and hyperpolarization, which appears to facilitate seizure initiation. In sharp contrast, sudden death is preceded by a marked suppression of these state transitions and the emergence of infraslow EEG activity, suggestive of spreading depolarizations. This pattern differed from the sustained spike-wave complexes and preserved state transitions observed during status epilepticus. These physiological differences are mirrored behaviorally: nonfatal events typically feature forelimb clonus and spike-wave discharges, whereas fatal seizures are characterized by kicking, tonic hindlimb extension, and diffuse EEG attenuation. Together, these findings suggest that cortical up and down states support seizure initiation, while their disruption and failure to recover postictally predisposes neocortical networks to spreading depression episodes that very likely propagate to brainstem circuits, ultimately triggering SUDEP. By delineating these divergent peri-ictal signatures, this study identifies candidate neurophysiological markers for SUDEP risk stratification.

items.title: Cross-species evaluation of commercial primary antibodies by Western blotting for immunohistochemical protein detection in mouse, rat, and human brain tissue.
items.abstract: Background Commercial antibodies show variable specificity and performance, limiting reproducibility of immunohistochemical studies. We systematically evaluated antibodies used to detect brain proteins across species. New method Established Western blotting (WB) and immunofluorescence (IF) validation approaches were applied systematically and in parallel to mouse, rat, and human brain tissue. The distinctive scope of the study was the comparative evaluation of 23 antibodies targeting 17 proteins, with WB results interpreted in the context of expected molecular weights, isoforms, post-translational modifications, and published evidence concerning each target. Antibody performance was further compared with publicly available validation information, and logistic regression was used to assess whether antibody citation count and manufacturer-provided validation information predicted successful experimental validation. Results Ten antibodies (43%) showed supportive WB results, and eight (35%) were validated by both WB and IF. Several antibodies produced unexplained or non-specific bands, while others showed speciesdependent performance. Validated antibodies displayed appropriate neuroanatomical and subcellular staining patterns. Antibody citation count was moderately associated with successful validation, whereas manufacturer-provided validation information did not improve predictive performance. Comparison with existing methods The overall validation rate was comparable to previously published antibody validation studies and Human Protein Atlas results. The present study extends existing work through its broader antibody panel, parallel cross-species evaluation, detailed target-protein assessment, and quantitative analysis of antibody metadata. Conclusions Commercial antibodies require independent validation before use in cross-species immunohistochemical studies. Our results provide a practical resource for antibody selection and highlight limitations of manufacturer claims and citation counts as indicators of antibody performance.

items.title: Baseline Adjustment and Normalisation in Neurite Outgrowth Assays: A Simulation-Based Comparison of Analytical Methods.
items.abstract: Background When baseline neurite lengths differ between experimental groups, analytical methods may detect, miss or overstate treatment effects. We assessed how commonly used methods recover a baseline-adjusted treatment effect. New method We developed a simulation framework comparing endpoint comparison, change score, percentage change, percent-of-control normalisation and ANCOVA. A known 8 μm treatment effect was simulated under varying baseline imbalances and baseline-growth relationships, with additional analyses of sample size and baseline measurement error. Results In the worked example, endpoint comparison and percent-of-control normalisation did not recover the true adjusted effect, whereas change score overestimated it by 55%. Across 20 parameter combinations, ANCOVA maintained nominal Type I error (3.8-5.8%) and remained essentially unbiased (mean absolute bias: 0.02 μm) when baseline was measured without error. Small-sample analyses showed that systematic bias persisted while error rates varied with sample size. Substantial baseline measurement error reduced ANCOVA's bias advantage and could inflate its Type I error. Comparison with existing methods Endpoint and percent-of-control approaches estimate unadjusted endpoint differences. Change scores can be distorted when baseline predicts subsequent growth, while percentage change additionally introduces denominator-related distortion when baselines differ. ANCOVA directly estimates the treatment effect at a common baseline under its standard assumptions. Conclusions When the target is a baseline-adjusted effect and baseline is measured reliably, ANCOVA provides the most appropriate analysis under the conditions examined. Baseline values, the target estimand and assumption checks should be reported explicitly.

items.title: A study protocol of fasting to provide energy needed to help adults in need of cognitive enhancement (Fasting ENHANCE).
items.abstract: Background Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) is defined as a self-perceived reduction in cognitive function and is associated with future cognitive impairment. However, few clinical trials have explored the impact of nonpharmacological interventions in older adults with SCD. Time-restricted eating (TRE) restricts food intake to a daily eating window and has shown improvements in cardiometabolic markers associated with cognitive impairment. Objective The Fasting to provide Energy Needed to Help Adults in Need of Cognitive Enhancement (Fasting ENHANCE) study is a rater-blinded, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial, designed to evaluate the effects of TRE on cognitive function in overweight older adults with SCD. Methods The study aims to enroll older adults (aged ≥65 years) who are overweight (BMI ≥25 kg/m 2 ) and have SCD without objective impairment. Participants are randomized to either a 6-month TRE or Successful Aging (SA) group. The TRE group is instructed to restrict eating to an 8-h window, and the SA group to maintain current lifestyle behaviors. The primary outcome is change in cognitive function, assessed using the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status and Montreal Cognitive Assessment at baseline, 3 months, and 6 months. Secondary outcomes include physical function, blood biomarkers, and self-reported mood, sleep, and quality of life. Conclusion The Fasting ENHANCE study protocol outlines the methodology for evaluating the effect of TRE on cognitive and metabolic health in older adults with SCD. Results will inform future nonpharmacological interventions aimed at attenuating cognitive decline. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT05732935.

items.title: Zinc activates autophagy by regulating HDAC6 expression following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion injury.
items.abstract: Intracellular zinc accumulation and excessive autophagy have been reported to contribute to neuronal death following cerebral ischemia/reperfusion (I/R). Histone deacetylase 6 (HDAC6), which contains a zinc-dependent active site, is closely associated with autophagy. However, the relationship between zinc, HDAC6 and autophagy following cerebral I/R remains unclear. In this study, we aim to investigate whether ischemia-induced zinc accumulation activates autophagy through HDAC6. Rats were treated with zinc chelator, autophagy activator/inhibitor or HDAC6 inhibitor during a 90-minute middle cerebral artery occlusion. Infarct volume, neurological deficits, protein expression, and the colocalization of HDAC6, Beclin1, and zinc in neurons were evaluated. Our results demonstrate that beclin1 expression was significantly increased after cerebral I/R and this elevation was markedly attenuated by zinc chelation. Notably, reactivation of autophagy with rapamycin significantly, though not completely, diminished TPEN-mediated neuroprotection, suggesting that zinc-induced autophagy is an important contributor to neuronal injury following cerebral I/R. Moreover, immunofluorescence revealed that HDAC6 was colocalized with Beclin1 in the penumbra of ischemic rats, and inhibition of HDAC6 reduced Beclin1 expression and alleviated brain injury. Molecular docking analysis suggested a potential interaction between HDAC6 and α-tubulin, which may influence autophagy by regulating microtubule stability and autophagosome transport. Furthermore, chelating zinc decreased HDAC6 expression, while HDAC6 inhibition did not influence zinc levels, demonstrating that zinc acts upstream of HDAC6. In conclusion, our findings identify a novel zinc-HDAC6-autophagy signaling axis underlying neuronal injury following cerebral I/R, suggesting that targeting zinc homeostasis or HDAC6 may represent a promising therapeutic strategy.

items.title: Behavioral and motor deficits following traumatic brain injury: implications for post-traumatic epilepsy.
items.abstract: Post-traumatic epilepsy (PTE) is a severe complication of traumatic brain injury (TBI). Patients with PTE often experience comorbid neurobehavioral deficits, which further reduce the quality of life and impede the recovery of patients. This review examines behavioral and motor deficits associated with PTE across clinical and preclinical studies, with an emphasis on the need to identify PTE-specific phenotypes that may serve as biomarkers of disease development and progression, as well as distinguish PTE from other forms of epilepsy. Despite growing evidence of post-TBI behavioral and motor abnormalities, their relationship with PTE remains unclear, particularly in preclinical models where direct comparisons are limited between animals that do and do not develop PTE. We further evaluate the application of artificial intelligence (AI) for characterizing these phenotypes throughout post-traumatic epileptogenesis, highlighting its potential to provide automated, objective, and sensitive measures of functional outcomes.

items.title: Brain-State-Resolved Consistency of Corticospinal Responses to TMS.
items.abstract: Background An important feature of motor-evoked potential (MEP) responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over the primary motor cortex (M1) is their substantial trial-to-trial variability. Ongoing brain activity at the time of TMS, such as the power and phase of the sensorimotor mu rhythm, influences MEP amplitude. It is unclear to what extent these endogenous brain states also shape the consistency of MEP amplitude across trials. Objectives We investigated trial-to-trial variability of MEP amplitude as a function of pre-stimulus mu dynamics. Methods Twenty-nine healthy participants received 1200 single TMS pulses over the left M1 during simultaneous electroencephalography (EEG) recording; 10 participants completed two sessions to assess inter-session reproducibility. Trials were stratified based on pre-stimulus mu power, phase, and interhemispheric M1-M1 functional connectivity. Brain-state-resolved MEP variability was quantified using the coefficient of variation (CV) within subsets of trials defined by similar pre-stimulus mu dynamics. Results Trial subsets characterized by high mu power were associated with reduced MEP variability, indicating more consistent corticospinal output. In contrast, mu phase did not significantly influence MEP variability at the group level. Mu power group-level effects were reproducible across sessions in an exploratory test-retest analysis and across experimental sites. Conclusions We show that inter-trial consistency of MEP amplitude reflects a structured, brain-state-dependent feature of the sensorimotor network. These findings contribute to our mechanistic understanding of trial-to-trial variability in TMS-evoked responses. This may provide a basis for future TMS approaches aimed at reducing response variability and improving the consistency of neuromodulatory effects.

items.title: Systemic D1-like receptor activation during song exposure biases the emergence of song selectivity in the juvenile zebra finch NCM.
items.abstract: Vocal learning requires juveniles to form auditory representations of adult vocal models that guide vocal practice. The caudomedial nidopallium (NCM), a higher-order auditory pallial region in songbirds, has been implicated in tutor-song memory and receives dopaminergic input, but whether dopamine receptor activation biases the emergence of song-specific selectivity during development remains unclear. We recorded NCM single-unit activity in juvenile male zebra finches with limited tutor-song exposure. One adult song was repeatedly presented after systemic administration of the D1-like receptor agonist SKF-38393, the D2-like receptor agonist quinpirole, or saline, and neural selectivity was assessed before and after pairing. Pairing did not produce a uniform population-wide shift in average selectivity. However, a linear mixed-effects model accounting for pre-pairing selectivity and multiple units per bird revealed significantly higher post-pairing selectivity in SKF-treated units than in saline-treated units. SKF-treated units also differed from quinpirole-treated units, whereas quinpirole and saline did not differ. Among initially non-selective units, threshold-defined gains occurred in 31.3% of SKF, 15.4% of saline, and 10.8% of quinpirole units, with SKF showing the highest gained fraction across all tested thresholds. Although the exact bird-label permutation test was not significant, continuous and threshold-based analyses provided convergent unit-level evidence for an SKF-associated enhancement of paired-song selectivity. These findings support neuromodulatory gating as a potential mechanism by which developmental auditory experience shapes stimulus-specific sensory representations.

items.title: An MRI-compatible electrode implantation system for linking behavioral neurophysiology and stimulation-evoked fMRI in non-human primates.
items.abstract: Local electrophysiology and microstimulation reveal site-specific neural activity and physiological effects but do not directly link these local effects to whole-brain responses from the same target site. We developed an MRI-compatible electrode implantation system for macaques that enables CT/MRI-based localization, postoperative depth adjustment, neural recording, microstimulation during behavioral testing, and subsequent electrical microstimulation combined with functional MRI (EM-fMRI) using the same implanted electrode. The system supported local field potential recording, a stimulation-induced reduction in pupil size, and distributed stimulation-evoked blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) responses. This approach provides a practical framework for linking local neural activity and stimulation-induced physiological responses with whole-brain responses at the same target site.

items.title: Frustration Induction Alters Reward Prediction Error Encoding in Pediatric Irritability.
items.abstract: Background Irritability is a prevalent, impairing, transdiagnostic affective symptom domain in youth associated with elevated risk for adverse outcomes. Theoretical models of irritability implicate disruptions in reward learning and frustrative nonreward. This is the first study to investigate reward prediction error (RPE) signaling before and after frustration as a neural correlate of irritability. Methods We used reinforcement learning modeling to derive individualized trial-by-trial RPEs from behavior during a child-friendly, fMRI-based probabilistic reward learning task in 88 youth (M age =14.43 years, 48.86% female). Irritability severity varied across participants and was characterized dimensionally. Neural encoding of RPEs was examined across prefrontal, ventral striatal/pallidal, and insular regions of interest (ROIs). To test the impact of frustration, RPE-modulated BOLD activity was assessed before and after an acute frustration induction. Results Prior to frustration induction, higher irritability was associated with enhanced positive coupling between trial-by-trial RPEs and BOLD activity in the ventral striatal/pallidal ROI. Following frustration, this pattern reversed, such that higher irritability was associated with attenuated positive coupling between RPEs and BOLD activity in ventral striatal/pallidal and right insular areas, indicating decreased neural encoding of reward outcomes. Irritability was not associated with RPE-modulated orbitofrontal or left insular activity. Conclusion Findings provide computationally-grounded evidence linking youth irritability to altered neural RPE encoding during learning and a reversal following task-induced frustration. This emotional state-dependent change in RPE-BOLD coupling suggests that frustration disrupts the neural encoding of reward outcomes during reward learning in youth with elevated irritability and highlights a candidate target for interventions addressing frustration reactivity.

items.title: Infant Negative Affect During Mother-Infant Interaction Is Associated with Neonatal Limbic-Prefrontal Connectivity in the First Month of Life.
items.abstract: Background Early caregiving may shape neonatal limbic circuit organization, yet whether microanalytically coded interaction quality relates to neonatal limbic-prefrontal connectivity is unknown. We tested associations between infant and maternal affect during mother-infant interaction and neonatal limbic-prefrontal cortex (PFC) connectivity. Methods At approximately 30 days postnatal, 143 mother-infant dyads from the Healthy MiNDS cohort (São Paulo, Brazil) completed a video-recorded interaction coded with the Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB) system; infant negative affect was the percentage of interaction time in distress. Neonates underwent resting-state fMRI; limbic-PFC connectivity was quantified by principal component analysis of amygdala and hippocampus seed-to-ROI maps. Covariate-adjusted regressions tested associations. Results Infant negative affect was associated with right amygdala-PFC (β = -0.247, p = .003) and right hippocampus-PFC connectivity (β = -0.202, p = .021), both surviving FDR correction and robust across multiple analytic approaches. The amygdala association was limited to infant distress-related behaviors, whereas maternal positive expressiveness showed an independent, opposing association (β = 0.202, p = .019); no other CIB measure was significant. Exploratorily, connectivity was associated with sleep problems at 18-24 months in females (r = -.324, p = .030). Conclusions The emotional quality of early caregiving is associated with neonatal limbic circuit organization: infant distress is selectively associated with weaker amygdala-PFC connectivity, whereas maternal positive affect shows an independent opposing association. These findings identify the mother-infant relationship as a modifiable input to neonatal brain development.

items.title: Decoding individual differences in mental information from human brain responses predicted by deep neural networks.
items.abstract: Brain decoding using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has high potential for evaluating unobservable mental information that varies across individuals in everyday situations. Although estimating individual differences in mental information using brain decoding could be effective for social applications, especially in neuromarketing, the physical constraints and high costs of fMRI limit the practical application in real-world settings. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework to estimate individual differences in decodable mental information using brain responses predicted by deep neural networks (DNNs). In this framework, DNN-based models are trained to predict fMRI responses to natural movie scenes. Then, additional fMRI measurements are no longer required because mental information for new movie scenes can be decoded from the predicted responses instead of the measured ones. A large-scale analysis revealed that the proposed predicted-response decoding captures individual difference patterns consistent with those derived from conventional measured-response decoding across various cognitive domains. Of the 88 cognitive labels associated with movie scenes, individual difference patterns could be captured for more than 70% of the labels. This framework offers a promising approach for evaluating personal mental information with substantially reduced reliance on fMRI, thereby expanding the potential for social applications of brain decoding.

items.title: Neurodegeneration in Sub-Saharan Africa: Intersections of Biological Ageing, Genomic Diversity and the Lifetime Exposome.
items.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases are emerging as an important consequence of population ageing in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), but their scientific relevance extends beyond a projected rise in case numbers. SSA combines exceptional human genomic diversity with marked heterogeneity in vascular and metabolic risk, infection, nutrition, occupational exposures, air pollution, and access to health care. This combination creates an underused setting in which to study why biological ageing produces neurodegeneration in some individuals but relative resilience in others. This review critically synthesises evidence on Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, Parkinson's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis/frontotemporal degeneration, Huntington's disease and related disorders, focusing on the intersection between hallmarks of ageing, disease-specific proteinopathies, ancestry and the lifetime exposome. Age-associated loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, impaired autophagy, chronic inflammation, neurovascular injury and genomic/epigenomic instability provide a mechanistic scaffold on which genetic susceptibility and cumulative exposures may act. Yet African evidence remains dominated by cross-sectional clinical phenotyping; neuropathology, longitudinal biomarkers, multi-omics and measured environmental exposures remain sparse. Recent African-ancestry Parkinson's disease genomics and emerging plasma biomarker studies demonstrate that ancestry-inclusive molecular neuroscience is feasible and can generate findings not predictable from European-ancestry datasets. The next phase should therefore move beyond documenting underdiagnosis toward longitudinal, biologically anchored cohorts that integrate phenotype, genomics, blood biomarkers, neuroimaging, exposomics, digital measures and health-system outcomes. This review proposes a research framework centred on biological ageing, gene-environment interaction and resilience. Such work would improve the validity of prevention, diagnosis and therapeutic translation in African populations while contributing globally to a more complete biology of neurodegenerative ageing.

items.title: Circulating immune cells phenotypes discriminate bipolar disorder from major depressive disorder during a depressive episode: A machine learning elastic-net approach.
items.abstract: MDD and BD are characterized by differences in peripheral immune markers, in frequencies of T helper, T cytotoxic, Natural Killer (NK) and T regulatory cells that may contribute to the development of mood disorders. However, few studies have used immune cells populations to discriminate MDD from BD with inconsistent findings. We applied an elastic-net machine learning pipeline predictive model using 5-fold nested cross-validation based on a wide panel of immune cell populations to discriminate between MDD and BD. The sample included 124 MDD and 89 BD hospitalised for depressive episode, and 40 healthy controls (HC). The predictive model achieved an accuracy of 78%, with 76% sensitivity, 80% specificity. The model performed significantly better than chance (p + IFN-γ, CD4 + IL-17, CD4 + TNF-α, CD8 + TNF-α, NK cells/TNF-α), and regulatory cells (FOXP3), whereas MDD diagnosis was associated with elevated frequencies of early activating memory cells both T helper and cytotoxic (i.e. CD4 + CM/CD69 + , CD4 + EM/CD69 + , CD8 + CM/CD69 + ), and cytotoxic effector cells producing apoptotic proteins (CD8 + EM/Perf + GrzB + , NK cells/Perf + GrzB + ). Excluding patients in lithium only early activated and cytotoxic cells differentiated the two diagnoses. Limitations include possible residual instrument-related effects and cryopreservation effects, lack of generalization to other phases of the illness, lack of external validation. Our data confirm that MDD and BD show different immune signatures and suggest a more pronounced alteration of immune cell populations in MDD especially in cytotoxic CD8+ cells. Future studies should address these differences to develop more effective therapies for mood disorders.

items.title: An accidental ultrasonic noise source in the mouse facility activating a band of neurons in the inferior colliculus.
items.abstract: Experimental animals are housed under tightly regulated conditions to standardize experiments and minimize the number of animals per experiment. Ultrasonic noise pollution is a potential problem in housing as it is inaudible for humans, and may thus remain undetected, whereas most laboratory animals can hear ultrasound. Compared with sounds audible to humans, ultrasonic noise has received much less attention, yet it can likewise induce physiological and behavioral effects in animals, including deleterious effects on welfare and on experimental reproducibility. In this study, we accidentally discovered that our mouse stable was polluted by an ultrasonic beep emitted by a radio. To investigate the impact of this beep, we tested under which conditions this beep would activate neurons in the inferior colliculus (IC) using the c-fos promotor in TRAP2 mice as a marker for activation. Exposure to the beep of the radio activated a band of neurons. A similar band was observed in the TRAP2 mice following exposure to a beep with the same frequency as the radio beep, and the location of the bands in both cases agreed with the tonotopic organization of the IC. A similar ultrasonic tone was observed in more than half of commercially available radios, indicating that the presence of a radio is likely to expose animals to a continuous tone that is inaudible to humans. Based on our findings, we therefore recommend that animal facilities routinely check for ultrasonic noise contamination to increase animal welfare and enhance study reproducibility.

items.title: Alerting acoustic stimuli enhance the internal representation of head direction.
items.abstract: Animals rapidly execute goal-directed spatial behaviors in response to threats, yet how alerting cues engage spatial representations remains unknown. Here, we tested whether head direction (HD) neurons-key components of the brain's navigation system-are recruited by alerting stimuli. We recorded thalamic and cortical HD cells in head-fixed mice during alerting acoustic stimuli while monitoring arousal via pupillometry and facial motion. Identified HD cells in the anterodorsal thalamic nucleus exhibited ectopic axons and projections to the thalamic reticular nucleus. These cells responded to artificial and natural alerting sounds, with frequency tuning closely matching facial motion patterns. Thalamic responses comprised fast and slow components, whereas cortical responses in the dorsal presubiculum were sparser and dominated by the slow component. In the thalamus, the fast component was independent of HD tuning, whereas the slow component was selectively amplified by alerting stimuli. This gain modulation enhanced HD coding, with decoding accuracy scaling with facial motion. Together, these findings identify the thalamocortical HD system as a non-canonical auditory pathway relaying alerting signals to spatial navigation circuits, providing a mechanism by which alerting stimuli sharpen the internal compass for goal-directed behaviors.

items.title: Feasibility and preliminary psychological effects of bedside immersive Virtual reality in prolonged bedridden neurosurgical Patients: A Single-Arm pilot study.
items.abstract: Background Prolonged immobility is a common consequence of neurosurgical spinal pathology and is associated with significant psychological morbidity, including anxiety, low mood, and reduced quality of life.[1,2] Conventional psychological support is often impractical in high-volume neurosurgical ward settings. Virtual reality (VR) has shown promise as a non-pharmacological adjunct in several clinical contexts,[3-10] though its specific application in prolonged bedridden neurosurgical patients has not been systematically explored. To evaluate the feasibility, tolerability, and safety of delivering structured VR sessions to prolonged bedridden neurosurgical patients (primary objective), and to obtain exploratory estimates of any associated change in anxiety, affect, mood, and quality of life to inform a future controlled trial (secondary objective). Methods Ten patients (5F/5M; mean age 38.3 ± 15.73 years) with spinal pathologies at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences (AIIMS), New Delhi, bedridden ≥ 15 days, underwent seven VR sessions delivered every third day (5-30 min each). GAD-7, PANAS, and POMS were assessed pre- and post-each session; WHOQOL-BREF before Session 1 and after Session 7. Wilcoxon Signed-Rank, Friedman and Spearman tests were used, with a random-intercept linear mixed-effects model fitted to all 140 pre- and post-session observations per measure, estimating cumulative (across-session) and acute (within-session) effects separately. Results The intervention was feasible and well tolerated: all ten patients completed all seven sessions (100 % completion) with no adverse events. Within-patient psychological measures all moved in the direction of improvement, providing preliminary effect-size estimates to inform a future controlled trial. GAD-7 declined by a median of 5.0 points (bootstrap 95 % CI 3.0 to 7.0; p = 0.002), shifting the cohort from the upper-moderate into the mild anxiety range. Positive affect improved (p = 0.006), negative affect declined (p = 0.002), and POMS-TMD fell (p = 0.008). WHOQOL-BREF domain scores rose in the physical (21.4 to 27.5), psychological (8.8 to 20.4) and environment (8.1 to 17.5) domains (all p = 0.016), with no change in the social relationships domain. Because all participants changed in the same direction, the corresponding effect-size r values reach their mathematical ceiling for n = 10 (≈0.89) and indicate consistency of direction rather than magnitude; all estimates are exploratory given the single-arm design. An exploratory association between bedridden duration and GAD-7 change (ρ = 0.854) is hypothesis-generating only. Conclusions These preliminary findings suggest that immersive VR is feasible, well-tolerated, and associated with preliminary improvements in psychological well-being in prolonged bedridden neurosurgical patients. The results support further evaluation through a randomized controlled trial.

items.title: Translational evidence for habenula's role in human addiction: A scoping review.
items.abstract: Addiction is characterized by persistent substance use or engagement in behaviors despite adverse consequences and impaired control, but its expression varies substantially across individuals, substances, and severity. Within one influential neurocircuitry framework, addiction processes are organized into binge, withdrawal, and preoccupation stages. Preclinical research implicates the habenula across these processes but indicates that its contribution varies across drugs, subdivisions, and experimental models. Research on the human habenula in addiction remains fragmented, and the extent to which it converges with preclinical mechanisms is unclear. This scoping review synthesized evidence on the human habenula in addiction and examined its convergence with preclinical findings. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, databases and grey literature were searched in November 2025, with literature surveillance continued through April 2026. Human studies reported reduced fronto-habenula white-matter integrity, elevated habenula-striatal resting-state functional connectivity, withdrawal-related habenula-frontal connectivity, increased habenula blood flow during opioid withdrawal, altered task-evoked responses to reward and feedback, and nicotine-related genetic signals. By contrast, morphological studies found no consistent differences in habenula structure across addiction samples. Most human neuroimaging studies could not distinguish the medial and lateral habenula, limiting direct comparison with subdivision-specific preclinical mechanisms. Overall, across human and preclinical studies, the evidence does not support a unitary habenular alteration across addiction. Cross-species convergence was strongest for withdrawal-related activity, particularly for opioids, and for nicotine-related molecular mechanisms, but remained limited by differences in substances, circuits, measures, and paradigms. Future studies using subdivision-sensitive imaging and more comparable cross-species designs are needed.

items.title: BodyScreen: A pilot evaluation of a mobile app intervention targeting social media engagement and eating disorder risk in adolescent and young adult women.
items.abstract: Appearance-focused social media use contributes to body dissatisfaction and elevated eating disorder (ED) risk in adolescents and young adults. Scalable, digitally delivered interventions targeting social media behaviours alongside psychological risk factors remain limited. This pilot trial evaluated BodyScreen, a 4-week mobile app designed to reduce maladaptive social media engagement while promoting self-esteem and body appreciation. Eighty adolescent and young adult women in Canada aged 15-29 with elevated ED risk participated in a single-arm pilot trial. Assessments were conducted pre- and post-intervention. The primary outcome was ED symptomatology. Secondary outcomes included body dissatisfaction, self-esteem, perfectionism, social media use, psychological adjustment, and quality of life. Linear mixed-effects models examined pre-post changes, and semi-structured interviews assessed user experience. Sixty-eight participants (85%) completed post-intervention assessments. ED symptoms decreased significantly (d = -1.12). Improvements were also observed across secondary outcomes: body dissatisfaction (d = -1.30), self-esteem (d = 0.84), perfectionism (d = -0.85), social media use (d = -0.46), psychological adjustment, and quality of life (d = 0.50). Engagement was high (73% completing ≥70% of exercises), and few negative effects were reported, while usability was moderate. Qualitative feedback highlighted structured daily routines and skill acquisition as facilitators, with repetitive self-monitoring and minor interface challenges as barriers. BodyScreen is a feasible, safe, and promising early intervention for young women at elevated ED risk, particularly those with appearance-motivated social media use. Future trials should include a control group, recruit more diverse samples, evaluate longer-term outcomes, and incorporate qualitative feedback to enhance usability and engagement.

items.title: Predictive dendrites as a foundation for biological learning
items.abstract: A fundamental challenge for neuroscience is to identify laws of synaptic plasticity that are consistent with experimental observations at the level of individual neurons, whilst also explaining the ability of neural networks to learn complex tasks. Here we investigate a candidate law in which neurons adjust synaptic strengths to minimize the mismatch between somatic and dendritic activity. We demonstrate that models based on this rule can effectively adjust synaptic weights across network layers to learn non-linear tasks. Moreover, minimizing mismatch between spiking activity and dendritic inputs leads to integrate-and-fire dynamics and spike-timing-dependent plasticity. The model reproduces the experimentally observed dependencies of plasticity upon initial synaptic weights and spike patterns, whilst also generating a series of testable predictions. Our results show that a single principle - minimization of somato-dendritic mismatch - links learning at the network level with fundamental properties of individual neurons, including membrane potential dynamics and canonical features of synaptic plasticity.

items.title: Neural circuitry mediating hypercapnia-induced microarousal and impaired sleep depth.
items.abstract: Sleep disruption in obstructive sleep apnea syndrome is characterized by frequent microarousals and reduced sleep depth, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Here, we show that intermittent hypercapnic air (HA) induces time-locked microarousals, fragments sleep, reduces non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep depth, and diminishes rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. HA exposure activates glutamatergic neurons in the nucleus tract solitary (NTS Vglut2 ), and their optogenetic or chemogenetic activation is sufficient to trigger arousal and impair sleep. Projection-specific activation reveals that NTS Vglut2 projections to the paraventricular nucleus (PVN), parabrachial nucleus (PB), paraventricular thalamus, and locus coeruleus (LC) promote arousal, whereas projections to the PB and LC additionally reduce NREM sleep depth. Inhibition of NTS Vglut2 projection to the PVN significantly postpones HA-induced arousal. NTS Vglut2 terminals monosynaptically activate corticotropin-releasing hormone neurons in the PVN (PVN CRH ), and inhibition of PVN CRH neurons or knockdown of Slc17a6 (encoding Vglut2), but not Crh , delays hypercapnia-induced arousal. These findings identify neural circuits underlying hypercapnia-induced microarousal and reduced sleep depth.

items.title: Learning by moving: Physical motion accelerates category learning.
items.abstract: Categorization is crucial for survival, helping animals forage, navigate, and avoid predators-all tasks involving movement. Yet, dominant theories of category learning treat it as a purely cognitive or perceptual process. Here, we challenge this view by demonstrating that physical movement can enhance category learning-but selectively. Using immersive virtual reality, we found that performing large actions, such as swinging a lightsaber, substantially improved learning of categories requiring integration of multiple cues (e.g., distinguishing aggressive from noncancerous lesions), while having minimal impact on categories involving independent evaluation of features (e.g., sorting by color and shape). This selective enhancement reveals a previously unrecognized motor contribution to categorization and may explain why prior studies missed it, opening avenues for optimizing training in critical categorization tasks.

items.title: How unequal is unequal? Turn-taking simulation for benchmarking participation and opportunity inequality in small-group collaboration.
items.abstract: Participation equity is essential for ensuring that students gain cognitive and social benefits from collaborative learning, yet there is a lack of quantitative benchmarks for interpreting participation and opportunity distributions in small-group collaboration. This study focuses on two turn-based analytical dimensions of participation equity: participation equality, measured by students' shares of speaking turns, and opportunity equality, measured by students' shares of addressed opportunities. Using the standard deviation of these rates, the study establishes preliminary, context-specific simulation-based reference values for identifying departures from an idealized triadic turn-taking baseline. The empirical dataset included 117 fourth-grade primary school students from two classes in mainland China, who worked in heterogeneous triads on mathematical and reading tasks. Using agent-based modeling and Monte Carlo simulation, the study estimated local turn-taking parameters from empirical data, generated reference distributions under an ideal-equity baseline, and conducted sensitivity analyses to examine model stability. Results support the internal stability of the model and provide turn-count-specific reference values for interpreting participation and opportunity inequality. The findings offer preliminary reference values for interpreting participation and opportunity distributions in collaborative learning and highlight the importance of turn count when evaluating structural patterns of participation and opportunity in triadic classroom dialogue. These reference values describe structural participation patterns rather than collaboration quality and require recalibration and independent validation before application in other educational settings.

items.title: Normative modernization, social integration, and collective wellbeing: Evidence from a cross-national dynamic panel study.
items.abstract: Cross-national evidence does not establish whether changing normative environments are associated with population wellbeing independently of social integration. Using repeated International Social Survey Programme data, the reported analysis aggregates individual responses into 286 country-wave observations across 52 countries. Two-step System GMM models estimate persistence and conditional associations while treating the lagged outcome as endogenous. Reported estimates indicate persistence in countries' relative wellbeing positions. Social integration has a modest positive association with wellbeing, while the composite modernization association is small and imprecise. Gender egalitarianism and environmental concern show modest positive domain-specific associations; inequality attitudes, religiosity, and work modernization do not. The modernization association is more positive at higher integration levels. These findings are conditional associations, not causal effects. Interpretation is restricted by low ICC(1) values, incomplete cross-national measurement invariance, a changing-domain composite, and only three directly observed social-integration waves. The evidence therefore supports a bounded conclusion: aggregate normative indicators are associated with relative wellbeing positions differently across domains and integration levels.

items.title: The applications of artificial intelligence in liver transplantation: A comprehensive scoping review.
items.abstract: Liver transplantation (LT) is a complex surgical intervention, with intricate decision-making and risks at all stages before, during and after the procedure itself. Artificial intelligence (AI) may assist the process but has seen limited use. This scoping review assessed primary articles reporting on clinical AI in LT in MEDLINE and Embase from 2000 to September 2026. 196 articles were identified: focusing on the pre-operative period before transplant (21.9%), organ retrieval (9.7%), intra-operative issues (3.6%), short-term post-operative complications (16.8%), long-term post-operative complications (45.9%) and natural language processing (2.0%). 95.9% had retrospective designs and only 12.8% had direct multi-centre data, with the rest from national registries or single centres. 13.8% of studies externally validated their AI tools. Only one study performed a prospective evaluation of their tool with a randomized controlled trial. Progress towards clinically deployable tools will require harmonised, higher-granularity datasets, consistent reporting, and prospective evaluation within real-world transplant workflows.

items.title: Determine and compare limb specific predictors based on the foot pressure index of right and left foot among young adults in Saudi Arabia using machine learning models.
items.abstract: Foot posture is a key determinant of limb-biomechanics, gait balance as well as functional mobility. Usage of foot pressure index (FPI) is widespread to but the determinants of FPI without accounting to the left right foot differences. Therefore, identifying limb-specific determinants would enhance screening accuracy and help in more targeted interventions. The objective of the study was to determine and compare limb specific predictors based on the foot pressure index of right and left foot among young adults using machine learning models. A total of 581 (290 females and 291 males) 18-25-year-old young adults were assessed on anthropometric measures, joint hyper mobility and functional mobility. Using SAS-Viya, separate entropy-based decision trees, along with logistic regression models were developed and model performance was evaluated using validation-test accuracy and area under the curve (AUC). Decision tree models outperformed logistic regression for both FPI-Left (FPI-L) and FPI-Right (FPIR). FPIR was primarily predicted by joint hyper mobility, followed by stair ascent time, stability as well as BMI with stronger influence of both structural and load related factors. FPIL was predicted by closed-eye balance along BMI, open eye balance, stair ascent, Beighton score, underscoring the role of sensory motor control. The findings of the study reflect that young adults foot posture is complex, limb specific interactions among anthropometric, functional and sensory factors.

items.title: MF-TLMLP: A multi-channel fusion-based multi-fidelity transfer learning method for predicting the cutting performance of conical picks.
items.abstract: Conical picks are critical components in key excavation equipment (including shearers, continuous miners, and roadheaders) employed for rock fragmentation in mining and civil engineering. This study proposes the multi-fidelity transfer learning multi-layer perceptron (MF-TLMLP) method to predict cutting performance. Addressing the scarcity of high-fidelity (HF) data, MF-TLMLP integrates low-fidelity (LF) and HF data through a multi-channel fusion and transfer learning approach. Simulations using Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) generated 2500 LF samples and 500 HF samples. Compared to traditional Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and transfer learning models, MF-TLMLP demonstrated superior performance, achieving a higher coefficient of determination (R2) and a lower mean squared error (MSE). Morris screening based on mean absolute elementary effects revealed output-dependent sensitivities, with cutting thickness dominating the force responses and cutting speed dominating the pulse-number responses within the sampled domain. These results demonstrate the potential of MF-TLMLP for predicting HF numerical cutting responses for the investigated rock properties, parameter ranges, and adjacent double-pick configuration.

items.title: Creative ageing in a digital world: A protocol for a synthesis of arts-based innovations for culturally diverse older adults in Canada.
items.abstract: The forthcoming scoping review will synthesize evidence on arts-based and digital engagement initiatives that support social inclusion, mental health, and cultural expression among older adults, with a particular focus on structurally-disadvantaged populations. Rapid digital transformation in the arts, including virtual and augmented reality, digital storytelling, and generative artificial intelligence, has expanded opportunities for participation and creative expression. However, access remains uneven, and there is limited consolidated evidence on effectiveness, equity considerations, and best practices for implementation across diverse contexts. Guided by Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting standards, the forthcoming review will systematically search peer-reviewed and grey literature across major health, social science, and interdisciplinary databases from inception to October 2026. An integrated knowledge translation approach will be embedded throughout the review, engaging older adults, caregivers, community arts practitioners, and cultural leaders as active partners in refining search strategies, interpreting findings, and shaping dissemination. Data will be extracted and synthesized using both quantitative mapping and qualitative content analysis to identify program models, theoretical frameworks, implementation strategies, outcomes, and equity considerations. Findings will generate a comprehensive evidence map of effective and emerging practices, highlight barriers such as digital exclusion and cultural underrepresentation, and identify ethical and legal considerations in digital arts engagement. The review will inform the development of culturally safe, accessible, and inclusive arts and digital programming, and will provide actionable guidance for researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and community organizations seeking to enhance well-being, social connection, and cultural continuity among older adults.

items.title: Decoding motor imagery EEG signals by a deep learning network integrating multiscale filtering and temporal-channel attention mechanisms.
items.abstract: Due to their low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationarity, accurately classifying EEG signals is still one of the main hindrances that limit the real-world applications of a brain-computer interface (BCI). Deep learning (DL) is a potential method for addressing the problem. However, how to create a suitable DL network for motor imagery (MI)-based BCIs poses severe challenges in the case of insufficient training data. In this paper, a DL network based on multiscale convolutional neural network (CNN) and temporal and channel attention mechanisms is proposed for decoding MI tasks. Temporal and spatial features are extracted by four parallel CNN branches, each of which is followed by a Transformer block for learning the global correlations of local time features. The outputs from the four Transformer blocks are concatenated along channel dimension and then input into a channel attention module for channel fusion. The subsequent feature map is classified by a CNN, which replaces the commonly used fully connected layer for reducing computational complexity. The proposed network was evaluated on three publicly available BCI datasets and compared with five state-of-the-art DL networks. The training data sets are augmented using the approach segmentation and reconstruction. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed network achieved an average accuracy of 80.21% on Dataset 1 (4-class tasks), 90.19% on Dataset 2 (2-class tasks), and 97.32% on Dataset 3 (4-class tasks), surpassing the strongest baselines FBCNet on Dataset 1, MSFBCNN on Dataset 2 and MSFBCNN on Dataset 3 by 2.59%, 1.27%, and 1.99% respectively. The network effectively decoded the MI-based EEG signals, providing a potential method for BCI applications.

items.title: GAMPoint: Geometry-augmented vision transformer with a multimodal-ready interface for 3D point-cloud segmentation.
items.abstract: Various 3D point cloud semantic segmentation methods have been proposed, yet they remain challenged by limited use of geometric cues and inaccurate predictions around thin structures, object boundaries, and rare classes in cluttered indoor scenes. To address these limitations, we propose GAMPoint, a transformer-based framework for 3D semantic segmentation. Specifically, Enhanced Relative Positional Encoding (EnhancedRPE) augments relative positional modeling with local surface-variation cues to strengthen geometry-aware feature learning. In addition, Conditional Multimodal Gating (CMG) is introduced as an input-side embedding interface. In GAMPoint, XYZ coordinates provide the basic point-cloud geometry, while CMG incorporates available auxiliary attributes, such as RGB colors and surface normals, before the serialized encoder. For RGB-D reconstructed datasets such as ScanNet, XYZ coordinates already contain depth-derived geometric information; raw depth is not used as an additional per-point channel. GAMPoint incorporates EnhancedRPE and CMG into Point Transformer V3 and is evaluated on S3DIS and ScanNet. Experimental results show competitive performance and modest gains over strong point-transformer baselines. Class-wise and repeated-run analyses further indicate category-dependent improvements and consistent gains across matched repeated runs under the reported settings. Code is available at github.com/airmanss/ GAMPoint.

items.title: Intratracheal microspray delivery of iohexol for sustained lung-parenchymal enhancement in preclinical micro-computed tomography: A feasibility and acute-safety study in mice.
items.abstract: Preclinical thoracic micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) is constrained by the brief pulmonary enhancement window of intravenously (IV) administered iodinated contrast, which the kidneys clear rapidly. We performed a feasibility study in mice comparing IV tail-vein injection with intratracheal microspray instillation of the clinical agent iohexol. Mice received iohexol (100 µL, 500 mg/mL) by either route. Whole-body projections were acquired to 120 min and thoracic sections to 30 min, each animal scanned before contrast in the same session. Contrast distribution was recorded by compartment and quantified from regions of interest. IV delivery produced vascular and cardiac opacification with progressive bladder accumulation, which was the largest signal in every IV animal by 120 min. Intratracheal delivery produced widespread, comparatively uniform lung-parenchymal opacification at 5, 15 and 30 min with no discrete bladder opacity at any time; coronal thoracic signal was 0.77 at 5 min and 0.72 at 30 min, against 0.09 to 0.19 after IV injection. Acute safety was assessed at 5 and 29 h by serum biochemistry and histopathology against untreated controls. ALT, AST and blood urea nitrogen did not differ among groups. Creatinine was modestly higher than in controls after both routes, with no difference between routes, consistent with renal excretion of absorbed iohexol. Lung, heart, liver, spleen and kidney showed preserved architecture without acute injury. These data identify intratracheal microspray delivery as a practical way to hold iodine in the lung parenchyma across a thoracic micro-CT acquisition and provide the basis for a confirmatory quantitative study.

items.title: Modulation of human dorsal root ganglion neuron excitability by Nav1.7 inhibition.
items.abstract: Nav1.7 voltage-gated sodium channels are strongly expressed in human primary pain-sensing neurons (nociceptors), and selective Nav1.7 inhibitors have been developed as possible therapeutic agents for treating pain, so far with disappointing clinical results. In contrast, a selective Nav1.8 channel inhibitor (suzetrigine) has had successful clinical trials. Because nociceptors express both Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 channels, it is of interest to compare effects of Nav1.7 and Nav1.8 inhibitors on the excitability of human nociceptors. To compare with previous results with suzetrigine, we characterized the effects of a selective Nav1.7 inhibitor, AM-2099, on action potential generation and repetitive firing of dissociated human dorsal root ganglion (DRG) neurons, studied at 37°C. Inhibition of Nav1.7 channels by 600 nM AM-2099 generally produced a substantial depolarizing shift of action potential threshold, an increase in rheobase, a decrease in action potential upstroke velocity, decrease in action potential peak, and prolongation of the refractory period. Compared to inhibition of Nav1.8 channels, inhibition of Nav1.7 channels had larger effects on threshold and maximal upstroke velocity, while action potential peak was reduced similarly by both. Nav1.8 inhibition produced much more dramatic reduction of repetitive firing than Nav1.7 inhibition. The results show that although the excitability of human DRG neurons is affected by inhibition of Nav1.7 channels, most notably by an increase in threshold and increase in refractory period, repetitive firing of the neurons in response to strong stimuli is little affected.

items.title: Chromosome-scale genome assembly and annotation of the goldenrod gall fly, Eurosta solidaginis (Fitch) (Diptera: Tephritidae).
items.abstract: Eurosta solidaginis is a plant-parasitic insect that develops from egg to adult inside of a spheroid gall it induces on the stem of goldenrod plants (Solidago spp.). E. solidaginis is widespread across North America, with a geographic distribution that extends from Southern Canada to Texas and the Southern U.S. and from the Atlantic coast to the Great Plains and includes scattered populations reaching the West coast. The natural history, ecology and physiology of E. solidaginis are well-documented, and its overwintering physiology, multitrophic interactions, and ecological speciation have been well-studied. Surprisingly, genomic resources are restricted to an incomplete scaffold-level genome assembly lacking protein-coding gene annotation. To advance understanding of the physiology, gall-forming, and population structure of E. solidaginis, we sequenced and assembled the genome of a single pupa using PacBio HiFi sequencing and Hi-C chromatin proximity sequencing technology. Here, we present a fully-annotated, chromosome-level de novo assembly of the 1.9 Gb genome, spanning five autosomes and the sex chromosomes. The assembly has a contig N50 of 3.7 Mb and a scaffold N50 of 289.3 Mb, and 96.5% of expected Diptera BUSCOs in the genome found in single copy. We annotated 14,223 identified protein-coding genes, identifying 96.2% of BUSCOs in the protein set found in single copy. The 18,293 bp mitochondrial genome was assembled and subsequently annotated separately. Even though there are 400-450 gall-inducing tephritid species, this is the second high-quality, chromosome-level genome assembly of a gall-forming fly in the family, and the third freeze tolerant dipteran genome.

items.title: Sublethal effects of the organosilicone surfactant Silwet L-77 and its interactions with acetamiprid and sulfoxaflor on honeybee (Apis mellifera) gustatory responsiveness and olfactory learning.
items.abstract: Pesticides remain indispensable for global food security, yet their use must be reconciled with the preservation of biodiversity. Despite advances in developing 'safer' pesticides, their sublethal effects and synergistic potential with co-formulants in tank-mixtures, including 'inert' spray adjuvants, often remain poorly understood in beneficial insects like bees. In this study, we assessed the effects of acute oral exposure to both single compounds and adjuvant-insecticide mixtures on gustatory responsiveness, associative olfactory learning, and 90-minute short-term memory retention in honeybee foragers (Apis mellifera L.). Specifically, individual foragers were exposed to either single compounds (0.1%, 0.5%, 1% or 2.5% Silwet™ L-77; 6, 30 or 150 ng acetamiprid; 3, 9 or 27 ng sulfoxaflor), adjuvant-insecticide mixtures (0.5% or 1% Silwet™ L-77 combined with 6 or 30 ng acetamiprid, or 3 or 9 ng sulfoxaflor), a positive control (6 ng imidacloprid), or negative controls (0%, 0.1%, and 1% acetone). While we found no significant interaction effects for these adjuvant-insecticide mixtures, single-compound exposure to the highest doses of 2.5% Silwet™ L-77 and 27 ng sulfoxaflor significantly reduced gustatory responsiveness. Furthermore, all three agrochemicals alone weakly affected associative learning without impacting short-term memory retention. Although adjuvant-insecticide mixtures did not significantly impair learning ability, these adjuvants may impact sensory perception. Moving beyond mortality-based assessments and including behavioural assay to test sensory perception and learning ability is essential for gaining a more holistic understanding of pollinator health.

items.title: Copper exposure induces the release of methyl iodide from coastal wetlands and seawater.
items.abstract: Methyl iodide (CH 3 I) is the main organic carrier for iodine transport from both marine and terrestrial ecosystems into the atmosphere, playing an important role in the global iodine cycle and ozone depletion. The widespread input of heavy metal copper (Cu(II)) deposition in marine environments due to anthropogenic activities may affect the production of CH 3 I, yet relevant studies are still lacking. Here, we explored the effects of Cu(II) on emission of CH 3 I in coastal wetlands and seawater. The results showed that Cu(II) addition significantly enhances CH 3 I emission from coastal wetland soils, with emissions under hydrogen peroxide (H 2 O 2 ) co-addition reaching approximately five times those observed with Cu(II) alone. Notably, this promotional effect was more pronounced in coastal wetland soils with higher organic matter content. In seawater, addition of 400 nM Cu(II) further stimulated the abiotic processes, with emission of CH 3 I increased 136% (day 8) in filtered seawater (biologically reduced). In unfiltered seawater, despite 400 nM Cu(II) addition inhibition of biological activity evidenced by an 81.7% decrease in chlorophyll-a and a 49.2% reduction in bacterial abundance, the overall CH 3 I emission was further amplified, which we tentatively attributed to the release of organic matter from the decay of phytoplankton. These findings elucidate that elevated copper stress promote CH 3 I emission from both salt marsh soil and ocean into the atmosphere. This study provides an important scientific basis for assessing the impact of heavy metal pollution on CH 3 I emissions from coastal wetlands and seawater under climate change scenarios and anthropogenic perturbations.

items.title: Adaptive restructuring of organohalide-respiring microbial communities under salinity stress maintains reductive dechlorination capacity.
items.abstract: Elevated salinity constrains microbial reductive dechlorination in groundwater contaminated with chlorinated aliphatic hydrocarbons, and stepwise salinity acclimation offers a strategy to sustain dechlorination activity. In this study, an organohalide-respiring enrichment consortium supplied with both 1,2-dichloroethane and trichloroethylene was subjected to stepwise salinity acclimation and subsequently evaluated through batch dechlorination assays and microbial community analyses. The acclimated consortium achieved complete dechlorination at 40 g/L NaCl after extended incubation, whereas conversion at 50 g/L remained incomplete, with persistent vinyl chloride accumulation. Community richness declined with increasing salinity, whereas Dehalococcoides remained detectable across all salinity treatments. Proteiniphilum and Sphaerochaeta were identified as candidate salt-tolerant taxa. Community restructuring was further characterized by an increased relative contribution of homogeneous selection, reduced co-occurrence network connectivity, and increased modularity. Functional prediction analyses also revealed stage-dependent shifts in predicted metabolic and biosynthetic potential. These findings demonstrate that stepwise salinity acclimation can improve and sustain dechlorination performance under saline conditions, while terminal conversion remains a key functional constraint at high salinity. The results provide a basis for further development of salinity-acclimated consortia for groundwater remediation and highlight the importance of minimizing chlorinated intermediate accumulation and improving terminal dechlorination efficiency.

items.title: Gentiopicroside protects against kainic acid-induced excitotoxicity by preserving glutamate homeostasis in rats.
items.abstract: This study provides the first evidence that gentiopicroside, a bioactive constituent isolated from Gentiana scabra, protects against kainic acid (KA)-induced excitotoxicity in rats. Intraperitoneal pretreatment with gentiopicroside (50 mg/kg) 30 min prior to KA administration (15 mg/kg) significantly mitigated seizure severity and prevented KA-induced cerebral blood flow (CBF) deficits. Histological analyses revealed that gentiopicroside markedly attenuated KA-induced neuronal loss, ultrastructural damage, and glial activation in the hippocampus. Mechanistically, gentiopicroside preserved the homeostasis of the glutamate-glutamine cycle, thereby reducing pathologically elevated hippocampal glutamate concentrations. This protective effect was mediated by the upregulation of glutamate transporter-1 (GLT-1) and glutamine synthetase (GS), alongside with the downregulation of glutamine transporters (SNAT1/3), glutaminase, and vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (VGLUT1). Furthermore, gentiopicroside normalized KA-induced alterations in AMPA and NMDA receptor subunit compositions, specifically restoring decreased GluA1, GluA2, and GluN2A levels while suppressing GluN2B upregulation. Additionally, gentiopicroside alleviated KA-induced mitochondrial dysfunction by suppressing calpain expression, restoring calpastatin and mitofusin 2 (MFN2) levels, and downregulating apoptotic protease activating factor 1 (Apaf-1). These findings suggest that gentiopicroside exhibits neuroprotective effects against KA-induced acute glutamate excitotoxicity by maintaining glutamate homeostasis, preventing calpain-mediated mitochondrial impairment, and attenuating glial neuroinflammation. These results highlight its therapeutic potential for excitotoxicity-related neurological disorders.

items.title: Salt-ion etching induced transformation of granular ZIF-8 into Fe-doped nanosheets for activating peracetic acid toward pollutant degradation.
items.abstract: Conventional water treatment processes exhibit inherent limitations in the removal of trace emerging micropollutants. To address this challenge, we rationally designed ultrathin Fe-doped nanosheets via a one-step etching strategy using ferrous sulfate. This approach simultaneously transformed pristine granular ZIF-8 into a layered architecture and facilitated the uniform incorporation of iron active sites. The as-prepared catalyst was subsequently employed in a visible-light-driven peracetic acid (PAA) activation system for the efficient degradation of micropollutants. The etching treatment not only substantially increased the specific surface area of the nanosheets relative to their bulk counterparts but also ensured homogeneous dispersion of Fe species, thereby establishing stable Fe 2+ /Fe 3+ redox cycling centers that significantly accelerate electron transfer kinetics. In the ZIF-8-Fe-Nanosheets/PAA/simulated sunlight system, sulfamethazine (SMT) achieved near-complete degradation within 50 min. Moreover, the catalyst exhibited excellent broad-spectrum degradation activity, robust pH adaptability across a range of 3-9, and strong resistance to coexisting matrix constituents in real water samples. Radical quenching experiments identified hydroxyl radicals ( • OH) and singlet oxygen ( 1 O 2 ) as the dominant reactive oxygen species. Three plausible SMT degradation pathways were proposed, and toxicity assessment using quantitative structure-activity relationship analysis indicated lower biotoxicity of the transformation products compared to the parent compound. Overall, this work validates the Fe-doped nanosheet catalyst as an efficient PAA activator, and more broadly, paves the way for expanding PAA-based catalytic oxidation toward practical water treatment.

items.title: A kleptomyiophilous orchid exploits milichiid flies through mimicry of common pentatomoid bugs with high levels of toxicity.
items.abstract: To attract pollinators, mimetic flowers imitate the visual and olfactory cues that their pollinators use when responding to models. 1 , 2 However, it is unclear which processes influence the mimicry of particular models. One possibility is that selection favors mimicry of models that act as "magnet species" by attracting large numbers of potential pollinators. 1 , 3 , 4 , 5 According to this hypothesis, models should be highly common, even if they are not the most attractive resources. This may apply to kleptomyiophilous flowers that exploit kleptoparasitic flies by imitating injured insects. 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 , 10 In this form of mimicry, the injured insect models would be highly common, even if they emit toxic defensive volatiles that could impede pollinator activities. 11 , 12 We report that the eastern ecotype of Bulbophyllum claviforme attracts a specific kleptoparasitic milichiid pollinator Phyllomyza sp. 1. Orchid floral scent is similar to (E)-2-decenal-dominated emissions of multiple pentatomoid bugs in the families Pentatomidae, Scutelleridae, Plataspidae, and Acanthosomatidae. Bioassays suggest that undecane, (E)-2-decenal and (E)-2-decenyl acetate are critical for attraction. Three (E)-2-alkenals, namely (E)-2-hexenal, (E)-2-octenal, and (E)-2-decenal, are both toxic and attractive to Phyllomyza sp. 1, with the toxicity of dominant (E)-2-alkenals negatively correlated to attractiveness. The orchid paradoxically appears to mimic pentatomoids that are less attractive due to higher toxicity. Selection may have favored mimicry of these bugs because (E)-2-decenal is emitted by a wide range of species, representing 68% of the pentatomoid species sampled. Our findings are congruent with the hypothesis that magnet species effects on pollinator abundance are important for the evolution of floral mimicry.

items.title: Identifying predictors of resilience in European forests through stakeholders' perceptions.
items.abstract: Enhancing forest resilience to climate change requires operationalizing resilience assessments and engaging stakeholders to support effective decision-making. Here, we assessed stakeholder perceptions of resilience indicators (i.e., predictors and system variables) and their relevance for promoting the resilience of European forests across ecological and socioeconomic dimensions. Stakeholder profiles and regional systems were considered as complementary contextual dimensions to explore variability in resilience perceptions across different forest social-ecological contexts. Through bipartite networks and ranking analyses, we assessed whether stakeholders perceived modular relationships between resilience predictors and systems variables associated with forest ecosystem services and forest-based value chains, identified the predictors most broadly relevant for promoting resilience, and assessed their perceived operational applicability. Results revealed consistent modules linking biodiversity-related variables with key resilience predictors associated with forest management, conservation and forest structural attributes across stakeholder profiles and regional contexts. By contrast, productivity-related variables were associated with predictors related to harvesting intensity, land use, and forest economics, particularly within the socioeconomic dimension, among value chain actors, and in a central and northern Europe contexts. Forest management and forest structural attributes consistently emerged as the most broadly connected predictors across dimensions, whereas some predictors, such as deadwood, were perceived as having more specialized relationships with biodiversity-related variables. Perceived practicability was moderately correlated with explanatory strength and measurability, suggesting a gap between perceived relevance and operational implementation. Overall, our results highlight the value of perception-based network approaches for identifying resilience priorities and supporting resilience-oriented governance and decision-making under climate change.

items.title: Developing biodiversity indicators for monitoring agricultural sustainability: Insights from a Delphi expert process.
items.abstract: With agricultural activities widely cited as drivers of biodiversity loss globally, it is important to distinguish between agricultural practices that have negative impacts and those with positive impacts on biodiversity. To measure on-farm biodiversity outcomes, the direction and magnitude of impacts need to be assessed. Outcomes can be measured using indicators. However, there is currently a multitude of biodiversity indicators available. This abundance makes monitoring biodiversity outcomes challenging, as farmers lack clarity on what to measure. This study presents a shortlist of biodiversity indicators selected via an expert panel as part of a modified Delphi process. The modified Delphi implemented two scoring approaches across four rounds, exploring the decision-making behind indicator selection. Thirty-nine experts scored 58 indicators based on their appropriateness for evaluating on-farm biodiversity and the practicality of data collection by non-specialists. The variation in scoring approaches helped combat respondent fatigue and build robustness into the indicator selection process. At the end of the study, nine indicators were chosen for monitoring on-farm biodiversity: area of habitat types, a connectivity index, a diversity index (landscape), both a crop and livestock diversity index, in-field crop temporal heterogeneity, indicator species, species richness, and species rarity. A final step considering each indicator's ability to inform on-farm decision-making is likely to have increased the efficacy of the chosen indicators in driving practice change. This would ensure the selected indicators are multifunctional, providing an evaluation of impact while also highlighting the desired direction of travel for the farmer or landowner.

items.title: A sensitivity-informed correlation-based framework for detecting runoff pollutant hotspots in grazed catchments: Implications for precision cattle grazing to improve water quality.
items.abstract: Cattle grazing is a known source of water pollution. Identifying areas within grazinglands where cattle activity contributes most to downstream water quality impairment is important for effective management. This study presents a framework to detect these runoff pollutant hotspots. The framework is based on Pearson correlation coefficients between cattle presence across the catchment and water quality at the outlet. Cattle locations were recorded at 5-60 min time intervals using Virtual Fencing (VF) technology in three experimental catchments located in north-central Oklahoma, USA, two under rotational grazing and one continuously grazed. Escherichia coli (E. coli), total Kjeldahl nitrogen (TKN), and total phosphorus (TP) were measured during runoff events between March 2022, and June 2024. The spatial and temporal scales at which runoff quality was most affected by cattle presence were determined through a sensitivity analysis of grid cell size (GCS), time interval (ΔT) between consecutive cattle Global Positioning System (GPS) records, and pollutant half-life (HL) representing manure decay. The strongest grid cell-scale correlations between water quality parameters and cattle presence ranged from 0.48 to 0.83 for E. coli, 0.70 to 0.86 for TKN, and 0.67 to 0.90 for TP. These hotspots were detected using grid cell sizes ranging from 70 m × 70 m to 100 m × 100 m, and half-life values ranging from 3 to 12 days for E. coli, 3-23 days for TKN, and 3-20 days for TP. Compared to the continuously grazed catchment, hotspots in rotationally grazed, VF-managed catchments with cattle exclusion from riparian buffers were fewer, diffused, and located away from streams. Significant positive spatial autocorrelation was observed in five hotspot maps. Hotspot identification was influenced by pollutant persistence and grazing management, with rotational grazing showing fewer and more diffuse hotspots than continuous grazing.

items.title: Simultaneous multi-element recovery from spent LiFePO<sub>4</sub> batteries by diethyl tartrate-assisted hydrothermal leaching.
items.abstract: Sustainable recycling of spent LiFePO 4 (LFP) batteries is essential for protecting both resources and environment. Conventional hydrometallurgical methods focus primarily on Li recovery, yet they depend on corrosive acids and external oxidants while generating phosphorus-rich iron residues-posing significant economic and environmental challenges. To address these issues, we propose an innovative diethyl tartrate-based hydrothermal treatment method that facilitates acid- and oxidant-free recycling of spent LFP cathode materials. By carefully controlling the leaching conditions, selective release exceeds 98% for Li and P, whereas Fe leaching remains negligible at 0.3%. Mechanistic studies confirmed that the high-efficiency leaching of Li and P is attributed to the combined effect of acetic acid and tartaric acid produced by the hydrothermal reaction of diethyl tartarate. Moreover, the high-quality Li 3 PO 4 was prepared from leaching filtrate via purification-precipitation, and the purity of 99.08% FeC 4 H 4 O 6 was obtained from leaching residue via redissolving-precipitation. This work establishes a sustainable, efficient pathway to fully recover valuable resources from spent LFP batteries.
