items.title: Neurospirituality Reappraised: Brain Mechanisms of Transcendent Experience and Beyond
items.abstract: Background:Subjective experiences featuring altered self-awareness, temporal perception, or spatial boundaries—termed Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs)—occur across clinical neurology, psychiatry, and psychedelic medicine, including in insular ecstatic seizures, meditation, breathwork, hypnosis, and psychedelic therapy. Objective: To synthesize neurobiological and clinical literature on NOEs for neurologists by presenting three heuristic frameworks: 1.A six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy; 2.A tri-level descriptive taxonomy (computational "software", neuromodulatory-autonomic "firmware", and network "hardware"); 3.The Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model, which maps how acute neurodynamic shifts resolve into adaptive growth or clinical distress without reducing existential meaning to neural activity. Methods: Narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, coordinate-based meta-analyses, and key theoretical frameworks sourced via PubMed/MEDLINE. Results: Conflating spirituality, religion, and NOEs causes construct contamination in neuroimaging, compounded by unvalidated single-item measures and non-independent cohorts. An fMRI meta-analysis of meditation (34 studies, N=700) reveals aggregate recruitment of the right rolandic operculum, left insula, supplementary motor area, and hippocampus, arguing against a singular "spiritual center". First-person reports are mapped using a six-dimension schema (experiential content, temporal dynamics, spatial dynamics, volitional dynamics/agency, ownership/embodiment, cognitive stance). Mechanistically, states are organized across three bidirectionally coupled levels: computational inference ("software"), neuromodulatory-autonomic state-setting ("firmware"), and large-scale networks ("hardware"). Five entry routes (meditation, psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis, focal neurological events) are hypothesized to share shifts in Bayesian precision weighting and network decoupling within the master Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model. Crucially, long-term outcomes (integration vs. distress) are not dictated by acute brain states alone, but are mediated by contextual filtering through the 4E Appraisal Prism (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended dimensions). Conclusions: Neurospirituality bridges network neuroscience, clinical neurology, and person-centered care. Clarifying biological substrates does not resolve existential validity. Clinicians must maintain a strict distinction between biological mechanisms, subjective experiences, and personal meanings (the Epistemological Invariant) to avoid pathologizing adaptive states or romanticizing neurological disease. Key terms: Spirituality; Neuroimaging; Meditation; Hallucinogens; Epilepsy.

items.title: Attachment and Caregiving as Social Allostatic Inference: An Updated Social Neuroscience Account from Single Brains to Dyads
items.abstract: Humans are highly social, and much of that sociality is regulatory: individuals manage the demands placed upon their bodies not only alone but through and with others. Attachment science has pursued how the brain accomplishes this for the better part of a century, and its most recent contribution has been neurobiological. Within the Social Neuroscience of Human Attachment (SoNeAt) programme, we previously specified a neuroanatomical architecture of two interacting systems and four domain-general modules for organised attachment, extended it to attachment disruption and disorganisation, and moved it from single brains to dyads through hyperscanning as part of Relational Neuroscience. What that work established energetically, through social allostasis, it did not specify computationally. Here we close that gap. Drawing on active inference, allostasis as interoceptive inference, and recent constructs of attachment as prediction, we propose the term social allostatic inference: the attachment system is one predictive-allostatic loop, the four modules are its successive stages, and organised, disrupted, and disorganised attachment are characteristic settings of the precision parameters that govern it. We extend the account to the caregiving system, which shares this architecture but infers rather than senses both the error that initiates its loop and the signal that terminates it. At the level of the dyad, interpersonal neural and bio-behavioural synchrony are read as indices of where regulatory work is invested rather than of bond quality directly. We address persistent misconceptions in trauma-informed practice and set out a measurement programme.

items.title: Translational neuroscience in psychoeducation: Mapping nonmotor circuitry to clinical management in movement disorders
items.abstract: Non-motor symptoms (NMS) affect nearly all patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD)and related movement disorders, with a mean of roughly 8–10 discrete symptoms perindividual. Their effect on quality of life often exceeds that of motor features, yetNMS remain under-recognized and undertreated, partly because patients and caregivers lack a working model of why these symptoms arise in a “movement” disease.This chapter applies neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to that gap andpositions it relative to conventional psychoeducation, health communication, and behavioral science. We propose the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN)workflow as a movement-disorders-specific implementation of the NIPE frameworkdescribed in Chapter 1 of this volume. MNDN is a clinical proposal, not a validatedprotocol: its components are specified so that it can be tested, but its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated. Drawing on the tripartite cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop model and multi-transmitter degeneration, we provide modules for seven high-yield NMS: apathy, anxiety, executive dysfunction, REM sleepbehavior disorder, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, and fatigue. Eachmodule summarizes the neural systems implicated, at the level of certainty the evidence supports, together with common misattributions, reversible contributors thatmust be excluded, management options and their limits, and patient and caregiverhandout content. We describe delivery formats from 3 to 5 min “micro-NIPE” sessions in routine visits to group and telehealth programs, specify the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and proximal outcomes neededto test MNDN, and examine the ethical risks of neurobiological framing (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, and false reassurance), with particular attention to prognostic counseling in REM sleep behavior disorder. NIPE in movementdisorders is designed to reduce self-blame, support accurate symptom attribution, andimprove collaborative management. Whether it does so is an empirical question thatthis chapter aims to make answerable.

items.title: Measuring heart and breath: BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), a wearable open-source physiology recording platform
items.abstract: Psychology and social neuroscience study the biological basis of real-world interactive behaviors, such as dancing or playing music in groups. Autonomic nervous system reactivity, assessed through cardiac and respiratory signals, plays an important role in these behaviors. However, affordable, scientifically validated, research-grade devices for synchronous, real-time physiological monitoring of multiple individuals in natural settings remain scarce. We propose a wearable open-source physiological monitoring device, the BRAMS-Bio-Box (B3), that can record cardiac and respiratory signals simultaneously from multiple individuals. B3 can be built cost-effectively using open-source blueprints and software we provide to yield a transparent, flexible option for research-grade physiological data collection. We empirically validated B3 against a widely used reference device in nine participants performing various motor and guided-respiration tasks. Heart rate (HR) and heart rate variability (HRV) were derived from electrocardiographic (ECG) signals, while respiratory sensors were evaluated for respiration rate and the accuracy and consistency of exhalation event detection. B3 derived HR and HRV closely matched reference measures across tasks, with high quality ECG recordings and minimal data loss, except during vigorous arm swinging. Respiratory rate and pattern metrics, including exhalation peak timing, also showed strong agreement. The B3 thermistor accurately tracked respiration rate even at higher breathing frequencies, although minor timing offsets occurred during some guided respiration segments. Overall, B3 performed comparably to the reference system for cardiac and respiratory measures, offering an affordable, open-source solution for physiological monitoring in real-world interactive settings.

items.title: Everyone else does it? Self-reported and perceived questionable research practices in music psychology
items.abstract: Questionable research practices (QRPs) may inflate false-positive rates and have been surveyed in psychology, ecology, and education, but not in music psychology. In a survey, 198 researchers who had authored empirical music-psychology work reported how often they had used 22 practices and estimated how many colleagues had used each. Three quarters (75.1%) reported at least one of the 18 practices bearing on false-positive risk, and 82.8% at least one of all 22. The most common were citing irrelevant work to satisfy a reviewer (46.9%) and selecting the most favourable analysis after seeing the results (43.5%). Respondents estimated that colleagues used 20 of the 22 practices more than they did themselves, but this gap is largely produced by the response scale in the survey and is not evidence of under-reporting. Researchers who thought practices were more widespread reported more of them between persons (OR = 2.16, 95% CI [1.74, 2.68]) and within them (OR = 2.62, [2.32, 2.96]), consistent with false consensus as well as descriptive norms. Music-specific practices were reported less often than reporting and analysis practices, though this depended partly on item wording and on whether a practice applied at all. Career stage showed no detectable association with admissions. Researchers reporting more open research practices reported more QRPs, not fewer (OR = 1.28, [1.14, 1.44]), which may indicate differences in disclosure as much as in behaviour. These results provide a first baseline for the field.

items.title: Environment-dependent diversity-stability relationship in microbial communities
items.abstract: Abstract Understanding the biodiversity–stability relationship has been a central challenge in ecology. Classical ecology proposed that diversity stabilize communities by distributing fluctuations across redundant pathways1,2, whereas random-interaction theory predicts that large and complex communities are unstable3,4. Field observations and experiments have reported positive, negative or negligible relationship between diversity and stability5–10. It therefore remains unclear diversity-stability relationship is universal or not and when a particular diversity–stability relationship emerges. Here we show that diversity-stability relationship is not fixed but environment-dependent, by studying bacterial communities under daily dilutions across temperature (10–50 °C) and dilution-rate (10¹–10⁵) gradients. Communities exhibit two distinct fluctuation regimes: collective fluctuations and dominant-species fluctuations. In the collective fluctuation regime, many species interact and fluctuate together, and exhibit a positive diversity-instability relationship and turnover in the most abundant species. In the dominant-species fluctuation regime, only one or a few abundant species fluctuate and exhibit no significant diversity-instability relationship. Single species measurements show that the community fluctuation regime is determined by the balance between species growth and pH-mediated death. We developed a consumer-resource model with pH feedback reproducing both the fluctuation regimes and diversity–stability relationships observed in the experiment. We further tested our theoretical interpretation by performing another experiment tuning the dilution rate to shift between the same two regimes. Our results thus show that two distinct environment-dependent ecological mechanisms and fluctuation regimes lead to different diversity–stability relationships.

items.title: “We Are All Sick”: Sanitation, Structural Neglect, and the Embodied Politics of Informality in Cape Town
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the relationship between sanitation, systemic neglect, and embodied suffering in the RR Section of Khayelitsha, Cape Town. Drawing on thematic analysis of interviews with 30 residents and 16 activists, supported by computer-assisted coding in ATLAS. ti 22, it centres the statement of a resident - “We are all sick” - as a lens into perceived illness, infrastructural decay, and environmental degradation. Testimonies reveal how inadequate sanitation systems, including open toilets, bucket disposal, and stagnant wastewater, exacerbate illness and psychosocial stress in densely packed dwellings. Although authorities acknowledge the crisis, the continued classification of the settlement as “temporary” perpetuates inadequate service provision and entrenches vulnerability. Using Urban Political Ecology, the concept of slow violence, and embodied urbanism, the study demonstrates how informality produces material precarity and political marginalisation. Residents’ accounts highlight not only exposure and illness but also fragmented grassroots organising, civic disillusionment, and episodic resistance. These narratives transform private suffering into collective political speech, challenging invisibility and asserting claims to recognition and citizenship. The study contributes to debates on sanitation justice, health equity, and the politics of informality in African cities, advocating for infrastructure to be recognised as a fundamental right of urban citizenship rather than a conditional privilege.

items.title: The Evolutionary Self: Adaptive Prioritization as a Framework for Personality Structure and Change
items.abstract: Abstract Personality psychology has produced increasingly sophisticated accounts of individual differences through trait, motivational, interpersonal, developmental, and evolutionary approaches. Yet an important theoretical question remains: what principles organize these diverse sources of variation into coherent patterns of behavior across situations and over time? This integrative review proposes the Evolutionary Self, a framework that conceptualizes personality as a dynamic system of adaptive prioritization. Whereas existing models primarily describe personality traits, motivational systems, or the processes producing state variation, the Evolutionary Self focuses on how competing adaptive demands are weighted and coordinated when they cannot be simultaneously maximized. Drawing on evolutionary psychology, behavioral ecology, reinforcement sensitivity theory, attachment theory, self-determination theory, interpersonal models of agency and communion, and dynamic approaches to personality, the framework identifies three candidate domains of recurrent adaptive tension: Opportunity–Protection, Control–Accommodation, and Connection–Self-Reliance. These dimensions are not proposed as mutually exclusive psychological systems. Rather, they represent domains in which individuals must coordinate competing adaptive demands. The framework distinguishes capacities, priorities, states, positions, and trajectories. Capacities describe what an individual can potentially do; priorities describe which motives receive greater weight when competing demands become salient; states describe momentary configurations; position describes the person’s characteristic center of gravity; and trajectory describes systematic movement through adaptive space across situations and developmental periods. The model is offered as a theoretical synthesis that generates testable hypotheses concerning personality structure, contextual variability, development, stress response, and behavioral flexibility.

items.title: From Forest to Remedy: Medicinal Plants and Indigenous Therapeutic Knowledge among Naga tribes of Manipur, Indo-Myanmar Biodiversity Hotspot
items.abstract: Abstract Background The Rongmei and Tangkhul Naga tribes of Manipur are forest-dwelling communities that have traditionally relied on medicinal plants for primary healthcare. Ethnomedicinal knowledge has been documented for these tribes in the Tamenglong/Noney and Ukhrul districts, respectively, but populations in the ecologically distinct Churachandpur and Kamjong districts remain undocumented, and no study has applied a quantitative framework to compare the two tribes and prioritize species for pharmacological validation. We documented medicinal plant use among both tribes in these districts and evaluated informant consensus and cross-cultural patterns to inform pharmacological and conservation priorities. Methods Field surveys were conducted from July 2024 to April 2025 across ten villages using multistage sampling. Data were gathered from informal interviews and focus group discussions using modified semi-structured questionnaires, and plants were identified using regional floras and consultation with taxonomists. Relative frequency of citation (RFC), use value (UV), fidelity level (FL), and informant consensus factor (ICF) were used to assess species importance; the Jaccard Index (JI) and Rahman's Similarity Index (RSI) were used to assess cross-cultural similarity in taxa and therapeutic use. Informants were general community members rather than specialized healers, and because each tribe was sampled in a single district, tribal identity, local ecology, interviewer, and sampling intensity could not be disentangled. Effect sizes, an overlap coefficient that adjusts for unequal inventory size, and exact confidence intervals were added to the comparisons Results Among 373 informants (aged 21–86 years), gender, age, and education were not significantly associated with plant-use knowledge in either community. We recorded 131 taxa from 117 genera and 57 families, used to treat 83 human ailments, including a distinctive Rongmei practice of using burnt Goniothalamus sesquipedalis ash for gastritis, fever, and warding off evil spirits. Species overlap between communities was low (JI = 16.03%), and RSI (9.16%) indicated modest concordance in therapeutic use of shared taxa. Plant-part use differed significantly in five of ten categories, though leaves dominated in both. Brassaiopsis glomerulata , Phlogacanthus thyrsiformis , Mikania micrantha , Goniothalamus sesquipedalis , Zanthoxylum acanthopodium , and Clerodendrum colebrookeanum emerged as the strongest candidates for pharmacological screening based on RFC and FL. Several taxa, including Aquilaria malaccensis (Critically Endangered), are of global conservation concern. Conclusion The study documents rich community-level ethnomedicinal knowledge among the Rongmei and Tangkhul Naga and shows that low taxonomic overlap can coexist with substantial agreement in the use of shared plants. Pharmacological validation and safety screening of promising species, targeted conservation of threatened taxa, and community-controlled benefit-sharing are needed to safeguard this cultural and botanical heritage.

items.title: Twenty Years of Agricultural Mechanization Practices in Northern Nigeria: Bibliometric Insights into Research Trends, Productivity, Labor, and Technology
items.abstract: Abstract Agricultural mechanization significantly boosts farm productivity, reduces labor effort, and promotes rural development, especially in developing economies. This study investigated trends in mechanization, productivity, labor, and technology in northern Nigeria. A total of 735 open-access articles published in English from 2004 to 2025 were extracted from the Dimensions.ai database and analyzed using R's Biblioshiny package ver.5.0. The tools of analysis used include co-authorship networks, keyword co-occurrence, citation patterns, co-citation, and word cloud generation, etc. The results show a 20% annual growth rate and a peak in 2025 with 138 publications, reflecting increasing academic, policy interest in mechanization and agricultural modernization. The average citation count was 14.82, highlighting the relevance of the field. Collaboration involved 4,530 authors, with an average of 6.84 co-authors per-paper and 16.55% international partnerships, highlighting global cooperation. Chinese scholars dominate publication volume. With citation analysis, the distribution of research impact by region is seen to be diverse from Asia, Europe, and Africa. Mechanization’s impact on sustainability and livelihoods is illustrated in the research clusters identified and the core themes of agriculture, employment and climate change. The word-cloud analysis reveals that mechanization research in northern Nigeria is multi-faceted, local, and integrative, connecting technology, socio-economics, sustainability and ecology. The results indicate the influence of mechanization in rural development in different ways, so region-specific results are necessary. It is necessary to have policies and investments in local research for effective implementation. Inclusive mechanization policies should promote smallholder farmers, dissemination of knowledge, and resource access in region for sustainable rural development.

items.title: Reevaluating Body Size in Fossil Physeteroids Using Cranial Proportions
items.abstract: Fossil physeteroids exhibited substantially greater diversity in body size and feeding ecology than their extant relatives, yet body-length estimates for many taxa remain dependent on incomplete skeletons and proportional scaling from a limited number of reference species. This study reassesses body-size estimates in fossil physeteroids using a cranial proportion-based framework centered on bizygomatic width (BZW) and condylobasal length (CBL). The reference body lengths of Zygophyseter varolai and Brygmophyseter shigensis were reevaluated using published vertebral measurements, preserved skeletal length, and scale-bar-based skeletal data, and were conservatively set at approximately 6.5 m and 6.0 m, respectively. These revised reference values were then used to generate updated body-length estimates for a broad sample of extinct physeteroids. Revised estimates indicate that large-bodied physeteroids were relatively uncommon. Among the non-kogiid genera examined, only seven reached or exceeded 6 m in estimated total length, whereas Livyatan and Eophyseter were the only fossil genera estimated to exceed 9.5 m. Macroraptorial physeteroids ranged from approximately 4.0–4.3 m in Acrophyseter spp. to approximately 15–16 m in the giant Livyatan melvillei. The results further suggest that large body size evolved under multiple ecological regimes. Some large-bodied physeteroids were macroraptorial predators, whereas others show adaptations consistent with suction feeding or predation on smaller prey. The temporal distribution of giant forms is therefore more consistent with repeated, independent increases in body size than with a single evolutionary trend toward gigantism. However, incomplete preservation and uncertainty in the body lengths of reference taxa remain important limitations. The framework presented here provides a more consistent basis for reassessing body-size diversity in fossil physeteroids and can be refined as more complete cranial and postcranial material becomes available.

items.title: Transparency Is Necessary but Not Sufficient for Trust: Information Leakage and Procedural Overfitting in Supervised Machine Learning for Psychology
items.abstract: Min et al. (2026) provide a timely checklist for improving the transparency and trust of supervised machine learning (ML) research in psychology. I strongly endorse this goal and recognize that their focus on retrospective reporting is both valuable and the appropriate scope for an article. However, I suggest that two related issues warrant greater emphasis in their framework: information leakage and procedural overfitting. Both can produce optimistic estimates of model performance despite apparently transparent reporting. I propose two extensions to the checklist: reporting requirements that make information leakage auditable and prospective specification of key analytical decisions through preregistration. I argue that these additions would further strengthen the ability of readers and reviewers to evaluate the trustworthiness of supervised ML analyses in psychology. Moreover, comprehensive guidelines that do not sufficiently emphasize these issues may create unwarranted confidence that threats to valid model evaluation have been ruled out, allowing information leakage or procedural overfitting to remain undetected.

items.title: More Visibility for Diversity? A Systematic Review of LGBTQ+ Representation in Educational Psychology Journals
items.abstract: Students identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or otherwise non-heterosexual or non-cisgender (LGBTQ+) are increasingly represented. However, they still face additional challenges in educational settings, so Educational Psychology needs to research these issues. In this preregistered systematic scientometric literature review, we investigate (a) the extent of LGBTQ+ centered research in Educational Psychology journals, (b) common themes and trends, and discuss systematic gaps for future research. After searching all 41,992 articles on ERIC, published in the most impactful (Q1 and Q2) Educational Psychology journals, we combined scientometric-quantitative and qualitative methods to review 68 eligible articles. We found a surge in publications from 2000 onward, driven by special issues. For almost half of these high-impact journals, we found no published articles on LGBTQ+ issues on ERIC; most publish only a few per thousand, even though this topic falls within their scope. Most often, these articles were empirical, correlational, and US-based, with inconsistent measures of LGBTQ+ identities. Through qualitative thematic analysis, we identified seven research themes and highlighted pertinent research gaps. To strengthen the evidence base in the field, future research should conduct rigorous longitudinal and intervention studies with culturally diverse samples and adhere to open science standards.

items.title: Artificial Agents as Leaders and Followers: An Integrative Role-Congruity Review
items.abstract: Artificial agents such as algorithms, virtual agents, and robots increasingly occupy organizational roles as leaders, followers, and partners. However, evidence on how people evaluate these nonhuman role occupants is mixed. We systematically review 107 empirical studies across management, psychology, engineering, and computer science through a role-congruity lens. A consistent pattern emerges: Artificial agents in leader roles face role incongruity, driven largely by perceived deficits in morality (e.g., fairness, trustworthiness). Agents in follower roles are evaluated as largely congruent with role expectations. Agents in partner and teammate roles show conditional congruity that depends on task context and design-based social cues (e.g., appearance, voice). We integrate these patterns into the Artificial Agent Role Congruity (AARC) model, a conceptual model that extends role congruity theory to artificial agents: perceived role (in)congruity occurs when observers compare role prescriptions with the attributes they ascribe to an agent from its design-based cues along a task dimension (competence, assertiveness) and a social-emotional dimension (warmth, morality). Based on this synthesis, we outline theoretical extensions, an agenda for future research, and guidance for managers and designers deploying artificial agents in organizational roles.

items.title: Avoiding the worst leaders is more important than getting the best
items.abstract: Society and organizations invest heavily in selecting the best leaders 1, and existing research shows a positivity bias by focusing on the bright side of leadership 2–4. Yet, according to Popper 5, the central question of institutional design is not who should rule, but how to prevent bad leaders from doing too much damage. This raises the question of which approach is more consistent with human psychology: Aim for the best leaders, or avoid the worst? We provide robust evidence for an “avoid-the-worst” principle in human leadership preferences. Although text analyses indicated that the top 100 business schools emphasize good leadership far more than the prevention of bad leadership, actual employee experiences from 9.9 million Glassdoor reviews show that people mentioned their leader 70% more often in the negative than positive section, and negative leader mentions predicted company ratings 1.5 times more strongly. Providing causal evidence, five high-powered experiments across 40 countries (N = 51,433) revealed that people were more willing to sacrifice time and money to avoid a bad leader than obtaining a good leader—across morality and competence, hypothetical and incentivized choice, ideology and culture. People care more about avoiding the worst leaders than getting the best.

items.title: The Prevalence of Bayesian Inference, Preregistration, and Open Data in Psychology, 2004-2024
items.abstract: Psychology has undergone substantial methodological changes in the past two decades. We tracked the adoption of Bayesian inference and two open science practices across 28,738 articles from six ‘top-tier’ (15,634 articles) and six ‘mid-tier’ (13,104 articles) psychology journals in 2004–2024. In ‘top-tier’ journals, human (50%) and LLM-assisted (50%) full-text coding revealed that in 2024, 26% of articles reported a Bayesian analysis, 41% included a preregistration, and 73% provided open data. In ‘mid-tier’ journals, LLM coding showed corresponding rates of 16%, 18%, and 40%. From 2004 to 2012, these practices were virtually nonexistent. Bayesian logistic growth modeling suggests further increases, although their extent remains uncertain. Mixed-effects models became more prevalent, software reporting improved, with greater use of R and less reliance on SPSS, but estimation-focused (vs. hypothesis-testing-focused) reporting showed only modest gains. Despite heterogeneity across journals, psychology articles published in 2024 differ markedly from those published only a decade earlier.

items.title: Sleep quality, chronotype, and psychological distress in adults with chronic conditions: independent associations and nonlinear sleep-quality gradients
items.abstract: Abstract Background We examined associations of sleep quality, chronotype, and chronic-condition burden with psychological distress in adults with chronic conditions and explored nonlinearity. Methods We analysed cross-sectional data from the Sichuan component of the 2023 Psychology and Behavior Investigation of Chinese Residents (PBICR-2023), collected from June to September 2023. Of 1,932 Sichuan respondents, 611 adults with at least one chronic condition were included. Chronotype, sleep quality, depression-anxiety symptoms, and perceived stress were assessed using the reduced Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (rMEQ), Brief Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (B-PSQI), Patient Health Questionnaire Anxiety and Depression Scale (PHQ-ADS), and four-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-4), respectively. Hierarchical multivariable linear regression with HC3 robust standard errors estimated adjusted associations. Unadjusted four-knot restricted cubic splines characterised nonlinear association patterns. Results PHQ-ADS and PSS-4 differed by age, household registration, income, education, body-mass-index category, relationship status, debt, recent life events, and chronic-condition count. They were strongly correlated ( r = 0.795; P P P P = 0.027); its PSS-4 association did not reach conventional significance (B=-0.31; 95% CI, -0.64 to 0.03; P = 0.075) and attenuated after broader adjustment. Splines indicated nonlinear B-PSQI associations with both outcomes ( P for nonlinearity P = 0.029), with fitted minima near 2.96 and 2.65, respectively. rMEQ nonlinearity was not statistically significant. Conclusions In this cross-sectional sample, Poorer sleep quality and greater chronic-condition burden were consistently associated with greater psychological distress. Morningness showed a weaker inverse association that attenuated after broader adjustment. Longitudinal studies with objective sleep and circadian measures are needed.

items.title: A complex systems approach to health workforce modelling: Simulating regional psychology workforce capacity and mental healthcare access to 2050
items.abstract: Abstract Background. Mental health workforce projections estimate future workforce supply and demand for services but seldom represent nonlinear feedback and behavioural adaptation through which population need, workforce capacity, service access, and system performance change over time. We examined these dynamics within a community-based psychological treatment pathway funded through Australia’s universal health insurance system and delivered by a Primary Health Network in southern Queensland. Methods. We developed and calibrated a 2013–2050 system dynamics model using workforce, Medicare-funded psychological therapy and population time series data. Model parameters were optimised against observed data, and uncertainty analyses identified plausible parameter combinations. The calibrated model generated a business-as-usual (BAU) projection and three stress test scenarios: (i) a future ceiling on workforce recruitment; (ii) increasing pressure from rising mental ill-health driven by compounding effects on onset; and (iii) their combination. Paired simulations compared each stress test with BAU. Results. The model reproduced broad historical trajectories. By 2050, mean paired differences from BAU under the recruitment ceiling were − 163 clinical FTE [-420, 0.0] and − 4,800 monthly services [-12,500, 0], with poorer access and workforce indicators despite a smaller visible treatment queue. Compounding onset pressure increased the population living with mental ill-health by 32,100 [24,100, 42,600]; workforce and services expanded but did not fully offset rising need. Combined pressures produced the clearest deterioration: +38,200 people living with mental ill-health [24,900, 55,200], -147 clinical FTE [-421, 84] and − 4,000 monthly services [-12,500, 2,900], alongside lower supply-demand balance and greater care-seeking suppression and pipeline attrition. Conclusions. BAU stability depended on recruitment keeping pace with demand. The combined pressures produced the clearest overall system-wide deterioration and showed that smaller queues can coexist with poorer access. Interpreting FTE, service volume and waiting alongside care-seeking, attrition and workforce conditions could support more complete whole-of-system planning. More broadly, these findings suggest that human resources for health planning may benefit from approaches that explicitly represent feedback processes, delays, behavioural adaptation, and other emergent system dynamics that influence how workforce capacity, service demand, and access evolve over time.

items.title: Beyond Correct Letters: Cognitive Foundations of Spelling in Multilingual African Contexts
items.abstract: Abstract Spelling is frequently characterised as the accurate reproduction of conventional written forms, a definition that can obscure the cognitive and linguistic mechanisms underpinning its acquisition and development. This conceptual article reframes spelling as an integrated cognitive–linguistic process and considers what this means for multilingual education in African contexts. Drawing on a qualitative, theory-driven synthesis of literacy studies, cognitive psychology, linguistics, and multilingual education, it combines research on phonological, orthographic, and morphological awareness with evidence on memory, vocabulary, and multilingual resources. The synthesis advances the position that spelling competence arises from dynamic interactions among these component systems rather than from a strictly linear process of grapheme sequencing. It also argues that multilingualism is not mainly a source of cross-linguistic interference; rather, it offers resources learners strategically draw on across languages to develop literacy. With specific attention to African educational contexts in which learners negotiate languages differing in orthographic depth, morphological structure, and instructional status, the article proposes a Multidimensional Cognitive–Linguistic Spelling Framework that embeds core cognitive processes within multilingual ecologies and schooling conditions. The proposed framework aims to guide empirically grounded spelling instruction and assessment by considering learners’ linguistic repertoires and the cognitive processes underlying orthographic learning.

items.title: Temporal associations between pain and anxiety/depression in young people: A systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal, prospective, population- and community-based studies
items.abstract: Pain, anxiety, and depression are common among young people, frequently co-occur with each other, and may be longitudinally related. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to synthesise the direction and strength of the temporal associations between pain and anxiety/depression among young people. PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, Proquest Dissertations and Theses, Google Scholar, and OSF Preprints were searched from inception until 3 July 2026. Additional studies were identified through citation searching and references of existing systematic reviews. Longitudinal, prospective, population- or community-based studies examining temporal associations between pain and anxiety/depression among young people (0-24 years) were included. Two independent reviewers screened studies, extracted data, assessed risk of bias using ROBINS-E, and evaluated certainty of evidence using GRADE. Data were synthesised using three-level meta-analysis and narrative synthesis. Forty-two studies from 31 longitudinal cohorts were included. Anxiety, depression, and combined anxiety/depression were positively associated with subsequent pain. However, after adjustment for confounders, only depression remained significantly associated. Pain was positively associated with subsequent anxiety, depression, and combined anxiety/depression both before and after confounder adjustment. Heterogeneity was moderate to considerable and was partly explained by sex, baseline age, follow-up duration, pain type, pain informant, pain and anxiety/depression operationalisation, and risk of bias. Two of 14 outcomes had high quality of evidence, whereas the remainder ranged from very low to moderate quality. These findings highlight longitudinal associations between pain and anxiety/depression among young people and should be considered in the screening, treatment, and public health management of these problems.

items.title: Acceptability and perceived effectiveness of health warnings and calorie labels on alcohol products: An online experimental study
items.abstract: AimsImproved alcohol labels are a population-level intervention with the potential to reduce selection and consumption of alcohol. The primary aim of this study was to assess the acceptability of implementing (i) alcohol calorie labelling, (ii) alcohol health warning labels (HWLs), and (iii) both types of labels combined, each presented with or without images. The specific labels used were based on those being proposed for national implementation in Ireland.MethodsParticipants (n=994) were randomly assigned to one of six groups in an online experiment with a between subject 3 (Label Type: HWL only; calorie labelling only; combined label [HWLs and calorie labelling]) x 2 (Message Type: description; description plus example image) factorial design. The primary outcome was acceptability of implementing the labelling policy. Secondary outcomes were perceived effectiveness and potential harms. Free-text comments were analysed using content analysis.ResultsThere was a significant main effect of Label Type (F(2, 990)=4.27, p=0.014, ηₚ²=0.01), with acceptability lower for HWLs (p=0.01, d=0.23). There was no main effect of Message Type or interaction. All types of labels were perceived as relatively acceptable. There were no overall differences in perceived effectiveness or harms of the labels. ConclusionsHWLs and calorie information were both perceived as relatively acceptable, although HWLs were less accepted. The way the labelling policy was presented did not affect acceptability. Although further evaluation with other labelling interventions is warranted, this suggests giving the public more detailed and visual information about a labelling policy does not decrease acceptability of the policy. items.title: The Relationship Between Problematic Social Media Use and Sleep Quality Among University Students : A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Abstract Problematic social media use has emerged as a significant global public health concern, particularly among university students. This systematic review synthesizes contemporary evidence across diverse geographical contexts to evaluate the relationship between social media addiction and objective sleep quality parameters. Following strict inclusion criteria, ten high-quality empirical studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses published between 2023 and 2026—representing populations in Bangladesh, China, India, Malaysia, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom, Nigeria, and Brazil—were synthesized. The collective findings across a cumulative sample size of over 40,000 participants demonstrate a robust, negative correlation between excessive digital exposure and sleep duration. Late-night screen time, driven by Fear of Missing Out (FoMo) and digital fatigue, severely alters circadian rhythms and suppresses melatonin secretion, leading to fragmented sleep, daytime sleepiness, and heightened depressive symptoms. While protective behavioral strategies like physical exercise offer a viable mitigation buffer, their efficacy is heavily undermined by extreme digital dependencies. In conclusion, unregulated social media consumption poses an escalating threat to student well-being. Immediate multi-sectoral interventions, digital literacy programs, and campus-based health policies are required to safeguard the physical and psychological health of the higher education workforce.

items.title: Sport Is Social Medicine: A Conceptual Review of Loneliness and Social Health
items.abstract: Abstract Background Loneliness has emerged as a major public health challenge associated with adverse biological, psychological, and social outcomes. Although traditionally conceptualized as an individual psychological experience, contemporary perspectives increasingly emphasize social connection and social health as important determinants of well-being. Sport and physical activity have received growing attention as potential strategies for addressing loneliness; however, the mechanisms through which sport may influence loneliness and social health have not been clearly synthesized within a single conceptual framework. This review aimed to examine how sport participation may contribute to reducing loneliness through biological, psychological, and social pathways and to explore its potential role in promoting social health. Methods This study was conducted as a conceptual review using a narrative synthesis approach. Literature related to loneliness, social connection, social health, physical activity, sport participation, social prescribing, and relevant theoretical frameworks was reviewed across multiple disciplines. Evidence was examined and synthesized to identify the biological, psychological, and social mechanisms through which sport may influence loneliness and social health. Based on this synthesis, a conceptual model was developed to explain the relationships among sport participation, social connection, social health, and loneliness. Results The reviewed evidence suggests that sport participation may influence loneliness through interconnected biological, psychological, and social pathways. Biological mechanisms include improved stress regulation, reduced inflammation, and enhanced cognitive health. Psychological mechanisms involve greater self-efficacy, self-esteem, resilience, and well-being. Social mechanisms include strengthened social support, belongingness, social identity, and community participation. Building upon these findings, the Biopsychosocial Loop Model is proposed to explain how sport participation may strengthen social connection, promote social health, and reduce loneliness through mutually reinforcing processes. The review further introduces the Sport is Social Medicine (SSM) perspective, which conceptualizes sport as a social health resource that extends beyond its traditional role in physical and mental health promotion. Conclusions Current evidence suggests that the relationship between sport and loneliness cannot be explained through a single mechanism. Rather, sport appears to operate through interconnected biopsychosocial pathways that strengthen social connection and support social health. The proposed Biopsychosocial Loop Model and Sport is Social Medicine perspective provide complementary conceptual frameworks for understanding how sport may contribute to addressing loneliness and promoting social health across the lifespan. These frameworks may inform future research, public health strategies, and community-based interventions aimed at strengthening social connection and well-being.

items.title: Digital Transformation of Public Finance and Fiscal Depth: Impact on Spending Efficiency to Achieve the Sustainable Development Goals in Iraq

By enhancing transparency, reducing waste, and improving efficiency in the allocation and use of public resources, digital transformation directly contributes to raising the level of efficiency of public spending. This efficiency, in turn, is a vital factor in countries’ ability to finance and achieve the Sustainable Development Goals, which positively impacts the long-term well-being and sustainability of societies. items.title: Maltreatment predicts centiles of individual variation from normative brain growth in children
items.abstract: Abstract Exposure to maltreatment in childhood is posited to profoundly disrupt brain development with adverse consequences for cognitive development and health across the lifespan. Here we use “brain charts” from the largest available neuroimaging database to quantify individual brain volumes relative to normative brain growth distributions in 299 children, aged 3 to 13 years, including 123 children with clinically verified maltreatment exposure. Using magnetic resonance imaging, we obtain volumes of cortical grey, total white, and subcortical grey matter and derive chart-based centiles for each child and tissue type. In our sample, children with maltreatment exposure exhibit lower mean brain centiles across tissues than unexposed children. Associations of greater maltreatment severity with lower brain centiles do not survive correction for multiple comparisons. Lower brain centiles are associated with lower intellectual ability and more behavioural problems. These findings provide evidence for widespread differences in brain structure associated with childhood maltreatment and their relevance to intellectual ability and behavioural functioning.

items.title: Experience affects novel object aversion and the use of human cues in rural and urban American crows
items.abstract: Abstract Population differences in behavior can result from experience, which can be drastically different between environments such as urban and rural areas. Urban areas may be more complex, contain more human-made objects but fewer natural objects, or have more non-threatening people. Consequently, animals in urban and rural populations may differ in neophobia levels, what is novel, and attention to human behavior. We conducted two experiments with a common urban bird, the American crow (Corvus brachyrhynchos). On home territories of urban and rural crow family groups, we presented objects that were either equally novel in both environments or more common in one environment than the other. Separately, we measured flight initiation distance (FID) from an approaching person using either a direct or averted, less threatening gaze for individual crows across an urban gradient. We found that urban crows were more neophobic than rural crows, as measured by the probability of feeding near an object that is equally novel in both environments. There were no differences in approach and feeding latencies for the least neophobic family member. Both urban and rural crows were less averse to objects that were more common in their respective environments. In the FID experiment, crows in highly urbanized areas had FIDs 25 m shorter for an indirect gaze, while rural crow FIDs were unaffected by gaze. FIDs were best predicted by crows’ experiences with people in a relatively large area around each trial. These results highlight how experience must be accounted for when considering population differences in behavior.

items.title: A meaningful framework for change for the Police
items.abstract: Background This PhD project evolved from MSc research by the author into stressors in a UK police force. The findings from both the MSc study and existing literature suggested that the UK police need a new way to support their officers and staff in reducing psychological distress. This led the author to want to create a Meaningful Framework for Change, moving the police from being reactive to psychological distress to being proactive and preventative. Aim and Research Question This PhD project aimed to develop a Framework for Change within a specific UK police force to determine its feasibility and identify what might be required to achieve this goal. In this sense, the PhD project is somewhat untraditional, as the author is an applied psychologist and the work is hands-on and practical, involving support methods that are to be tried and tested within the pilot force. Methods Due to its applied and practical nature, the author was embedded with the pilot police force, and the most logical method for this project was to be autoethnographical in its approach. The thesis is subsequently written in the first person and is less traditional than the reader may be used to seeing. Results/Findings The findings showed that it is possible to design a Meaningful Framework for Change for a police force, introducing new methods of supporting officers and staff. The Framework for Change was partially achieved, with some elements still to be developed by the end of the project. Conclusion Although the project was successful, it took longer than the usual three years of full-time PhD study because of COVID delays. However, from a cultural change perspective, the extra time was beneficial in securing the organisational uptake that made a difference for officers and staff, providing a new and meaningful way to support them.

items.title: Developing a multisensory smell retraining programme
items.abstract: Olfactory training (OT) is a well-established intervention for enhancing smell function, but questions remain about the mechanisms underpinning its effectiveness and the features that optimise outcomes. This thesis investigates how factors such as odour pleasantness, training duration, subjective experiences, and multisensory integration contribute to OT efficacy, drawing on both quantitative and qualitative approaches. A systematic review of the OT literature revealed that improvements in olfactory function are influenced by elements such as training duration, odour selection, and adherence. However, the review also highlighted substantial methodological variation across studies, underscoring the need for more standardised and theory-driven approaches. To facilitate experimental control over odour valence in subsequent work, a stimulus set of pleasant and unpleasant odours was developed and validated through hedonic ratings, enabling precise manipulation of this dimension. Building on these foundations, a 16-week longitudinal OT study was conducted with participants with and without olfactory dysfunction who trained using a set of pleasant, unpleasant, or mixed odours. Results indicated that olfactory function improved over time regardless of odour valence, suggesting that a longer training duration may be more influential than odour pleasantness in driving improvement. To better understand the lived experience of individuals undergoing olfactory training, a qualitative study explored participants’ perceptions, and revealed four key themes: lived experiences of olfactory dysfunction; OT challenges; noticeable changes in olfactory function; and training techniques and strategies employed to facilitate training. Finally, a short-term study tested whether visual-olfactory congruency could enhance training effects over a one-week period. No significant gains were observed, indicating that brief multisensory training may be insufficient without longer engagement or additional support. Together, these findings advance understanding of how OT works, highlighting the importance of duration, baseline ability, subjective engagement, and adherence. The work contributes to the development of more effective, personalised OT interventions, particularly for use in clinical settings with individuals experiencing olfactory loss.

items.title: How Australian fire and rescue service personnel would like to improve their decision-making learning and training programs
items.abstract: Effective management of the response to an incident or emergency event is critically dependent on the decision-making skills of incident and emergency management (IEM) personnel. In a series of workshops conducted in 2022 by Natural Hazards Research Australia, priorities were identified that specified future needs for the practice and training of IEM decision-making. The research in this paper contributes to the understanding of how to address these priorities by considering the views of a sample of fire and rescue service personnel about their agency’s current decision-making training program and aspects to improve. This paper provides findings from 34 semi-structured interviews with fire and rescue services personnel in Australia. The sample comprised 29 men and 5 women. Participants worked in rural fire services (n=17), urban fire services (n=9) and State Emergency Services (n=8). The findings suggest that there is need for greater training focus on emergency management decision-making, greater use of exercise-based training activities, a formal approach to mentoring and coaching staff development programs and mandatory refresher courses and review exercises to maintain incident management skills. Australian fire and rescue services agencies need to ensure they are taking a strategic and holistic approach to emergency management learning and development programs.

items.title: The Influence of Self-Esteem and Gender on Judgments of Sociosexuality and Romantic Desirability in a Hypothetical Dating Context
items.abstract: In forming first impressions of others, people may notice and attend to cues about the others’ self-esteem, argued to function as a “proxy trait” that can influence inferences of other traits, including relationship desirability (Cameron et al., 2016 ). Our study provided a further test of this lay theory of self-esteem by examining how information about a hypothetical person’s self-esteem not only affects participants’ judgments of the romantic desirability of the target (from a third person perspective), but also estimates of the target’s sociosexuality (degree of being restricted vs. unrestricted in sexual attitudes and behaviors). Using a vignette experimental design, we manipulated the self-esteem (low or high) and gender (man or woman) of a hypothetical target in an online dating profile. Results indicated that a high self-esteem (HSE) target was estimated to be more attractive and desirable to online daters, and also assumed to have higher sociosexuality compared to a low self-esteem (LSE) target. Our study also contributes to the literature on gender stereotypes related to sexuality; a male target was assumed to be more unrestricted in their sociosexuality than a female target. However, the gender of the target did not interact with the self-esteem of the target to affect impressions of targets’ sociosexuality. Beyond extending past research, our results provide implications for interventions in clinical, educational, and relational contexts.

items.title: Khawf, Huzn and Sakinah in Islamic finance
items.abstract: This article analyses the way in which Islamic finance incorporates certain psychological and emotional states known in Islamic thought, namely khawf (fear and apprehension in the face of the unknown future) and huzn (sadness and regret for choices made in the past), within a system of welldefined norms and operational structures. This methodology is compared with that of traditional finance and behavioral finance, stating that the Islamic approach proposes a structurally different solution to economic precariousness. The study adopts a qualitative conceptual methodology that combines Qur'anic textual analysis, regulatory examination of Islamic finance standards issued by the Organization of Accounting and Auditing for Islamic Financial Institutions (AAOIFI) and the Islamic Financial Services Board (IFSB), and contextual analysis of macrofinancial data from international institutions. The focus is on institutional design rather than causal inference. The analysis shows that Islamic finance institutionalizes khawf and huzn as economic constraints through prohibitions of gharar and ribā, risk-sharing, and zakāt. In contrast, conventional finance monetizesfear and regret via debt and risk transfer, while behavioral finance remains primarily descriptive. This article contributes to the literature conceptualizing Islamic finance as a normative institutionalization of behavioral insights and promoting sakinah (tranquillity) as a systemic goal of financial design. The study is conceptual and does not empirically test causal relationships. Selected principles of Islamic finance can inform ethical screening, debt regulation, and financial consumer protection frameworks. By structurally addressing debt-related uncertainty and distress, Islamic finance contributes to financial well-being and social stability

items.title: INTEGRASI NILAI-NILAI BUDAYA LOKAL SUMATERA UTARA DALAM DESAIN PEMBELAJARAN BAHASA INGGRIS BERBASIS KARAKTER
items.abstract: This study aims to develop and evaluate a character-based English language instructional design that integrates the local cultural values of North Sumatra to improve students’ English proficiency and multicultural character. The approach incorporates the traditions and local wisdom of ethnic groups, including the Batak, Malay, Nias, and Karo, to strengthen linguistic competence while fostering cultural awareness and identity. It also seeks to prepare graduates who are globally competitive and remain rooted in their local cultural heritage. The study employed a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group pretest–posttest design. It was conducted during the fifth semester of the 2026/2027 academic year in the English Literature Study Program, Faculty of Literature, Universitas Islam Sumatera Utara (UISU). The sample consisted of 72 undergraduate students, with 36 assigned to the experimental group and 36 to the control group. The experimental group received local culture-based instruction, whereas the control group received conventional instruction. The instruments measured English proficiency through locally relevant cultural content and multicultural character across four dimensions: cultural awareness, appreciation of diversity, cross-cultural empathy, and cultural identity. Data were analyzed using multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA) and normalized gain (N-gain). The results indicated significant improvements in English proficiency (F = 29.47, p < .001, d = 0.94) and multicultural character (F = 34.82, p < .001, d = 1.07). The N-gain scores were 0.68 for English proficiency and 0.71 for multicultural character. These findings support integrating North Sumatra’s local cultural values into character-based English language instruction.

items.title: Land-based search and rescue training: evolution and simplification
items.abstract: Land-based search and rescue training in Aotearoa New Zealand has undergone substantial change, yet there has been limited examination of how these changes have affected the analytical foundations of search management. This review was undertaken to identify what concepts, tools and competencies have been retained, modified or lost in the Managing Land Search Operations course that evolved into Manage the Initial Response and Extended Search Planning. Using 8 analytical domains and a continuity scoring approach, this longitudinal review examined the evolution of 3 core courses. Findings indicate improvements in operational rhythm, interoperability, safety and alignment with the country’s Coordinated Incident Management System. However, these gains are accompanied by a reduction in analytical depth, probability-based reasoning and decision traceability. Key frameworks, including the Probability of Success equation and the Bike Wheel model, have been simplified without clear justification. This review concludes with recommendations to restore analytical foundations and strengthen evidence-based decision-making within the search and rescue training system.

items.title: SUPRIATNOKO’S FIVE-FINGERS TECHNIQUE MODEL: INNOVATION IN ENGLISH GRAMMAR LEARNING TO IMPROVE INDONESIAN STUDENTS’ COMMUNICATIVE COMPETENCE
items.abstract: Mastery of grammar, especially English tenses, is a fundamental component in developing effective communication skills among Indonesian EFL students. However, in practice, tenses remain one of the most challenging aspects for students across educational levels to comprehend and apply. Despite the wide range of instructional methods available, tense instruction in Indonesian classrooms still predominantly emphasizes formula memorization rather than functional use in real communication. Consequently, students tend to forget grammatical rules easily, struggle to apply tenses flexibly, and experience low confidence in speaking and writing. This study aims to (1) develop the Supriatnoko Five-Finger Technique Model as an innovative instructional framework for teaching English tenses, (2) examine its theoretical foundations in embodied learning and communicative language teaching, and (3) evaluate its preliminary effectiveness in improving students’ functional use of tenses in speaking and writing. The study employed a research and development (R&D) design combined with a limited pilot implementation. The development phase included conceptual design, model formulation, and instructional material preparation. The pilot implementation involved classroom application at Sekolah Terbuka Madani Depok using a quasi-experimental approach with comparative observation of students’ performance before and after the intervention. Data were collected through speaking and writing assessments, classroom observation, and student feedback questionnaires. The Supriatnoko Five-Finger Technique Model is a visual and kinesthetics’ instructional approach that maps five major English tense categories—present, past, future, perfect, and continuous—onto the five fingers of the hand. Each finger is associated with a distinct communicative question type: WH-questions, Yes/No questions, Negative tag questions, Positive tag questions, and Assumption questions. The novelty of this study lies in its integration of embodied learning, functional tense categorization, and communicative question-based interaction into a single instruction model that operationalizes grammatical tenses to support functional language use, rather than focusing on vocabulary acquisition or classroom commands. Preliminary findings indicate that 97.4% of students demonstrated measurable improvement in their speaking and writing performance compared to conventional teaching methods. Although promising, the model requires further large-scale testing and refinement across diverse secondary and language training contexts to ensure broader applicability and effectiveness.

items.title: Individual differences and grade-related changes in sensitivity to the statistical structure of word forms in a shallow writing system
items.abstract: Abstract The present study investigates a principal mechanism underlying reading development and individual differences in reading skills, namely sensitivity to orthotactic regularities in lexical processing. This sensitivity can be seen as a reflection of statistical learning (SL), as it pertains to accumulated experience with statistical regularities in print. However, empirical evidence regarding the link between such sensitivity and reading skills remains mixed, and it is particularly unclear what role it plays in orthographically shallow languages. The present study addressed this issue by assessing sensitivity to orthotactic regularities in Finnish pseudowords using a lexical decision task, and examining how this sensitivity depends on vocabulary skill and grade by comparing students from grades 3, 4, and 7 ( N = 818). We identified distinct differences between grade levels, with the orthotactic sensitivity effect being significantly stronger in higher grade levels. Furthermore, we observed substantial within-grade individual differences, with higher vocabulary proficiency predicting greater effects of orthotactic regularities in pseudowords. These findings demonstrate a link between sensitivity to orthotactic constraints and linguistic skills. Importantly, our findings indicate that sensitivity to statistical information is critical even in markedly shallow orthographies, challenging earlier literature. We discuss the implications of our findings for SL views of reading. We also discuss whether sensitivity to regularity exists at the level of orthotactics, phonotactics, or both, given that in the shallow writing system of Finnish the distinction between these levels is blurred.

items.title: Delusions and Compelling Experiences
items.abstract: Abstract Delusion is one of the most puzzling doxastic phenomena: on the one hand, the subject appears irrational, holding a delusion despite counterevidence; on the other hand, the subject appears otherwise rational, apportioning their non-delusional beliefs to the evidence. Leading theories of delusion, despite their strengths, still face notable limitations. This article argues that they may benefit from a new empiricist approach. Drawing on insights from Hobbes and Locke, it proposes that the subject may have a distinctive kind of compelling experience that is phenomenologically analogous to, and can effectively be more compelling than, the Cartesian ‘clear experience’. How the experience may, in various ways and to varying degrees, compel domain-specific irrational belief in the face of counterevidence will be articulated.

items.title: ASSESSING THAILAND’S COMMUNITY CRAB BANKS THROUGH INTERNATIONAL CRITERIA FOR SUSTAINABLE MARINE CONSERVATION
items.abstract: This qualitative study evaluates Thailand’s Blue Swimming Crab Bank Expansion Project against five international criteria for sustainable community-based conservation: measurable ecological impact, community participation, scientific credibility, knowledge transfer, and policy alignment. To overcome the persistent limitations of purely narrative assessments, the research systematically triangulates empirical evidence from official operational reports, rigorous peer-reviewed publications, and external international endorsements. The findings show that the project aligns with all five multidimensional criteria. Notably, the initiative transformed local fishers into active co-managers, established fifty-two dynamic learning centers, and demonstrably increased juvenile crab survival rates from one percent to between forty and sixty percent. Furthermore, this robust integration of community empowerment and scientifically verifiable ecosystem recovery contributed directly to upgrading Thailand’s Fishery Improvement Project status from level C to level A. Ultimately, the study argues that international-standard success in marine conservation emerges not from a single isolated factor, but from these five dimensions mutually reinforcing one another. By utilizing this rigorous criterion-based assessment, the framework provides funding agencies and policymakers with a highly replicable, evidence-based tool for designing sustainable natural resource management globally.

items.title: Integrative approach reveals hidden diversity in the Brachionus (Rotifera, Monogononta)
items.abstract: The phylum Rotifera has many species complexes that require integrative analyses to resolve their taxonomic identity. Brachionus angularis comprises different morphotypes. In Aguascalientes, Mexico, we observed two of these morphotypes coexisting. To explore their species identity, we applied an integrative approach that combined taxonomical, ecological, and molecular data. Our results demonstrate taxonomic differentiation in the lengths of females, males, and diapausing eggs between the two morphotypes. We also observed distinct hatching patterns and clearly different ornamentation in diapausing eggs between the two morphotypes. Genetic variation between one monoclonal culture of each morphotype revealed distances of 18.8% for mitochondrial COI and 13.73% for nuclear ITS1 regions. These marked, concordant divergences in mitochondrial and nuclear markers across the closely related Brachionus species, together with diagnostic morphological and ecological differences, support the recognition of the two morphotypes as distinct species. Accordingly, we describe Brachionus agsensis sp. nov. and Brachionus hydrocalidensis sp. nov. as new species.

items.title: Fine-scale characterization of dispersed-village landscapes: data challenges and methodological advances for rural landscape mapping and assessment in Pomerania, Poland
items.abstract: Abstract Dispersed-village landscapes in Pomerania are shaped by local environmental conditions and long-term farming practices, yet standard spatial datasets generalize many fine-scale landscape elements. In this pilot study, we developed and tested a fine-scale mapping and assessment approach at the 64-ha Knyki-1 reference site using a custom 3-level land-use/land-cover (LULC) scheme, an uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)-derived digital surface model (DSM), field mapping, plant-cover inventories, and GIS analysis. We compared custom mapping with CORINE Land Cover (CLC) and the Topographic Objects Database (BDOT10k) using landscape- and class-level metrics. At the Knyki-1 site, standard datasets strongly generalized or omitted small patches, linear elements, woody structures, and structural transition zones that may correspond to ecotonal structures. The custom mapping represented 21 LULC classes and 148 patches, versus 2–6 classes and 6–28 patches in the standard datasets, showing how dataset choice affects landscape representation and structural inference. Field inventories documented ancient-forest indicators, archaeophytes, and protected vascular-plant taxa across multiple landscape components. The resulting fine-scale baseline may support future repeated monitoring and, after multi-site validation, regional landscape assessment, conservation planning, and management. These natural–cultural rural landscapes remain absent from national landscape classifications and are increasingly vulnerable to pressures from the abandonment of traditional agriculture.

items.title: Population consolidation and head-starting as demographic rescue of a low-density gopher tortoise population
items.abstract: Context Gopher tortoises, Gopherus polyphemus, are a keystone species of south-eastern North America due to their historically high density, grazing habits, and the burrows that they maintain across upland landscapes. Many gopher tortoise populations are demographically non-viable due to low population density and/or population size. Management for this species frequently utilize measures such as translocation and head-starting. Aims Between 2020 and 2024, we used short-distance translocation to consolidate a low-density resident population of gopher tortoises and monitored spatial biology and apparent survival in the translocated animals immediately following translocation. We also conducted head-starting of tortoises collected as eggs from the same site and manipulated head-start release conditions to test whether soft- versus hard-release affected apparent survival. Methods We tracked both wild and head-started tortoises via radiotelemetry for 1 year during and 1 year after penning; we determined apparent survival by direct observation of individuals remaining alive and within the site approximately 1.5 years after all enclosure pens had been removed. Key results Home ranges of free-ranging tortoises were approximately the same in the enclosure pen as they were after the enclosure pen was removed, but apparent survival of free-ranging tortoises at the study site was only 56% after the enclosure was removed. Male adult tortoises had higher apparent survival in the site than did females, and translocation distance was a negative predictor of apparent survival. Release condition did not affect head-started tortoise apparent survival, and overall apparent survival of head-started tortoises was 70% 2 years after release. Conclusions Head-starting and direct hard release of juveniles are likely to be successful tools for gopher tortoise conservation, whereas population consolidation may cause poor adult survival and/or site fidelity. Implications Short-distance translocations of wildlife populations should be further studied before this tool is more broadly applied in conservation projects.

items.title: Contrasting responses to climate change in two Dianthus species of the Irano-Anatolian biodiversity hotspot
items.abstract: The Irano-Anatolian biodiversity hotspot harbors exceptional plant richness and endemism but faces severe threats from climate change. I used MaxEnt-based ecological niche models to evaluate the current and future distributions of two closely related species, Dianthus floribundus and Dianthus szowitsianus . Models were projected for mid-century (2041–2070) and late-century (2071–2100) under SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios. Temperature-related predictors, particularly annual mean temperature (bio1) and temperature seasonality (bio4), were the dominant drivers, yet the species showed markedly different responses to future climates. D. floribundus , characterized by a narrow thermal niche, is predicted to undergo severe habitat contraction (up to 60%) and pronounced elevational and latitudinal shifts toward northern high-elevation refugia, consistent with the “escalator to extinction” paradigm for cold-adapted mountain taxa. In contrast, D. szowitsianus displayed a broader modeled climatic suitability, maintaining most of its core range while expanding into newly suitable habitats, with projected gains exceeding 50%. These asymmetric outcomes highlight the species-specific nature of climate change impacts even among closely related endemics and forecast a decoupling of historical assemblages, with potential consequences for montane community structure and species interactions. Moreover, the reduction of overlap between the two species and the limited representation of persistent habitats within current protected areas underscore the urgent need for forward-looking conservation strategies. My findings emphasize that conserving montane biodiversity in global hotspots requires species-focused vulnerability assessments, identification of future refugia, and adaptive management frameworks to mitigate differential risks and preserve endemic diversity under climate change.

items.title: Standardizing freshwater macroinvertebrate taxonomy: a Lithuanian operational taxa list for ecological quality assessments and biodiversity research
items.abstract: Taxonomic discrepancies pose a significant barrier to national data synthesis and accurate biomonitoring reporting. We compiled a standardized operational taxa list of freshwater macroinvertebrates known to occur in Lithuania, with the goal of improving comparability and ecological quality assessment reliability of biomonitoring data. A national list of freshwater macroinvertebrates was created by synthesizing literature and biomonitoring data. We standardized the synthesized taxa list according to contemporary nomenclature and integrated ecological and genetic information for each species. Using a rule-based approach, we assigned operational taxonomic units to each validated taxon according to the taxonomic level required within each of the Lithuanian river macroinvertebrate index’s constituent metrics. We tested the impact of operational taxonomic unit assignment on the calculation of ecological quality using national biomonitoring data from 401 sites (931 samples) collected between 2014 and 2022. Three out of four tested metrics were practically indistinguishable from the originally reported ecological status values, with the final ecological status classes matching in 91.4% of samples. For the fourth metric, which encompasses the proportional contributions of Malacostraca (formerly Crustacea), we found taxonomic inconsistencies in originally reported results, with recalculated values for this metric being consistently lower. Our findings indicate that Lithuania’s current ecological assessment method is not adversely sensitive to changes in taxonomic resolution, even when standardization led to a 61.3% reduction of taxonomic richness across all groups of macroinvertebrates. The present study is a step toward more reliable and consistent biomonitoring in Lithuania, especially with the anticipated uptake of DNA-based monitoring methods.
