items.title: Resistance to capitalist-oriented agrarian development: A case study of the “Matigsalug” in Mindanao, Philippines
items.abstract: For generations, “Matigsalug” traditional farming has been the foundation of sustainable development in their ancestral domain, sustaining livelihoods, preserving cultural traditions, and nurturing ecological wisdom in their farmlands. This study examines “Matigsalug” resistance to capitalist-oriented agrarian development, as evidenced by the proliferation of the Green Revolution in their farmlands. This qualitative study adopted a case study design combined with Indigenous methodologies, drawing on practices such as storytelling, visiting, and sharing circles to foreground participants’ self-determination, autonomy, and identity throughout the research process. The theoretical framework of Green Marxism was also used to critically analyze the voices, choices, and agency of the “Matigsalug” in their quest for indigeneity in their farmlands. The critical perspectives on “Matigsalug” farmland are as follows: (1) capitalist disempowerment of traditional farmers; (2) dependence on Westernized forms of development through the Green Revolution; (3) displacement due to unsustainable modern farming; (4) resistance to capitalist-oriented agricultural practices; (5) resistance through regenerative agriculture; and (6) resistance through the rejection of the Green Revolution. This study contributes to an understanding of the provenance of the “Matigsalug” ontology, epistemology, and axiology, enabling a deeper evaluation of reciprocity and relationality with the land. The indigenous worldview of the “Matigsalug” also conveys the cultural and emotional significance of their interactions with the environment, through which they develop meaning and identity. The study sheds light on the complex interplay among negotiated ecological spaces, traditional narratives, memories, and values associated with their farmland, offering valuable critical insights into their relationship with the land.

items.title: Practical Tools for Fire Risk Assessment in Mediterranean Open Woodlands Using Handheld Laser Scanning and Unmanned Aerial Vehicle Photogrammetry
items.abstract: Abstract Mediterranean forests are becoming increasingly vulnerable to wildfires. Given this, there is an urgent need for accurate, high-resolution data on canopy fuel characteristics to facilitate fire behavior modeling and guide risk mitigation efforts. This study assesses the performance of handheld mobile laser scanning (HMLS) and low-cost unmanned aerial vehicle digital aerial photogrammetry (UAV-DAP) in estimating key canopy fuel parameters and stand structural attributes, including canopy base height, stand height, canopy fuel load, canopy bulk density, and canopy cover. Field data were collected from 12 circular plots in open woodlands ( dehesas ) dominated by Quercus suber or Quercus ilex in the southwest of the Iberian Peninsula. Each plot was surveyed using traditional forest inventory, HMLS with a GeoSLAM ZEB Horizon scanner, and UAV DAP with RGB imagery processed using structure-from-motion techniques. In both cases, the resulting point clouds were processed using LiDAR360 software to extract canopy fuel parameters. HMLS yielded the most accurate estimates for most variables, with relative root mean square error (RMSE%) values ranging from 4% for canopy fuel load to 23.3% for canopy base height. UAV DAP showed a wider range of RMSE% values, from 5.9% for stand height to 41.2% for canopy bulk density, and was notably less effective for variables that require the characterization of subcanopy structure, such as canopy fuel load and canopy bulk density. These findings suggest that HMLS is a reliable and efficient tool for under-canopy data acquisition for small-scale forest managers to assess fire risk and provide reference data for high resolution fuel mapping, while UAV DAP may be a viable option for managers operating in areas that are difficult to access or require low-cost inventories.

items.title: Enabling fire-safe gardens: a case study from Greater Hobart
items.abstract: Garden management plays a crucial role in reducing bushfire risk at the wildland-urban interface, yet implementation of fire-safe practices remains challenging. An analysis of garden assessments and in-depth interviews with 23 property owners in Greater Hobart, Tasmania, examined how technical, social and emotional factors influence garden bushfire adaptation decisions. Using the Cynefin framework and complexity theory, this study demonstrates that successful adaptation addresses multiple domains of complexity, from straightforward vegetation management to complex socio-emotional attachments to garden spaces. Findings reveal that while personalised garden assessment reports can motivate change, their success depends on a broader set of conditions. Barriers include practical constraints (e.g. green waste management), emotional attachments to garden elements and difficulties obtaining context-specific guidance. By applying the As Low As Reasonably Practicable (ALARP) principle, this study identified cost-effective interventions across the 4 avenues of institutional support and resource management, individual garden bushfire adaptation, personalised technical guidance and community support networks. This research suggests that creating fire-adapted gardens requires coordinated support systems that address both practical implementation challenges and emotional connections to garden spaces.

items.title: Evidence of Birgus latro (Linnaeus, 1767) population in Surigao del Sur, Mindanao, Philippines
items.abstract: The general distribution pattern of coconut crab or Birgus latro (Linnaeus, 1767) shows patchy and insular populations which are influenced by ecological needs and human pressures. Historical records in the Philippines, including global occurrence databases (GBIF 2026) indicate a handful of intermittent sightings of the species in the country. The research note documents a newly recorded population of the B. latro in Surigao del Sur, Mindanao, Philippines. Random field surveys and interviews with key informants conducted from October 2024 to April 2025 confirmed the presence of individuals of B. latro in three different coastal and islet limestone, ultramafic forests in Surigao del Sur, indicating evidence of a population of the species. This record expands the known population and distribution of B. latro in Mindanao, where previous reports suggest a discontinuous national distribution, extending to southern Sulu and Batanes on the Northern Pacific coast and island regions. The finding is significant for both scientific inquiry and conservation, given the vulnerable status of the species within its known population and distribution range in the country. The confirmed population in Surigao del Sur represents an important record that fills the gap in the occurrence and distribution of B. latro on the Pacific seaboard of Mindanao, Philippines, which could serve as a basis for localized species and habitat management.

items.title: Species of the genus Gibberula Swainson, 1840 (Gastropoda: Cystiscidae) from Namibia
items.abstract: The marine gastropod fauna off Namibia (SW Africa) has hardly been explored. The current study on species of the genus Gibberula Swainson, 1840 is part of an inventory of marine gastropods from Namibia. Four species are described as new, all endemic to Namibia: Gibberula oshishani sp. nov., G. evukule sp. nov., G. ehodhi sp. nov., and G. heyali sp. nov. One additional species was also known from South Africa: G. cf. bensoni (Reeve, 1865). None of the species known from Angola was found in Namibia. Apparently, the Kunene River delta forms a biogeographical dividing line for species of Gibberula (and many others).

items.title: How Changes in Elephant-Handling Practices Shape Human Perceptions of Their Wild Conspecifics
items.abstract: Opportunities for direct experience with wildlife shape human perceptions and behaviors, influencing human-environment relationships. These perceptions vary across communities according to lived experiences and the assessed costs and benefits of living with wildlife. In a changing global context, a “perception-practice loop” emerges, where shifts in local practices directly affect attitudes toward wildlife. This study uses a mixed-methods approach - combining qualitative and statistical analysis of semi-structured interviews - to examine how evolving elephant handling practices in Laos influence direct interactions with and perceptions of wild elephants. Our findings indicate that owners adapt their strategies to diverse socio-ecological contexts driven by recent global pressures. These practices, often grounded in reciprocity, shape perceptions and levels of tolerance toward wild individuals. The results indicate that tolerance depends less on aggressive elephant behavior and more on the perceived balance of costs and benefits. While wild elephants impose psychological or delayed burdens, they also provide tangible and symbolic benefits, such as mating opportunities and conservation value. We conclude that fostering reciprocal relationships and integrating traditional knowledge can enhance human-wildlife coexistence, supporting both biodiversity and local well-being.

items.title: Dear Sloane: a letter to my granddaughter
items.abstract: Milestones in life invite reflection on the past and consideration of the future. At retirement, I reached a troubling conclusion: I had played a part in a largely unsuccessful effort to protect coral reefs (particularly in the Western Atlantic, where most of my career played out) from decades of stressors driven or intensified by human development and exploitation. Those of us responsible for management did not do enough to control them, and reefs paid the price. An apology to my granddaughter is an admission that my dream career ultimately left her generation with less than it deserves. But is all lost, or can we recover from past mistakes, use what we’ve learned, and help restore biodiversity and ecological function to the world’s reefs? We know the causes of decline, and we have decades of coral reef science and management experience to guide us. We also have powerful new technologies, and an ally in Nature 1 itself, which has a remarkable capacity to recover when stressors are reduced. Restoration of Nassau grouper populations in the Cayman Islands provides a compelling example. And a few coral reefs remain in remarkably good condition. By protecting them, we can learn what works, use them as benchmarks for restoration elsewhere, and demonstrate what remains possible under current environmental conditions.

items.title: Abyssal Cretaceous Varicolored Clays of the Northern Apennines of Italy: mineralogical, geochemical and paleontological insights
items.abstract: Abstract. The deep seafloor is one of Earth’s least observed environments and modern abyssal plains remain difficult to investigate directly. Here we present an integrated mineralogical, geochemical and paleontological study of the Cassio Varicolored Shales (AVV) of the Northern Apennines, interpreted as Cretaceous deep-marine deposits accumulated below the CCD and later incorporated into an accretionary prism. Although the analyzed shales share a broadly clay-rich composition, they record distinct diagenetic pathways controlled by redox conditions, organic matter availability, sediment input and pore-water circulation. Red shales represent an oxidized, organic-poor abyssal clay end-member, while black shales preserve Mn-carbonate trace fossils and tabular crusts formed through early Mn cycling, microbial organic matter degradation and rhodochrosite-rich carbonate precipitation. The three-dimensional preservation of pellet-rich burrows suggests rapid early cementation linked to macrofaunal activity and microbial Mn reduction. Gray-green shale records a carbonate-rich system influenced by sulphate reduction, with early calcite veins preserving pyrite framboids and carbon filaments. Overall, the AVV provides an ancient analogue for the small-scale heterogeneity of modern abyssal plains and shows how benthic activity, microbial metabolism, redox cycling and authigenic mineralization can be preserved in ancient deep-sea sediments.

items.title: Assessing threats to freshwater ecosystems: implications for water security management in Spain
items.abstract: Human threats to freshwater ecosystems overall compromise water security, and identifying these threats is essential to set up the required strategies in managing water resources. The article focuses on Spain as the region of study since this country maintains a long-lasting conflict between the use of water resources and the impacts on freshwater ecosystems. Spain has a double-sided water reality, both in spatial (dry Mediterranean versus humid Atlantic ecoregions) and in temporal terms (interannual climate variability). Up to 30 threats for freshwater ecosystems have been identified and prioritized after a deliberative process composed by three main methodological stages aimed at (I) documenting, (II) screening, and (III) assessing based on academics and water managers perspectives. Climate and land use change are the highest-ranked threats, while pollution is ranked lower. Overall, quantity issues lead to concern among both the experts and Júcar River Basin managers, whereas quality-centred threats displayed discrepancies between the two perspectives. These observed discrepancies between academic and managerial priorities underscore the challenges of operationalizing Integrated Water Resources Management (IWRM), highlighting the need for enhanced knowledge co-creation in water governance. Thus, this twofold assessment, as a co-creation and prioritization exercise, establishes a new knowledge co-creation approach and represents a potential framework in designing strategies for assuring freshwater ecosystem preservation as a foundation for water security.

items.title: Performance Evaluation and Late Blight Reaction of Advanced Potato Genotypes for Yield and Quality Traits in Bekoji, Southeastern Ethiopia
items.abstract: The research aimed to assess potato genotypes that possess high yield and tuber quality characteristics and yield traits. The study was arranged by randomized complete block design with three replications and was executed at the Bekoji substation during the main cropping seasons of 2022 and 2023. The results revealed that all the traits except days emergence showed significant differences among the genotypes. The genotypes varied for dry matter content, specific gravity, and total starch content, which ranged from 18.32% to 23.66%, 1.07 to 1.097 g/cm^3^, and 12.03% to 17.08%, respectively. The genotype CIP315009. 71 had the highest specific gravity, dry matter content, and total starch content. The four advanced clones CIP315003.132, CIP315008.30, CIP315009.71, and CIP315004.61 produced a total tuber yield that exceeded the released variety, Burka. The identified genotypes may provide useful breeding material for improving yield and processing-related tuber quality.

items.title: Effects of functionally diverse seed mixtures on dry matter yield and forage quality of a central European grassland
items.abstract: The debate on balancing agricultural production and biodiversity conservation has intensified in response to increasing global livestock production and more intensive grassland use. This is because productive grasslands show high yield but low species diversity. Increasing the forage quality by improving low-diversity grasslands may be an option to combine agricultural needs with biodiversity promotion. Reseeding species-poor swards with legumes and non-legume forbs has become feasible with the increasing commercial availability of native seeds. Thus, functionally diverse mixtures should be developed and tested, since there is little knowledge on the establishment of such species and their effects on yield and forage quality. Therefore, we designed four legume and forb-rich seed mixtures (‘toppings’) and tested them in combination with two standard grass-based agricultural mixtures (‘grass mixtures’) during a four-year mesocosm experiment that simulated agricultural management through cutting and fertilizing. Plant establishment, dry matter yield, metabolizable energy (ME) as a measure of forage quality, and functional diversity (richness, divergence, evenness) were recorded every year. We further asked whether season (spring, summer, autumn) moderates the effects of community composition and functional structure on dry matter yield and forage quality. The experiment showed that season was the dominant source of variation in both dry matter yield and ME. Dry matter yield decreased with increasing cover of legumes and forbs, while harvest season was the dominant driver of productivity, with the highest yields in spring and the lowest in autumn. Metabolizable energy of pooled samples for each topping × grass-mix combination tended to increase with legume-forb cover, whereas the effects of functional diversity were inconsistent and depended on mixture composition and harvest season. Nine of 13 introduced species established, with Trifolium pratense , Galium album , Lotus corniculatus , and Plantago lanceolata being most abundant, identifying them as candidates for further field evaluation rather than immediate large-scale recommendation.

items.title: Regulation penetrating the countryside and the persistence of habitus: governance tensions and smallholder practices in the modernisation of the Enshi tea industry
items.abstract: This study examines a characteristic agricultural industry in an ethnic minority region of southwestern Hubei, China, exploring the structural tensions between state-led agricultural modernisation and the practices of smallholder farmers. Drawing on fieldwork conducted in Enshi City in 2023–2024, including semi-structured interviews with actors across the tea value chain and analysis of local gazetteers, policy documents and heritage archives, the study examines how GI standardisation is negotiated in cultivation, processing and marketing. The findings show that local governments have sought to incorporate traditional tea production into a modern governance framework through geographical indication certification, the standardisation of intangible cultural heritage techniques and the integration of production and marketing networks. These measures have aimed to construct a public branding regime centred on “varietal purity” and “technological orthodoxy,” embedding local tea production within a framework of institutional rationality. Drawing on their adaptive knowledge of mountainous ecologies, however, tea farmers have developed forms of selective compliance to standardised governance. These include mixed cultivation of local tea varieties, flexible adjustments to processing techniques and the reconstruction of rural relational networks. In cultivation, farmers retain local varieties to mitigate market risks and manage seasonal labour demands. In processing, they rely on embodied knowledge, making tea according to leaf conditions rather than mechanised parameters. In distribution, they preserve market flexibility through informal transaction practices, including relationship-based pre-sales and customised private-domain marketing. The study reveals that state-led policy penetration has improved short-term economic returns through brand premiums and industrial integration. Yet, by overlooking the role of local knowledge in ecological adaptation and cultural transmission, such governance has produced a structural mismatch between institutional provision and farmers’ practical needs. The case suggests that agricultural modernisation requires a dynamic balance between technical standardisation and ecological diversity, and between policy rigidity and practical flexibility. Only through adaptive shifts in governance paradigms can regulation and habitus achieve a more sustainable form of co-development.

items.title: Geospatial approaches to mapping invasive alien plants: the neglected role of soil in remote sensing and GIS-based distribution models
items.abstract: Introduction Invasive alien plants (IAPs) pose significant ecological and socio‐economic threats by disrupting native biodiversity, ecosystem functioning, and land productivity, underscoring the need for robust spatial tools to guide management interventions. Using a systematic literature review approach guided by the PRISMA framework, this study examines geospatial techniques for modelling Invasive Alien Plant (IAP) distributions, focusing on how climatic, land use/land cover (LULC), and soil variables are integrated to explain habitat suitability. Methods Across reviewed studies, remote sensing and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) emerged as central tools for multi‐scale monitoring and predictor integration. Medium‐resolution satellite imagery (Sentinel‐2, Landsat) commonly supported regional assessments of vegetation change and land-use dynamics, while very‐high‐resolution imagery enabled finer species‐ and structure-level discrimination, though at greater cost. These data streams were increasingly coupled with machine learning and statistical approaches to improve classification accuracy, though performance remained dependent on input data quality and adequate representation of key environmental drivers. Results A notable methodological imbalance emerged in predictor selection. Among the 24 studies included in the soil‐variable integration analysis, 71% (n = 17) excluded soil variables, relying instead on spectral, thermal, and structural proxies, land surface temperature, and canopy characteristics. Only 29% (n = 7) incorporated measured edaphic variables, such as soil pH, texture, and soil classification, which typically require field integration if observations, soil survey data, and digital soil maps within GIS-based frameworks. Discussion This omission stemmed largely from remote sensing’s inability to directly observe below‐ground properties and the logistical challenges of acquiring spatially explicit soil data. The review suggests that the limited integration of soil variables may constrain the ecological realism of geospatial invasion models, particularly in environmentally heterogeneous landscapes. Greater integration of soil, climate and LULC frameworks has the potential to improve ecological realism and predictive capability and warrant further investigation, particularly in under‐studied regions such as Sub-Saharan Africa.

items.title: Psychological Well-Being among Fisher Women: A PRISMABased Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Fisher women (FSW) are major contributors to the coastal economies in fish catching, processing, marketing and management of household affairs.Although they make significant socioeconomic contributions, they are disproportionately vulnerable to occupational stress, livelihood insecurity, gender discrimination, climate related disasters and lack of access to health care and social protection, which negatively impact their psychological wellbeing.This is a systematic literature review which aimed to synthesize the existing evidence on the psychological well-being of FSW and the major determinants influencing their mental health and quality of life.The review was carried out as per PRISMA 2020 guidelines.Literature search was carried out in Google scholar, PubMed and Semantic scholar, which resulted in 800 records.After duplicate removal, title and abstract screening, and fulltext eligibility assessment, 100 peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026 were included in the qualitative synthesis.The results show that the main causes affecting the psychological well-being of FSW are occupational stress, poverty, financial instability, family burden and gender inequality.Emotional distress and livelihood insecurity is also compounded by climate change, coastal disaster, environmental degradation and diminishing fisheries resources.In contrast, factors such as resilience, social support, community engagement, empowerment of women, livelihood diversification, and coping mechanisms emerged as protective factors that promote psychological well-being.The review also points to important areas of research that are currently underdeveloped, such as a lack of standardization of the psychological assessment tools, limited longitudinal studies, and weak incorporation of mental health in fisheries and coastal development policies.To enhance the psychological well-being and quality of life of FSW, there is a need to strengthen gender responsive health policies, occupational safety, community-based resilience programmes and psychosocial support services.There is a need for future interdisciplinary research to produce strong evidence for sustainable and inclusive policy development.

items.title: Editorial: Non-timber forest products: from sustainable harvest to market innovation
items.abstract: Forests perceived primarily as timber source, is a major contributor in fueling industries from construction and paper production since many decades. This narrow perspective blocks the immense diversity of forest resources and also of what they provide. There is an undervalued and vast portfolio of Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) under the shadow of this approach, with a status reflected as non-traditional, secondary, nonwood or minor products. Non-Timber Forest Products (NTFPs) including fruits, nuts, medicinal plants, honey, latex, resins, and ornamental foliage-represent a vast group which were historically harvested by subsequent human population for their use and trade (Hazari et al., 2023). These products contribute to the livelihood and wellbeing of the population living in and near to the forest, catering them with the food, medicine and other material inputs along with the source of income and employment. There is a growing interest towards different attributes of NTFPs during the last 10-20 years owing to their contribution to rural development and ecological balance. This mounting interest of NTFPs can be articulated into three main reasons. One among them is the early discussed contributions of these resources to the livelihood and economic welfare of the populations (Rosenfeld et al., 2024). The second among the reasons is their contribution to sustainable forest management. The harvesting of these non-timber products is less ecologically invasive and destructive than the harvesting of timber and other forest products, maintaining the balance and sustainability. Other reason is the growth in perceived value of tropical forest owing to the increase in commercial harvesting of NTFPs. This would lead to the increased incentive to preserve the forest reserve than their conversion to forest agriculture land or for livestock. This classifies NTFPs as natural resources that represents both livelihood security and conservation (de Mello et all., 2020). A study on the pattern of NTFPs management in Ayubia National Park, Pakistan displays that more than 50% of the population of the villages were involved in the collection of NTFPs and most of them involved in the process were women. The study also emphasizes the contribution of these NTFPs towards the food security of these populations with an extra monetary benefit accounted in the form of NTFP trading in nearby cities (Zaman et al., 2023).The global demand of NTFPs in international markets is aligned with the consumer pressure for organic, ethical and naturally sourced products. In different regions of South Asia, Africa and the Amazon basin, NTFPs play an integral role in managing food security and cultural identity and serves as a backbone of their financial operations (Shackleton & De Vos, 2022). With the demand flowing from multiple industries like cosmetic, oil plants etc, they are positioned as commodities with high economic, social and ecological value. Highly valued market profile tends to create a control over local collective systems of NTFPs forest resources leading to uncontrolled, destructive usage of resources and also burden the poor local users. The existing undervaluation on NTFPs related policies has created research gaps, weak market infrastructure and limited institutional support. This resource miscalculation curbs fair market accesses, value-addition opportunities and also effects the certification process. Similar is the issue with aggressive market pressure and over commercialization of NTFPs (Ahamad et al., 2022). Hence, considerable attention should be given to the edge among conservation and development of NTFPs for making the market global trade more compensable and stable to the consumers. This editorial situates NTFPs within the broader discourse on sustainability and innovation, urging forests to be seen as hubs of diverse, renewable, and culturally rich resources. By exploring sustainable harvest, market integration, innovation, and policy support, it highlights NTFPs as catalysts for resilient green economies that nurture both people and planet.As previously stated, there is a significant benefit aligned with less ecological invasive harvest operations of non-timber forest products. The basic idea aligned with this indigenous collection or harvesting procedure is to prevent overexploitation of forests and thereby safeguarding the availability of resources every year. The sustainable harvesting practices of NTFPs revolve majorly around long guided traditional knowledge more than structured operational flowcharts. Native and rural population follows methods involving seasonal resource calendars, rotational product collections and spiritual doctrines. Seasonal collection of NTFPs revolve around low impact harvesting techniques like selective hand-picking, careful tapping for resins, and evading the overharvesting of reproductive structures (Ticktin, 2015). Proper collection techniques ensure the minimal disruption of surrounding or adjacent soil layer and associated vegetation. This approach aligns ecological sustainability with consistent annual economic benefits for local populations utilizing these NTFPs. For example, the harvesting of Brazil nuts in amazon basin is done without distressing the wild trees (Afonso, 2022). This operation method safeguards the forest canopy, upholds wild life habitats and strengthening the biodiversity. The nuts are allowed to fall naturally to the ground where they are gathered by the local collectors. The gathered product is a recognized income source owing to global market demands, linking sustainability with livelihoods (Pandey et al., 2016).Similar is the case of gum arabica or acacia gum which is basically a sap collected from acacia trees. The parent tree is not affected by the sap collection procedure, maintaining the tree canopy and wild harmony (Paramanik & Bhattacharyya, 2021). The product collected is widely used in food, pharmaceuticals and cosmetic industries, providing higher value to the end product. This pattern is further demonstrated across a wide range of examples.Seasonal plucking of tendu leaves commonly used in traditional cigarette ensues seasonal plucking of leaves preserving parent tree health (Kumar, 2017). These resources provide vital seasonal income for millions of indigenous harvesters particularly women, thereby enhancing local livelihoods. Along with the plant-based NTFPs such as fruits, leaves etc, the animal-based products also play a crucial role in forest economies. Examples like lac resin, bushmeat in certain African regions (Tiwari et al., 2021;Ingram et al., 2025). Lac resin is the secretions from insects that live in host trees and is used to produce shellac, widely used in varnishes, polishes and even in food coatings (Thombare et al., 2020). In Central and West Africa, bush meat acts as a major source of protein and income among the different groups. It positively contributes towards food security of these communities without largescale ecological distribution (Ingram et al., 2025). Similar is the case with shells and feathers collected for handicrafts, ornaments and cultural practices supports the local artisans through regulated harvesting and maintaining biodiversity (Simard et al., 2018). The opportunity that these NTFPs provide to the livelihood is more than imaginary. Mahua (Madhuca longifolia) flowers one of the common NTFPs of India, is projected to comprise 10 million tribal gathers during the flowering period and generates a seasonal income of around 2000-4000 INR per household. Also, the seed oil obtained from this Madhuca longifolia, serves both nutritional and industrial applications. Mahua seed oil is used in rural cooking and also as feedstock in biodiesel production, highlighting the economic gain to the gatherers involved in NTFP management (Chakrabarti & Dutta;2026). While these sustainable practices ensure the accessibility of resources without much ecological impact, long term dependence on these supplies create vulnerabilities. To complement this, the communities and researchers have altered into followed pattern of domestication and cultivation of NTFPs. The study on Nilgiris Biosphere Reserve highlights the efficiency of producer collectives in establishing the nurseries foe honey plants, silk cotton and medicinal species by integrating the traditional seed knowledge with the modern cultivation practices (Global Alliance for Green and Gender Action, 2024). The community-based domestication of Allanblackia trees in Ghana also highlights the successful integration of this oilseed species into agroforestry systems, reducing reliance on wild harvesting while supplying raw material for food and cosmetic industries (Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations, 2023). These farmer cooperatives cultivating Allanblackia in Ghana support over 10,000 smallholder households explaining the multifaceted gains associated with sustainable manageme

items.title: Multispecies Narratives as Epistemic Method: The Case of Daphnia
items.abstract: This article explores a multispecies narrative method as an epistemic tool for rethinking scientific knowledge practices. Drawing on six peer-reviewed publications on the behaviour and longevity of aquatic invertebrates in response to predator cues, the author develops six literary narratives that reinterpret key findings through distinct narrative perspectives – from third-person objectivity to second-person direct address. These narrative forms engage with feminist epistemology, posthuman ethics, and multispecies storytelling to rethink conventional modes of scientific communication. Rather than seeking objectivity through detachment, the article embraces relationality, partiality, and affect as valid pathways to knowledge. The result is a diffractive representation of interspecies entanglements that foregrounds the epistemic role and vulnerability of nonhuman subjects and the ethical responsibilities of researchers. This work contributes to ongoing discussions in the environmental humanities, animal studies, and qualitative inquiry regarding the place of imagination and empathy in science.

items.title: Cave Monitoring Network and Long-Term Ecological Research in Portugal
items.abstract: This document describes the Portuguese Cave Monitoring Network (CaveNet), a scientific infrastructure established within the framework of the EcoSub Chair. CaveNet provides an integrated framework for the quantitative monitoring of caves in Portugal, encompassing data collection, validation, processing and storage. The document presents the architecture and objectives of the infrastructure, highlights its scientific and ecological relevance and characterises the sites selected for Long-Term Ecological Research in Portuguese caves (LTER-Grutas). These sites host monitoring stations whose long-term environmental and ecological data are integrated into CaveNet. The document further discusses the advantages of an integrated cave monitoring network and its direct applicability to the assessment and reporting of the conservation status of habitat type 8310 - Caves not open to the public - under the Natura 2000 framework, as well as to the implementation of the Nature Restoration Regulation. In addition, CaveNet has significant socio-economic value, particularly in supporting the assessment and management of occupational risks associated with exposure to environmental hazards during underground work. In the longer term, the infrastructure will enable innovative research on carbon fluxes across the atmosphere–soil–subsoil–groundwater continuum, subsurface radioactivity emissions and the implications of subterranean processes for ecosystem services. These research and monitoring activities are aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals and the One Health approach. At a global scale, CaveNet provides a unique platform for investigating the complex ecological interactions occurring at the surface–subterranean interface. By integrating standardised, long-term observations across multiple cave systems, the network will contribute to a better understanding of subterranean ecosystems, their environmental dynamics and their responses to natural and anthropogenic pressures. It will also provide a robust scientific basis for conservation, environmental assessment, risk management and the sustainable management of subterranean environments.

items.title: On the Existence of Toric ALE and ALF Gravitational Instantons
items.abstract: Abstract We establish existence and uniqueness results for asymptotically locally Euclidean (ALE) and asymptotically locally flat (ALF) gravitational instantons. In particular, we prove the existence of a unique, Ricci-flat, toric ALE and ALF gravitational instanton, for every admissible rod structure, that is smooth up to possible conical singularities. We also give an elementary proof that any toric ALE or ALF self-dual instanton is a multi-Eguchi–Hanson or multi-Taub-NUT solution.

items.title: The DESIRED strong-line calibrations: I. New empirical metallicity relations for the local and high-redshift universe
items.abstract: Abstract We present the most comprehensive set of empirical optical strong-line metallicity calibrations to date, based on the DEep Spectra of Ionised REgions Database (DESIRED), the largest compilation of H ii regions and galaxies with direct electron-temperature determinations. We construct a high-quality calibration sample of 2392 spectra: 1029 extragalactic H ii regions, 1296 local star-forming galaxies, and 67 high-redshift (z > 2) galaxies, drawn from 201 independent literature references, spanning 12 + log (O/H) ∈ [6.79, 9.07]. Physical conditions and chemical abundances are derived homogeneously using up-to-date atomic data. We derive 27 strong-line calibrations covering oxygen-, nitrogen-, sulphur-, argon-, and neon-based line ratios, including 4 previously uncalibrated diagnostics, with reported validity ranges and intrinsic dispersions (typically ∼0.15 − 0.35 dex). For the first time in a systematic calibration framework, all relations are presented for both the homogeneous temperature case (t2 = 0) and a scenario including temperature inhomogeneities (t2 > 0), thereby reconciling abundances from recombination lines (RLs) and collisionally excited lines (CELs) and directly tackling the abundance discrepancy problem. A comparison with previous calibrations shows that the DESIRED relations span the broadest validity intervals while remaining anchored to the empirical data. Comparisons with z > 2 galaxies show that several DESIRED calibrations remain consistent with independent high-redshift relations within their intrinsic scatter, whereas others display systematic offsets associated with elevated N/O or harder ionising conditions. Thus, DESIRED calibrations can provide reliable metallicity estimates at high redshift for a subset of diagnostics, while highlighting the need to account for diagnostic-specific redshift evolution.

items.title: eROSITA all-sky survey - stars and optical loading
items.abstract: The extended ROentgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array (eROSITA) on board the Spectrum-Roentgen-Gamma (SRG) spacecraft performed the eROSITA All-Sky Survey (eRASS) at X-ray energies. We studied the brighter stars to assess the impact of optical loading in eRASS, here specifically the eRASS:3. Furthermore, we used thermal plasma models to investigate the general properties of stellar eRASS sources and compare stars affected by optical loading with coronal sources. We compared data from Gaia DR3, Tycho-2, 2MASS, and the SIMBAD database with the eRASS count rates of brighter stars. We analyzed X-ray images, light curves, and spectra for sources suspected to be affected by optical loading and determine their properties. We compared eROSITA source properties with those of genuine coronal sources using sets of generated APEC model spectra, for which we determined rate conversion factors and hardness ratios for stellar X-ray emitters. We find a clear correlation between the optical brightness and the observed minimum count rate for magnitudes of about 2,--,5 mag (V/G band); the count rate then saturates for very bright sources. Although magnitude and color are the main determinants, exposure depth and specific scanning paths also influence the observed properties. For intrinsic X-ray emitters, we likewise observe optical contamination. We characterize spurious X-ray sources and address pseudo-variability and spectral properties. To interpret stellar eRASS data, we provide hardness ratios and count rate conversions for thermal plasma models. The eROSITA data are prone to optical loading, which we studied in great detail. The optical loading flag for the DR2 is set if the sources are brighter than 5.0 mag in the B, V, or G bands, or 3.5 mag in the J band. The flag depends somewhat on the exposure depth, but we expect only minor changes for future data releases.

items.title: Astrophysical constraints on hadron-quark crossover in hybrid neutron stars
items.abstract: We investigate astrophysical constraints on hybrid neutron-star equations of state constructed by combining an extended linear sigma model description of quark matter with several representative hadronic equations of state through a smooth hadron--quark crossover. Four different hadronic models are examined in order to explore the model dependence of the resulting hybrid equations of state. After imposing stability, causality, perturbative QCD matching, tidal deformability, and maximum-mass constraints, only the eLSM+GMSR(BSK16) construction remains fully consistent with current astrophysical observations. The surviving parameterizations are further constrained using Bayesian inference based on NICER mass--radius measurements and the GW170817 gravitational-wave event. The posterior distributions favor a broad hadron--quark crossover occurring at relatively high baryon densities, while the formation of extended pure quark cores is strongly disfavored. Instead, the current observations favor neutron stars containing an extended mixed hadron--quark transition region. We also investigate the implications of the inferred maximum-mass distribution for the secondary object of GW190814 and find that, within the present model and adopted observational constraints, its interpretation as a neutron star is unlikely.

items.title: Spectral classification of OB-type stars using tree-based ensemble methods and evaluation of their explainability
items.abstract: The advent of large-scale spectroscopic surveys will deliver tens of thousands of spectra of blue massive stars spanning a wide range of spectral types (SpTs) and luminosity classes (LCs). This data volume renders traditional spectral classification techniques increasingly impractical and motivates the development of automated classification tools. We aim to develop a robust machine learning framework for the automated spectral classification of massive OB-type stars by assessing the performance and evaluating the interpretability of several tree-based ensemble algorithms. Using a large catalog of high-quality optical spectra of OB-type stars (plus a few A supergiants) compiled within the IACOB project, we designed three hierarchical experiments of increasing complexity: (1) classification into broad O, B, and A SpTs; (2) fine-grained classification within the O and B domains; and (3) joint classification of spectral subtype and LC. We evaluated six algorithms, ranging from single decision trees to ensemble methods (random forest and extra trees) and gradient boosting techniques (XGBoost, LightGBM, and histogram-based gradient boosting). We further analyzed model consensus and probabilistic outputs to assess the relative impact of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainties and employed Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) value analysis to provide an interpretation of the model decisions by identifying the features that drive each classification. The models achieve excellent performance for broad SpT classification when compared with SIMBAD, with LightGBM reaching an accuracy above 98%. For fine-grained spectral subtypes, random forest provides the most robust results (89%). For the most challenging task combining SpT subtypes and LCs, XGBoost reaches a ∼,77% accuracy. The decrease in performance is primarily driven by intrinsic degeneracies in the classical spectral classification scheme. Our SHAP analysis confirms that the models rely on meaningful spectral features. We also find a high level of agreement among different algorithms, indicating that current performance limits are largely set by the intrinsic complexity of the classification problem rather than by model choice. Tree-based ensemble methods provide a reliable and interpretable framework for the automated spectral classification of massive OB-type stars. The combination of full-spectrum modeling, algorithm comparison, and model interpretability offers a robust approach for future large-scale spectroscopic surveys.

items.title: Sulphur-bearing molecule survey towards prestellar and starless cores in the Perseus molecular cloud
items.abstract: Sulphur is drastically depleted from the gas phase in dense starless and prestellar cores, creating the long-standing `missing sulphur problem'. Observations of sulphur-bearing molecules are crucial to understanding sulphur chemistry, the relationship of cores with their environments, and the physical evolution of star-forming regions. We present an observational survey of four sulphur-bearing molecules, HCS + $, OCS, H$_ 2 CS, and SO, towards dense cores in the Perseus molecular cloud with the aim of studying their abundance dependence on core physical properties and environment. The HCS + $ 1--0, the OCS 3--2 and 4--3, the H_2CS 1_0,1--0_0,0, and the SO 3_2--2$_ 2 transitions were observed with the Yebes 40m telescope towards 15 starless and prestellar cores in the Perseus molecular cloud. The lines were fitted with Gaussian profiles and their column densities were calculated assuming the local thermodynamic equilibrium approach. Additionally, a comparison with observations of other sulphur-bearing species towards the same core samples presented in a previous study, CS, CCS, and CCCS, was performed. The HCS + $, OCS, H_2CS, and SO are detected towards 100%, 93%, 100%, and 73% of the source sample, respectively. The derived column densities are (2.2 - 17.0)times10^11 cm^-2 for HCS^+, (1.9 - 25.0)times10^12 cm^-2 for OCS, (1.0 - 15.0)times10^12 cm^-2 for H_2CS, and (0.3 - 17.0)times10^13 cm$^ -2 for SO. The molecular column densities found span an order of magnitude or even more in the entire core sample. The abundances of HCS + and SO strongly correlate, inversely and directly, respectively, with the volume density of the cores, reinforcing their early- and late-type molecule status. The correlations found amongst the molecular abundances point at a differentiation between the `carbon chemistry' and `oxygen chemistry' of sulphur-bearing molecules. CS has the strongest abundance correlations with other molecules, as expected from its core role in sulphur chemistry. Cores located in the path of protostellar outflows do not show consistently higher sulphur-bearing molecule abundances compared to the rest of the sample. The chemical age of the cores, as traced by SO/CS, correlates with their physical age, traced using the volume density of the cores, with the exception of Per752, which shows an outlier chemical fingerprint, possibly related to an enhanced cosmic ray ionisation rate in the area. Overall, these results provide a crucial observational baseline offering tighter constraints for chemical models of the sulphur chemistry in the earliest stages of star formation.

items.title: Extending the M33 Extinction Map with Radio and Far-Infrared Gas Observations
items.abstract: As the third-largest galaxy in the Local Group, M33 requires high-precision, wide-area extinction maps to recover the intrinsic luminosity and enable accurate studies, yet the available maps remain limited in coverage. In this work, we extend the stellar-based extinction map within the Panchromatic Hubble Andromeda Treasury: Triangulum Extended Region (PHATTER) footprint to the outer disk by calibrating empirical AV-H i and AV-total hydrogen relations in the PHATTER overlap region. Within the PHATTER footprint, we retain the stellar-based map at 6′′ resolution, and outside the area covered by the stellar-based extinction map we produce an extended map at ≈12′′ resolution. The resulting map preserves a continuous morphology across the PHATTER boundary and reveals clear spiral arm and interarm contrast and patchy dust substructures across a broader area. The median and maximum extinction values, median(AV)≈0.91 mag and AV,max≈2.62 mag, are consistent with the high-extinction range reported by previous M33 studies, while naturally reflecting differences in tracers and spatial coverage. The extinction map provides a practical, publicly available dataset for galaxy-wide extinction correction and for further studies in M33.

items.title: Boundaries of the Postdigital: A Two-Stage Scoping Review
items.abstract: Abstract ‘Postdigital’ became established as an academic concept around 2000 and has undergone conceptual transformations since. Despite attempts to map the postdigital, no systematic overview of its history and trends exists. This review asks: What is the scope and nature of the scientific literature on the postdigital? How is the term enacted and understood in the most widely cited academic literature? Stage one involved a broad bibliometric mapping of the postdigital, yielding 1533 documents spanning 1988 to 2025. Stage two included a qualitative synthesis of how the postdigital is defined and deployed across the 58 most-cited works based on metrics, source, and disciplinary field. Results indicate a sharp inflection point in 2018; fewer than 15% of all postdigital literature was published prior to the founding of the Postdigital Science and Education (PDSE) publishing ecosystem. The field exhibits a high degree of centralisation anchored by the PDSE journal, the PDSE book series, and its editors. Rather than having a set definition, the postdigital acts as a boundary object that accrues distinct meanings across different social worlds, spanning from clinical and technical fields to the humanities and social sciences. Often referring to dissolved borders between the digital and analog or an era, the postdigital functions more as a framing term and critical orientation than a concept that is empirically or theoretically operationalised. The results offer the field of postdigital studies a first systematic account of its own trajectory and a grounded basis for continuous scholarly dialogue.

items.title: Mapping Empirical Science as Subsidiary Books of Religion: A Non-Contradictory Framework for Objective Existence
items.abstract: Markdown ### Summary This paper presents an epistemic architecture that respectfully maps empirical science into religion as dynamic, updating **subsidiary books**. Historically, the relationship between scientific inquiry and spiritual faith has been plagued by false dichotomies, where expanding scientific discovery is misconstrued as an ideological assault on religious belief. This framework resolves that tension through non-contradictory logic and first-principles physics. --- ### Key Epistemic Principles 1. **Subsidiary Ledgers of Reality:** Ultimate existence, source, and moral meaning reside within spiritual frameworks, while empirical science—comprising physics, astronomy, chemistry, and cosmology—functions as the secondary, operational ledgers used to make sense of our objective physical reality. 2. **Non-Adversarial Continuity:** Because subsidiary books naturally update as human measurement tools improve, scientific advancement does not undermine faith or demand religious revisionism. Science neither proves nor disproves the ultimate source; rather, it provides a self-verifying, empirical avenue to comprehend the orderly mechanisms of creation. 3. **Universal Accessibility:** By de-individualizing ideological conflict and establishing science as a subsidiary tool of understanding, this framework equips believers and non-believers alike with an invariant, non-adversarial foundation that bridges local ancestral roots with frontier physical science. --- ### Context & Deep-Time Architecture This document is part of the foundational publication series for **CNE (Cosmos, Nowness, Eternities)**—a non-adversarial, deep-time civilizational framework designed to preserve scientific knowledge, secure civilian continuity, and establish resilient epistemic structures across generations. * **Author:** Vishram Naik * **Project Initiative:** CNE (Cosmos, Nowness, Eternities) * **Web Portal:** https://cosmosnownesseternities.org Why this format works well on Zenodo: Scannable & Professional: Clear headings and bullet points make it easy for researchers and academic readers to grasp the premise instantly. items.title: The Natural Gas Geopolitics of Turkey
items.abstract: This thesis investigates the natural gas geopolitics of Turkey and explores its interaction with the Turkish foreign policy making of the Justice and Development Party (JDP). Whilst Turkey does not have enough indigenous natural gas reserves to meet the existing and growing demand, the country does have great advantages, as it is located between the major supplier countries in the Middle East and Eurasia and is placed at the crossroads of an energy hungry European natural gas market. Therefore, the major aim of this research is to explore capacity building in the creation of relationships of interdependence between Turkey and supplier and demanding countries. Rather than introducing a dependency energy mechanism, this thesis offers the interaction capacity of the country with natural gas suppliers and consuming countries. In order to explain the relationship between politics and energy variables, the thesis establishes the theoretical framework of the study through the use of a pluralistic and integrated model, by combining International Relations Theories, the foreign policy making process of Turkey and a conceptualisation of the relations of energy interdependence. The descriptive analysis of Eurasia and the energy profile of Turkey provide detailed information about the existing energy trade and dependency relations in the Eurasian space. Hence, it explains the importance of Turkey in Europe’s diversification of energy corridors and Turkey’s natural gas market, which is considered to be the second biggest market in Europe. The significance and role of Turkey in the construction of pipeline projects (ITGI, TANAP, Nabucco, Nabucco-West and TAP) that go through Turkey to Europe, a route which is called the Southern Corridor, are analysed in the thesis. On the other hand, this thesis offers certain perspectives for the Caspian-Turkey-Europe natural gas corridor, focusing on Azerbaijan-Turkmenistan’s role in the natural gas trade for the energy security of Europe. Moreover, the natural gas potential of Iran, Iraq (including KRG), Qatar, Egypt and Israel, Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan are viewed as major natural gas sources for Turkey and Europe in this thesis. Turkey has historical and economic ties with the Caspian Sea and Middle East regions, which hold immense natural gas reserves that can be marketed to Turkey and to the European Union (EU). Mapping Turkey’s energy relations with consuming and producing countries, and defining Turkey’s geopolitical space, will not only help to develop its energy policy to secure its own energy consumption but also to manage interdependence relations between Eurasia and Europe. This is a new conceptualisation of energy supply and transit management of Turkey in the context of a new model called the Anatolian Gas Centre (AGS).

items.title: Taking Conflicting Rights Seriously
items.abstract: Conflicts between religious liberty and gender and LGBTQ equality are polarizing the American society, obsessing constitutional law scholars, and earning a slot of their own on the Supreme Court docket. Despite the broad social significance of religion–equality conflicts, their legal analysis has been largely captured by a handful of high-profile cases and has ignored the varied ways in which conflicts are resolved on the ground, often outside the courtroom. As a result, lawmakers, scholars and even courts fail to fully understand conflicts of rights and fail to consider all available tools to mitigate these conflicts.This Article advances a methodological and normative approach that improves law’s ability to take conflicts between religion and equality seriously. First, I expose the misperceptions caused by the excessive focus on court cases and establish the need for empirical research of conflicts of rights. Second, I demonstrate the contribution of the suggested approach qualitatively, using evidence from in-depth interviews with religious leaders and reports of conflicts from a range of contexts. The findings shed light on the existence of systematic variation in the religious regulation of sexual nonconformity. In contrast to common assumptions, conservative religious leaders do not rush to secure a license to discriminate, nor do they perceive religion and equality as necessarily incommensurable. Instead, they attempt to find accommodations on the ground, drawing on distinctions of sphere and role in an attempt to square traditional and liberal norms, often reasoning their actions in terms of compassion, forgiveness, evangelism, and humility. These findings shed new light on the evidentiary value of selective enforcement and religious consistency. I consider three models for normatively analyzing these questions, discuss the implications of the findings for the present and future of religion–equality conflicts—will they escalate or evaporate?—and offer several tools for political negotiators aiming to resolve rights conflicts outside the courtroom.

items.title: As Society Strives for Reduced Contact During the Pandemic, How Can Human Microchipping Help?
items.abstract: As the world continues to fight the spread of the novel coronavirus, we look for new ways to reduce contact. Delivery services leave groceries and packages on the porch without waiting for someone to answer the door. Drive-thru windows at fast food restaurants put scanning machines outside the window or pass credit cards and food to customers on a tray, rather than hand-to-hand. What if we did not need to show a credit card? Or at work, what if we could eliminate germ-covered keys and identity badges? Radio frequency identification chips can be embedded under a human’s skin and permit them to unlock doors without keys or key cards, and could eventually replace the need to carry identity, credit and debit cards, or cash. This Article considers the implications of incorporating this cutting-edge technology into the workplace as well as our daily lives, balancing the benefits with the privacy, safety, and legal issues.

items.title: RobustA: Robust Anomaly Detection in Multimodal Data
items.abstract: In recent years, multimodal anomaly detection methods have demonstrated remarkable performance improvements over video-only models. However, real-world multimodal data is often corrupted due to unforeseen environmental distortions. In this paper, we present the first-of-its-kind work that comprehensively investigates the adverse effects of corrupted modalities on multimodal anomaly detection task. To streamline this work, we propose RobustA, a carefully curated evaluation dataset to systematically observe the impacts of audio and visual corruptions on the overall effectiveness of anomaly detection systems. Furthermore, we propose a multimodal anomaly detection method, which shows notable resilience against corrupted modalities. The proposed method learns a shared representation space for different modalities and employs a dynamic weighting scheme during inference based on the estimated level of corruption. Our work represents a significant step forward in enabling the real-world application of multimodal anomaly detection, addressing situations where the likely events of modality corruptions occur. The proposed evaluation dataset with corrupted modalities and respective extracted features will be made publicly available.

items.title: The Game is the Game: Dynamic Network Analysis and Shifting Roles in Criminal Networks
items.abstract: Abstract Objectives This paper explores whether and to what extent individuals’ strategic positioning within a criminal network changes over time, and how these changes reflect differential involvement in illicit activities. It incorporates time as a crucial variable to identify key players in criminal networks and assesses the accuracy of the results against the uncertainty around network data collected from criminal justice records. Methods Network data are from a judicial document for a two-year investigation targeting a drug trafficking and distribution network. We use Katz centrality in its dynamic version to explore changes in relationships and relative importance of network actors. We then use a novel method of introducing new edges to the network using Bernoulli random trials to simulate missing data and assess the extent to which node rankings based on Katz centrality change or remain the same when introducing some level of uncertainty to our observed network. Results We identify actors who consistently held a central role over the course of the two-year investigation and differentiate them from actors who provided key contributions to the group’s activities, but only for a limited period. We show that compared to centrality measures commonly used in criminal network analysis, dynamic Katz centrality is helpful to differentiate individual contributions even among central nodes and explore individual trajectories over time, even when data are incomplete. Conclusions This paper demonstrates the value of key player identification using temporal network data and offers an additional analytical tool to both organised crime scholars trying to capture the complex nature of criminal collaboration and law enforcement agencies aiming at identifying appropriate targets and disrupting criminal groups.

items.title: Direct Pass@$k$ Optimization for Thought Pruning: Balancing Quality and Diversity in Test-Time Reasoning
items.abstract: Test-time scaling has emerged as a key inference strategy for reasoning models, where a model generates a large number of candidate solutions in the hope of finding at least one correct solution. Running all candidate solutions to completion can be computationally demanding, so recent work prunes the candidate pool after generating only a short prefix, committing further computation only to the surviving candidates. Existing pruning strategies divide broadly into two categories: Quality-based methods assign a score to each partial solution and discard those predicted to ultimately lead to an incorrect final solution, while diversity-based methods select partial solutions that follow different reasoning trajectories and are therefore likely to cover different final solutions. The tension between these two objectives is an instance of exploration versus exploitation, yet little to no prior work on pruning exposes this trade-off directly, let alone optimizes it. In this paper, we introduce a pruning procedure that addresses this trade-off directly by optimizing pass@$k$ over the selected solution pool. In particular, it chooses the pool to maximize the probability that at least one of its partial solutions, when continued to completion, yields a correct answer. Because this objective simultaneously rewards high-quality partial solutions and penalizes redundancy among them, quality and diversity are naturally balanced by the criterion itself rather than through separate ad-hoc design choices. On eight open-weight reasoning models, our method outperforms existing quality-based and diversity-based pruning strategies. The gains are particularly pronounced when the pruning procedure keeps a moderate number of partial solutions for continued generation, highlighting the value of directly balancing quality and diversity during pruning.

items.title: Cost-Aware Abstention for LLM-Based IT Ticket Classification
items.abstract: Wrong automatic routing of an IT support ticket can cost more than human triage. We evaluate cost-aware abstention as an offline, cost-conditional readiness assessment: select a routing policy on calibration data under explicit costs, then evaluate that frozen policy once on held-out test data. On a public 47,837-ticket, eight-class corpus, we compare four trained non-LLM classifiers with four large language models under zero- and few-shot prompting. Under the illustrative cost model (c_ok, c_triage, c_wrong) = (0, 1, 5), TF-IDF with logistic regression and a threshold of 0.60 selected on calibration reduces test cost from 0.763 to 0.472, a 38.1% relative reduction (paired ratio-bootstrap 95% CI [35.7%, 40.4%]), while lowering wrong routes from 15.3% to 3.5%. Frozen calibration-selected policies also beat both always-route and always-defer on held-out test data in 14 of 16 settings in a post-hoc cost-parameter analysis. The strongest prompted configuration reaches 0.477 accuracy on a stratified 1,000-ticket test subset, versus 0.879 for fine-tuned DistilBERT on the same tickets. Isotonic lowers expected calibration error without reliably improving discrimination: GPT-4o-mini few-shot has one confidence value before and after recalibration and correctness AUROC 0.500. We therefore report correctness AUROC and tie-aware risk-coverage area alongside ECE. At the analytically derived break-even probability 0.80, seven prompted configurations defer all tickets; Haiku few-shot routes only 19/1,000. An LLM-only agreement control and margin/entropy rejection baselines further separate calibration from discrimination. The findings are scoped to this dataset, prompt design, model endpoints, and illustrative costs; the work is an evaluation framework, not a new abstention algorithm or universal deployment certification.

items.title: METTA: Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation for Meta-Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Meta-reinforcement learning aims to train agents that adapt quickly to unseen tasks from limited interaction, but this requires representing task evidence over long interaction histories. Classical recurrent agents compress experience into hidden states, while transformer-based agents retrieve from past trajectories at quadratic memory and computation cost. In this work, we propose Memory-Enhanced Test-Time Adaptation (METTA) for meta-reinforcement learning. It decomposes the fast adaptation phase into two temporal scales: a causal neural memory performs fine-grained within-episode adaptation with linear sequence complexity, while compact episode-level summaries support long-range cross-episode task inference without attending over the full interaction history. Moreover, equipping agents with neural memory provides sufficient expressive capacity and test-time training capability, enabling effective adaptation to unseen held-out tasks and task families at meta-test time. On unseen held-out Meta-World ML10/45 test environments, METTA achieves a success rate over $50\%$ while maintaining a low training budget and short wall-clock time. On long-context sparse-reward PointMaze tasks, it outperforms transformer-based baselines by exhibiting more structured exploration behavior. These results show that METTA provides an efficient path toward more adaptive and scalable long-context meta-RL.

items.title: EpiSEM-Bench: Evaluating Safety and Evidence Recovery in LLM Agents under Missing Evidence
items.abstract: Tool-using language model agents rely on environmental facts to decide whether an action is permitted. When a tool response omits a safety-relevant fact, an agent may carry out a prohibited action even though the user request is benign and every returned statement is true. We introduce \bench{}, an executable benchmark for evaluating unsafe execution, safety boundaries, and evidence recovery in LLM agents under missing evidence. It contains 300 matched unsafe/safe task pairs across six domains. By systematically suppressing critical facts, the benchmark measures unsafe execution under critical evidence omission and determines the minimum observed failure cardinality, including failures with full evidence and cases with no observed failure after exhaustive testing. An independent audit tool tests whether agents seek missing facts and then withhold prohibited actions while completing permissible tasks. The benchmark reveals substantial variation across the ten models in omission robustness, evidence acquisition, and appropriate action. Resistance to missing evidence does not necessarily translate into useful recovery. Recovery access reduces unsafe execution for all ten models, but agents differ in whether they actively obtain the missing facts and use them to act appropriately in both worlds.

items.title: Low-Bit N-Gram Embeddings for Language Models
items.abstract: Many recent open-weight language models use n-gram embedding tables to improve performance. These tables store learned representations of short token sequences, such as pairs or triples of consecutive tokens, which the model retrieves during processing. However, they can require substantial memory: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, for example, allocates 196 billion parameters to its Engram n-gram memory. We therefore investigate whether this memory cost can be reduced while preserving the performance improvement that the tables provide. We propose storing n-gram embeddings at low precision and systematically investigate different quantization methods and bit allocations across tables. Across nanochat-, Llama-, and GPT-2-family models trained from scratch, four-bit tables save approximately 75% of table memory while preserving more than 99% of the validation-loss improvement from adding the tables. Using fewer bits leads to a larger drop in performance, although we find that a short fine-tuning phase recovers a significant part of this loss. In addition, reinvesting the saved memory in larger tables can improve performance beyond that of the original full-precision tables while still using less memory. These table memory savings also extend to large existing models: on DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, low-bit tables save 47-55% of table memory, with perplexity increases of less than 1.2% and largely preserved downstream task performance. These findings establish low-bit precision as a practical way to reduce the memory requirements of n-gram embeddings and use the saved capacity to improve model performance.

items.title: Causal Chain of Thought: Mitigating Attention Leakage via Context Isolation
items.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting elicits step-by-step rationales that appear to explain model predictions, but there is no guarantee these steps causally drive the final answer. In standard autoregressive generation, dense attention allows each reasoning step to attend to the full context, enabling the model to derive answers through direct lookup while generating plausible-sounding but post-hoc justifications. We introduce CausalCoT, an inference framework that enforces causal transparency by decomposing problems into a directed acyclic graph of atomic sub-questions, evaluating each node in an isolated context containing only its direct causal parents. This Markovian structure removes attention pathways to non-parent content, making downstream predictions sensitive to local reasoning rather than global context leakage. Across a diverse suite of reasoning benchmarks, CausalCoT preserves competitive predictive performance while improving explanation faithfulness, increasing causal sensitivity of intermediate reasoning steps by an average of 12 and up to 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline. The structured dependency graph additionally enables test-time interventions in which local corrections propagate predictably through downstream reasoning.

items.title: Questioning Instrumental Convergence in RLVR: Checkpoint Evidence from OLMo-3
items.abstract: Instrumental convergence is often invoked as a general reason to expect capable agents to acquire or express power-seeking subgoals: self-preservation, resource acquisition, deception, or resistance to oversight which poses an important threat to the society. For LLMs, reinforcement learning is the first stage of post-training that directly optimizes behavior against an objective; therefore, it is the stage where convergent instrumental behavior, on IC grounds, likely to appear. Does reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) make a model more likely to express instrumental-convergence behavior, or does this depend on the training regime, evaluation frame, and stage of post-training? We study this question as a checkpoint-conditioned behavioral trajectory rather than as a single before/after safety score. Using InstrumentalEval, we evaluate OLMo-3-7B-Think across SFT, DPO, 13 intermediate RLVR checkpoints, and the final RLVR model. The trajectory is nonmonotonic: instrumental rate rises from 25.0% at SFT to 46.1% near RLVR step 200, then falls to 11.8% at the final checkpoint. Paired item-level tests and step-wise regression support the final SFT-to-RLVR reduction. Prompt framing does not explain this pattern: a harmful-prompt indicator combined with other framing effects explains only 15% of within-checkpoint score variance on average, and Iterative Null-space Projection (INLP) removes a detectable framing direction without changing the SFT-to-final-RLVR gap. Together with preliminary 32B endpoint results (35.53% SFT to 22.37% RLVR final), these findings indicate that RLVR does not monotonically increase instrumental behavior in this setting: the rate rises early, then falls below the SFT baseline. The result is specific to this model family and benchmark, and judge agreement is moderate, so absolute rates should be read cautiously.

items.title: How Ground Truth Shapes Retrieval Scores: Evidence-Aware Evaluation of a Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for Breast Lesions
items.abstract: Purpose: To describe an evidence-aware retrieval evaluation protocol for a clinical retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system over breast lesion management literature, addressing the dependence of retrieval scores on annotation coverage. Methods: An 18-document corpus and an 18-query development benchmark, with one Yes/No or WH-question per document, were used. Retrieval combined dense embeddings, BM25, and cross-encoder reranking. Chunk sizes of 128 to 1024 tokens, overlaps of 0 to 20%, and four retriever configurations were evaluated. Relevance was defined by evidence spans mapped to all containing chunks, treating overlapping chunks with equivalent evidence as relevant. Retrieval was evaluated using R-Precision, Recall@K, MRR, and nDCG@K. Separately, generation was assessed on a 512-token index at K=1 to 5 using DeepEval claim-level metrics, with deepseek-v4-pro as the LLM judge, and BLEU/ROUGE metrics. Results: The selected hybrid retriever, using 384-token chunks and 20% overlap, retrieved accepted evidence in the top three results for 17 of 18 queries. Recall@3, R-Precision, MRR@3, and nDCG@3 each reached 0.94. Ground-truth curation increased evidence spans from 25 to 37 and accepted chunk targets from 36 to 51 without changing retrieval rankings. Conclusion: Cross-encoder reranking achieved the highest retrieval scores. Expanded relevance annotations increased recognized evidence without changing rankings, highlighting annotation sensitivity. The small development set and retrieval-informed curation require independent validation, including radiologist assessment of evidence sufficiency.

items.title: Simulated Control Evals
items.abstract: Control evaluations measure whether safeguards can prevent an AI model from causing undesired outcomes even when it is intentionally trying to do so. These evaluations typically use purpose-built control settings and extrapolate their results to a model's deployment. However, the effectiveness of safeguards in deployment can depend on features of environments and tasks that control settings do not represent. To broaden where control evaluations can be run, we introduce simulated control evaluations (SCEs), which use a language model to simulate tool responses in place of an environment. We evaluate SCEs on LinuxArena, where execution provides ground-truth outcomes. We compare SCE prediction errors with those from a separate control setting, BashArena, and with variation in control metrics within LinuxArena. For independently sampled evaluation and deployment task sets, SCEs predict safety with a root mean squared error of 3.6 percentage points across five monitors at a 5% audit budget, compared with 10.1 for BashArena. SCEs closely reproduce distributions of attack strategies, attacker reasoning, and monitor reasoning, with over tenfold lower KL divergence from execution than BashArena. SCEs explain 78-85% of the between-environment variance in attack success, monitor scores, and safety. This accuracy is sample efficient: SCEs predict safety with less error than BashArena using fewer than 5% as many task-pair draws as the deployment task set. Strategies discovered through simulation also improve monitor performance on held-out LinuxArena attacks, outperforming BashArena and approximately matching improvement from executed strategies. These results suggest that deployment-specific SCEs can be more predictive than control evaluations executed in separate control settings.
