items.title: Radio and high-energy variable emission from a multi-wavelength follow-up of the infant planet-hosting star V1298 Tau
items.abstract: V1298 Tau is a very young and magnetically active K1V star which hosts a benchmark multi-planetary system to study planet formation and evolutionary history at the earliest stages. Between 2025 and 2026, we conducted a campaign to monitor the variability of V1298 Tau in radio (band C), X-ray, and NUV bands, with the support of publicly available contemporary optical light curve, and to investigate multi-band correlations to link the emission with stellar activity. Radio observations were carried out with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (JVLA) in band C (4.5--6.5 GHz). X-ray and NUV observations were carried out with the Swift satellite over 20 days, ending one month before the begin of the radio campaign. We analysed the temporal variability of peak (integrated) fluxes in the C-band and of X-ray (NUV) luminosities on various timescales, comparing it with the variability observed in the high-cadence optical light curve collected by the ASAS-SN survey. We observed both radio and high-energy time variable emission. JVLA detected emission in 90\% of the visits, switching between high ($\geq$0.1 mJy/beam) and low flux states in matter of days or hours. The fluxes show moderate correlation with the optical light curve, suggesting modulation with the stellar rotation period. Except for one visit, dynamic spectral analysis does not reveal short-term (minutes) variability, nor is there any evidence of circularly polarised emissions. Overall, the radio observations can be explained as gyrosynchrotron and/or cyclotron emission from the corona, and linked to stellar magnetic activity. At high-energy, we detected significant variability in X-ray luminosity (within the range ~1.2--2.5x10$^{+30}$ erg/s), the decay phase of a stellar flare, and evidence of correlation with the optical flux. Our data confirm that V1298\,Tau follows the near-linear Güdel-Benz relation.

items.title: Urban climate regressions require representative monitoring networks
items.abstract: Land use regression models relate intra-urban air temperature to spatial predictors such as building volume, tree canopy cover and topography, and are increasingly used to produce fine-scale temperature maps. However, the accuracy of these estimates can be compromised by unrepresentative monitoring networks. Here we show that reference weather station networks, designed for regional rather than intra-urban monitoring, sample only a narrow portion of a city's spatial heterogeneity, missing both the densely built core and the cool, vegetated periphery that set the two ends of the urban temperature range. As a result, city-wide predictions underestimate temperature differences, in ways that cross-validation against the station measurements does not detect. Using Zurich, Switzerland, as a case study, we compare multiple linear regression, generalized additive models and random forests as up to 117 low-cost temperature sensors are added to the four reference weather stations. When trained on reference stations alone, all three models achieve comparable cross-validated performance. As low-cost sensors broaden the sampled spatial heterogeneity, multiple linear regression scores lower on both metrics, whereas the non-linear models remain at their reference-only level. Although a third of the low-cost sensors already recovers nearly the full predicted temperature range, which predictors are identified, and with which sign, is determined by the station sample rather than the model class. At full coverage, only multiple linear regression leaves significant residual spatial autocorrelation, suggesting a linear form unable to capture non-linear responses of air temperature to urban form. Drawing on landscape ecology research on focal site study design, we provide a transferable framework for diagnosing station network representativeness and improving the reliability of city-wide environmental maps.

items.title: Surface regolith model of near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon
items.abstract: The near-Earth asteroid (3200) Phaethon displays activity as it comes close to the Sun and is presumed to be the progenitor of the Geminids meteor shower. Both CM- and CY-meteorites have been suggested as possible meteorite analogues for Phaethon. Previous spectral and polarization measurements of Phaethon indicate possible surface heterogeneity in the regolith properties. By combining mineral components and their size fractions, we present a regolith model for Phaethon that reproduces the spectral, polarization, and geometric albedo measurements presented in various studies, with the aim of quantitatively characterizing the surface material and structure, as well as the regolith heterogeneity. The best fit model able to produce the measurements is constructed from large olivine particles with troilite inclusions and small scale surface roughness, mixed with smaller, porous troilite aggregates comprised of monomers resembling interplanetary dust. Our model suggests that the different spectral and polarization responses of the regolith are caused by changes in the size and amount of the small dark troilite particles. Based on the amount of troilite in the regolith model, we propose that CM-meteorites are the preferable meteorite analogue for Phaethon.

items.title: An Eco-Friendly Tourism Trip Planner Driven by Z-Number Uncertainty: Evidence from Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul
items.abstract: Deployed tourism trip planners ingest travel times and ratings as exact numbers, although routing services return travel times that vary with the hour of departure and a platform rating may rest on a handful of reviews or on tens of thousands. We present an eco-friendly trip planner that represents both quantities as Z-numbers, which pair a fuzzy restriction on a value with a fuzzy reliability on the evidence behind it, and that constructs them directly from routing-service observations at six departure hours and from platform review counts rather than from linguistic elicitation. A hybrid loss combines score, carbon, travel-time, and reliability terms, and an adaptive large neighborhood search returns single-day itineraries with per-leg reliability annotations through a conversational front end. We compare the planner with a crisp-mean baseline under an identical optimizer in Baku, Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Tashkent, and Istanbul, with fifteen points of interest and thirty seeds per city, and we evaluate the selected itineraries on their trip carbon and their total travel time. Pooled over 150 seed-paired runs, the planner lowers trip carbon from 3.24 to 2.61 kg (19.3%, Wilcoxon p = 0.017; city-clustered bootstrap interval 6.4% to 26.7%) and travel time from 123 to 109 minutes per trip (11.5%, p = 2.8e-10; interval 5.0% to 18.2%). The travel-time reductions survive a Holm correction in Baku, Istanbul, and Abu Dhabi, the carbon reduction is significant in Baku and large but uncertain in the dispersed catalogs of Dubai and Abu Dhabi, and neither metric changes in Tashkent. Review counts were measured for Baku and estimated for the other four cities, and the comparison involves a single baseline, so the results establish feasibility and direction rather than a general advantage. Code, routing caches, frozen routing tables, and per-seed results are openly released.

items.title: Hollow homes: Roost selection and role of roost morphometrics in the cavity-roosting Bamboo Bat (Genus Tylonycteris) from the Western Ghats, southern India
items.abstract: Bat species occupy diverse day-roosting habitats, ranging from rock-based to plant-based substrates. Depending on the properties of roosting substrates and the ability of bats to adapt to them, roosts can be stable or ephemeral over time. Bamboo bats (genus Tylonycteris) occupy bamboo cavities and possess adaptations such as a flattened skull, thickened thumb pads and modified soles of the feet, making them specialised for roosting within often ephemeral bamboo internodes. The Western Ghats host a bamboo bat species that has traditionally been considered a subspecies of Southeast Asia's Tylonycteris pachypus. However, its precise taxonomic status is unresolved, and recent analyses suggest this population could be a potential new species. Nevertheless, their roosting ecology and the role of bamboo properties in occupancy remain unexplored. By comparing properties of used and unused cavities by the bamboo bats in the Western Ghats, we investigated how physical roost characteristics are associated with cavity occupancy and how the roost properties and space available differed between solitary and non-solitary roosts. We found that only the area of the cavity mouth was associated with occupancy, and all tested properties, including roost volume, were similar for solitary and non-solitary roosts. Our findings are similar to patterns reported from other Tylonycteris species, but these findings contribute to the comparative understanding of bamboo bat roost selection across the tropics. It also opens up future avenues to investigate the understudied ecological continuum in the Indian tropics that involves bats, bamboo, pest insects, cavity-dwelling taxa and bamboo harvesters in further detail.

items.title: The ontogeny of repeatability: measurement choices shape individuality estimates in a clonal fish
items.abstract: Consistent among-individual differences in behavior across time and contexts ("individuality", "animal personality") are increasingly recognized as playing an important role in both the ecology and evolution of species. Such individuality is not static: individual differences emerge, shift, and crystallize across ontogeny, shaped by developmental plasticity, stochastic processes, and gene-environment interactions. Despite growing awareness of this developmental dimension, the field has relied predominantly on snapshot designs with few repeated measures, raising the question of how much reported repeatability estimates reflect biology versus methodological choices. Here, we leverage high-resolution tracking data from 45 clonal Amazon mollies (Poecilia formosa) recorded at 5 frames per second across the first 28 days of life to systematically examine how temporal aggregation, sampling rate, frame rate, and the number and placement of measurement days affect repeatability estimates and their underlying variance components. We find that repeatability increases with higher temporal aggregation, decreases with lower sampling rates, and varies substantially depending on the developmental stage sampled. These results demonstrate that commonly used measurement practices can substantially distort repeatability estimates, and that conclusions about behavioral consistency may be as much a product of study design as of biology. We close with practical recommendations for researchers studying individuality across development.

items.title: A million orthopteran singers from a year of continuously operating field recorders detected, tracked and organized by song
items.abstract: Continuous acoustic monitoring has become an invaluable tool in ecology and conservation biology, with hundreds of thousands of automated recording units deployed worldwide. While semi-manual annotation is adequate for some uses, fully automated methods to segregate and identify the source of animal sounds are essential to utilize these data to their full extent. Significant progress has been made for birds, whose calls are generally discrete and structured, and where large annotated reference libraries are available. However these methods do not extend neatly to insects, whose choruses dominate nighttime, and often daytime, soundscapes across most of the world. While many approaches have been proposed to fill this gap, an efficient end-to-end system for annotating insect calls that can operate at the scale of available data has not emerged. Here we describe an unsupervised method that uses the intrinsic, highly repetitive structure of the songs of many insects, especially orthopterans, to identify and separate distinct songs in narrow (minute) time windows, connect them across windows for as long as entire nights as their carrier frequencies and syllable repeat rates vary with time, temperature and other factors, and assemble them across days and locations into a catalog of singers and song types across time, space and conditions. We apply this method to thirteen months (November 2024 to November 2025) of recordings from 27 autonomous recording units in different microhabitats at a field site in southwestern Arkansas, 175,896 recorder-hours in all. We detected 10.9 million singers in five-minute windows and linked them, within each night or day, into 911,005 tracks, of which 103,802 lasted two hours or more (71,770 at night, 32,032 by day), a total of 335,882 hours of song. In the plane of carrier frequency against syllable repeat rate these singers fall on discrete lines along which each slides with temperature, and we use this organization to define 45 song types, 37 trilling and 8 chirping, each composed of dozens to thousands of singer-nights. Within singers, syllable rate rises by about 3 percent per degree and carrier frequency by about 1.5 percent in nearly every type, recapitulating and extending classical observations on the temperature dependence of orthopteran song. Published and reference recordings placed on the same plane fall on these lines, and species of Anaxipha recorded by Walker and Funk land on single types at the right temperatures. More generally, this method and the data it produces provide a robust means of studying changes in insect song over time and space, and of understanding the behavioral and physical forces that shape its production.

items.title: Habitat use patterns and diet of Lontra longicaudis (Olfers 1818) in urban streams of southern Brazil
items.abstract: Abstract The Neotropical otter ( Lontra longicaudis ) is a semiaquatic mammal widely distributed throughout Latin America and is considered an important indicator of aquatic ecosystem integrity. This study evaluated the habitat use and feeding ecology of the species in three coastal streams in the municipality of Rio Grande, Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, representing different levels of urbanization and landscape modification. Sampling was conducted monthly from August 2024 to July 2025 in three streams along an urbanization gradient. Indirect signs of the species were recorded, the microhabitats used were characterized, and land use and land cover surrounding the watercourses were analyzed using imagery obtained from an unmanned aerial vehicle and processed through supervised classification. Diet was determined through fecal analysis. Habitat-use intensity was estimated based on sign encounter rates, while spatial and seasonal differences were assessed using non-parametric tests and multivariate analysis (PERMANOVA). A total of 175 signs were recorded, most of them in the intermediate-urbanization stream (133), followed by the most urbanized (29), and the least urbanized (13). Encounter rates differed significantly among streams and were highest in the intermediate-urbanization stream, with no significant seasonal variation. Sandbanks accounted for 95.1% of all records, highlighting their importance both as marking sites and for sign detectability. Diet was predominantly composed of fish, followed by crustaceans and birds, with no significant differences in diet composition among streams or seasons. The results indicate that habitat-use intensity was more closely associated with the availability of favorable microhabitats, landscape connectivity, and anthropogenic disturbance than with riparian vegetation extent alone. We conclude that the conservation of Neotropical otter in anthropized coastal landscapes depends on maintaining functional connectivity among aquatic environments and mitigating the impacts of urbanization.

items.title: From Microsatellites to SNPs: Improving hybridization rate estimation in non-invasive monitoring
items.abstract: Abstract The transition from traditional microsatellites to single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) markers is a major objective in modern DNA-based wildlife monitoring. However, empirical comparisons evaluating their relative performance on degraded, non-invasively collected DNA remain scarce. Using the European wildcat ( Felis silvestris ) as a biological model for hybridization with the domestic cat ( Felis catus ), we directly compared results obtained with a traditional 16-microsatellite panel to those obtained with a customized 96-SNP array on the exact same set of 133 wild individuals sampled via non-invasive hair traps. Our results reveal profound methodological divergences in resolution and assignment of hybrid category. While microsatellites indicated an homogeneous wild population, suggesting limited sensitivity for detecting advanced backcrosses, SNPs revealed greater genetic heterogeneity, assigning several individuals to first-generation hybrid or backcross classes. These misclassifications could explain why the overall hybridization rate appeared nearly three times higher with SNPs, a metric also affected by strict assignment thresholds. Furthermore, when considering individuals assigned as pure wildcats, microsatellite data indicated a higher inbreeding coefficient (Fis = 0.28) than SNPs data. These findings offer important insights for molecular ecology. While microsatellites remain cost-effective for assessing broad-scale population genetic structure, this study demonstrates how marker choice can influence hybridization diagnostics and estimates of genetic diversity, underscoring the need for careful calibration when assessing introgression in non-invasive samples.

items.title: Rethinking Ecosystems, Climate Change and Insecurity Through Indigenous Knowledge Systems
items.abstract: Abstract Climate change has aggravated environmental degradation, resource competition and human insecurity across Nigeria, threatening livelihoods and weakening ecosystem resilience. Although contemporary responses have largely relied on scientific and technological interventions, comparatively little attention has been given to Indigenous Knowledge Systems (IKS), which historically informed environmental conservation and community adaptation. This paper rethinks the relationship between ecosystem governance, climate change and insecurity by examining the significance of indigenous ecological knowledge to contemporary environmental and security challenges. It argues that indigenous practices such as sacred forest conservation, traditional weather forecasting, customary land-use regulation and community-based natural resource management provided sustainable mechanisms for ecological preservation, climate adaptation and conflict mitigation. The study adopts a qualitative historical methodology, drawing on historical literature, ethnographic studies, policy documents and documented case studies from Nigeria. Guided by Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Political Ecology perspectives, it analyses how indigenous environmental practices have shaped ecosystem governance and community resilience across time. The findings reveal that despite the erosion of many indigenous institutions through colonialism, urbanisation and changing socio-economic conditions, indigenous ecological knowledge remains a valuable resource for strengthening climate adaptation, environmental sustainability and local security. The study further contends that the marginalisation of indigenous knowledge in environmental governance has limited community participation and reduced the effectiveness of climate response initiatives. The paper concludes that sustainable responses to climate-induced insecurity require the integration of Indigenous Knowledge Systems with contemporary environmental policies and scientific innovations. It recommends the documentation and preservation of indigenous ecological practices, their incorporation into climate adaptation and environmental governance frameworks, and stronger collaboration among local communities, researchers and policymakers. Such an integrated approach offers a more possible pathway to ecosystem sustainability, climate resilience and community security in Nigeria.

items.title: Conceptualizing Cognitive Growth and Release: Integrating Adult Development into Contemplative Science
items.abstract: Adult developmental theory has the potential to contribute across many fields. This paper, authored by two developmentalists and a neuroscientist studying meditators, argues that developmental models are increasingly needed as contemplative science enters a “third wave” concerned with advanced meditation including highly skilled practitioners, deep meditative states, and enduring transformations. This leading edge also overlaps with wisdom studies, spiritual and transpersonal inquiry, and trauma theory, exposing important conceptual tensions. We argue that these arise from a common assumption that cognitive complexity and spiritual clarity or psychological wholeness necessarily develop together along a single vertical axis of developmental “altitude.” To clarify and resolve these tensions, we propose a framework distinguishing two quasi-independent developmental movements: ascending structural growth, the cumulative and hierarchical construction of cognitive capacities, and descending structural release, the loosening, deconstruction, or seeing-through of cognitive structures. Release exposes constrained or inaccessible cognitive resources, enabling deconditioning, reintegration, healing, and/or insight. We apply this framework to problems including the fallibility of spiritual adepts; relationships among states, stages, and stable “vantage points”; requisite complexity and adverse effects of intensive contemplative practice; disputes over maps of contemplative attainment; and the legitimization of traditional and Indigenous knowledge. The framework offers a heuristic bridge among contemplative science, developmental psychology, and adjacent fields, while generating theoretically and empirically testable hypotheses about increasingly deep possibilities for human development.

items.title: From student voice to visible influence: A mixed-methods needs analysis of medical student partnership engagement across Türkiye
items.abstract: Abstract Background Student engagement through partnership positions students as collaborators in educational design, research, governance, quality assurance, and community engagement. Although increasingly promoted in health professions education, less is known about how students experience partnership across national contexts or why some participation mechanisms produce influence while others remain symbolic. This study examined how medical students in Türkiye perceived and experienced engagement through partnership. Methods We conducted a nationwide, multiphase mixed-methods needs analysis. An online survey included five-point items, a five-level engagement continuum, and open-ended questions on facilitating and hindering factors. Medical education departments or units across Türkiye’s seven geographical regions were asked to distribute the survey. Survey findings informed two student-only online focus groups. Quantitative data were analysed descriptively in R. Open-ended responses and focus-group transcripts were analysed using an iterative, team-based codebook thematic approach and integrated during theme development and interpretation. Results A total of 144 students completed the survey; 130 (90.3%) attended public universities, and 80 (55.6%) reported no role in student representation or organisations. Partnership was rated at least moderately important by 82.6%, and 90.9% perceived at least a moderate contribution to educational quality; 59.0% rated institutional support at the scale midpoint or above. Across four domains, 89.5%–92.3% rated partnership at least moderately important, whereas 59.7%–70.1% reported engagement at involvement or higher. The integrated qualitative dataset comprised 639 meaning units and generated five higher-order themes: from student voice to visible influence; from goodwill to institutionalised partnership; building safe, respectful, and fair relationships; protected capacity for sustainable partnership; and enacting partnership through shared practice. Representation, feedback, and formal structures could facilitate or hinder partnership depending on their enactment. Conclusions Students valued partnership but perceived an implementation gap between its educational importance and institutional practice. Meaningful partnership requires student voice to have visible influence through institutionalised processes, psychologically safe and equitable relationships, adequate capacity, and shared practice. Medical schools should prioritise feedback accountability, inclusive representation, role clarity, partnership literacy, psychological safety, and protected capacity rather than simply increasing opportunities to speak.

items.title: Strong mnemonic prediction errors increase cognitive control, attention, and arousal
items.abstract: Ongoing experience is continuously processed in the context of past events. Divergence between current experience and memory-based predictions (i.e., a mnemonic prediction error; MPE) is theorized to be a signal for the hippocampus that encoding, as opposed to retrieval, should be prioritized. We asked how MPEs place demands on cognitive and neural resources beyond the hippocampus, and whether these demands differ as a function of prediction strength. We investigated these questions across two experiments, wherein we recorded scalp electroencephalography and/or pupillometry as 101 young human adults performed an associative memory task. Strong MPEs, more so than weak MPEs, increased physiological indices of cognitive control (frontal theta), attention (posterior alpha and pupil size), and arousal (pupil size). Trial-level pupil-linked MPE responses scaled with the amount of attention (posterior alpha) allocated during prediction generation. Finally, greater cognitive control (frontal theta) during strong MPEs promoted better learning of prediction violating (i.e., unexpected) stimuli. Collectively, these findings reveal how the mind and brain respond adaptively to violations of strong mnemonic predictions.

items.title: Language usage shapes neural mechanisms of code-switching
items.abstract: Linguistic environments play an important role in shaping the mechanisms of language processing. The current study examined how neural responses to bilingual code-switching vary as a function of ongoing language usage, and which control processes may underlie these differences. Forty highly proficient English-French bilinguals listened to continuous spoken narratives containing inter-sentential switches. Participants were matched for proficiency and language background but differed in their current L2 usage (Active vs. Inactive). Narratives alternated either between their first and second languages, or between language and an acoustically matched non-linguistic signal, providing a means to probe language disengagement and re-engagement. While comprehension and cortical speech tracking were comparable across groups, oscillatory analyses revealed a usage-dependent modulation of alpha-band activity. Active bilinguals showed comparable alpha responses to switch and non-switch sentences, whereas Inactive bilinguals showed reduced alpha power following language switches, emerging from 650 ms over parieto-occipital regions. The direction, timing, and location of this effect are consistent with later attention control processes rather than early perceptual responses to the switch. Further analyses suggested that group differences were more closely associated with language disengagement than re-engagement. Together, these findings demonstrate an association between current L2 usage and alpha-band responses during language switching, suggesting that ongoing language experience may be modulating the neural mechanisms of language control.

items.title: Social chatbots and character: Mind-modelling, mimetics, and postdigital misperception
items.abstract: This article examines how users cognitively process social chatbot output as a novel form of participatory, generative “character,” co-produced through human–AI interaction. Reporting on the results of empirical research on user responses to the social chatbot platform character.ai, it shows how cognitive stylistic and narratological approaches to character can be utilised but also must be developed to analyse and theorise users’ experience of and interaction with generative AI agents. It makes specific contributions to cognitive stylistics, rhetorical narratology, character studies, and research on gen AI chatbots by: (1) illustrating how the concept of mind-modelling can used to analyse the ways in which users linguistically anthropomorphise social chatbots; (2) developing two new audience response types – transmimetic and hypermimetic – to respectively capture ways in which users assess chatbots against prior knowledge of characters across media and cases where chatbots appear so convincingly human that users question their ontological status; (3) proposing the concept of ‘postdigital misperception’ to reflect the way that users of AI can misattribute the ontological origin of an LLM’s output. The article demonstrates how social chatbots are reshaping how users understand character, agency, and reality in interactive, participatory and generative digital contexts and argues that social chatbots epitomise postdigital experience in blurring the distinction between the digital and non-digital as well as fictional and real.
